en: The Yatidharmasamuccaya composed by Yādavaprakāśa: the first section.

We take refuge in Him, who is to be ascended by the ladder of the series of Vedic scriptures, and whose name "Hari" is heard at the time of yoga as the symbol of the rule for the wandering mendicant (pārivrājya). 1.1.
Victorious is the illustrious Lord of the worlds, whose banner bears Garuḍa; by him, in a former life as one bearing the marks of an ascetic, the three Vedas were protected from the heretics. 1.2.
Having collected all the Śruti and Smṛti texts concerning renunciation,
this *Yatidharmasamuccaya* is composed by Yādava.
The ritual procedure, the state of the agent, the gender, the application, and the primary action;
the conduct of daily activities throughout day and night, the duties pertaining to the marks, and the modes of movement and staying. 1.4.
Expiations, sacraments—these eleven sections constitute the duties of the ascetic, extracted here in their proper order from the treatises on Dharma. 1.5.
The exponents of the Dharmaśāstras are Manu, Viṣṇu, Yama, Aṅgiras, Vasiṣṭha, Dakṣa, Saṃvarta, Śātātapa, and Parāśara. (1.6)
Kātyāyana, Uśanas, Vyāsa, Āpastamba, Bṛhaspati, Hārīta, Śaṅkha and Likhita, Yājñavalkya, Atri, and Gautama. (1.7)
Bodhāyana, Vṛddhadakṣa, Kāśyapa, Kapila, Kratu, Śāṇḍilya, Vṛddhajābāla, Dattātreya, and Devala. || 1.8 ||
Gārgya, Vṛddhavasiṣṭha, Viśvāmitra, Gālava,
Medhātithi, Bharadvāja, Jamadagni, Śaunaka, Paiṭhīnasi, Satyakāma, Vāyu, and others such as these. || 1.9 ||
This dharma has been compiled specifically in those sections concerning renunciation within these scriptures; it is not found in other places, nor in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas.

In this regard, it is now examined whether the rule for renunciation exists or not. On this point, some say: "Since it is not seen in the Śruti and since Smṛtis lack authority when they contradict the Śruti, it does not exist at all. Thus says Gautama:
"The teachers maintain that there is only one stage of life (the householder's), because the householder's state is directly prescribed by the Veda" (GDh 3.36).
Bodhāyana said:

Regarding this very [life], some say there is a fourfold division. Others say there are four [stages] for the sake of the unseen (the spiritual goal); this is the doctrine of ritual action concerning the *iṣṭi*, *saumika*, *pāśuka*, *dārvīka*, and *haumika* sacrifices. On this point, there are these verses: "The student (*brahmacārī*), the householder (*gṛhastha*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*). The student serves his teacher until death. The forest-dweller, according to the practice prescribed in the *Vaikhānasa* scriptures, lives in the forest subsisting on roots and fruits, devoted to austerity. Having established the sacred fire according to the *Śrāmaṇaka* rite, he should perform ablutions at the three daily libations (*savanas*). He should eat non-village food and may even subsist on alms; however, he should not enter a village. Wearing matted hair and clothing of bark or skin, he should not eat more than once a year. The wandering mendicant, having abandoned his kinsmen and possessing no property, should wander forth. Having gone to the forest, shaven-headed or with a top-knot, covered only by a loincloth, he should stay in one place during the rainy season. Wearing ochre-colored robes, he should beg when the pestle has been laid aside, when the embers are extinguished, when the people have finished eating, and when the dishes have been cleared away. He should be free from malice toward living beings through the restraints of speech, mind, and body. Carrying purifying implements, he should perform his necessary duties with water drawn for the purpose of purification. Having cast aside the rituals pertaining to the gods and the sacred fires, they say: "We shall unite with the middle [state], being severed from both ends. However, the teachers maintain that there is only one stage of life (*aikāśramya*), because the others do not produce offspring. Regarding this, they cite an example: [The text continues with further verses.]

There was indeed an Asura named Kāpila, the son of Prahlāda; he created these distinctions while vying with the gods. Therefore, a wise person should not pay heed to them, because they have a visible purpose. This is also restated in the following verse: "This is his eternal greatness. [TB 3.12.9.7–8]
He should say:
"By whom the sun shines... concerning the world beyond" (TB 3.12.9.7). "These who move neither hither nor thither, who are neither Brahmins nor pourers of the Soma-juice..."
"Having resorted to speech with evil, they weave a web of deceit, lacking progeny" (RV 10.71.9). "O Agni, through offspring may I attain immortality" (RV 5.4.10).

"Indeed, at birth, a Brāhmaṇa is born burdened by three debts: to the seers by means of the student life (brahmacarya), to the gods by means of sacrifice, and to the ancestors by means of offspring" (TS 6.3.10.5). Thus, there are innumerable statements regarding the connection to these debts, as well as prohibitions (BDh 2.11.9–33). 1.14.
Āpastamba:

"The threefold knowledge, studentship, procreation, faith, austerity, sacrifice, and the giving of gifts—those who perform these, with them indeed we are; by praising anything else, one becomes dust and perishes" (ĀpDh 2.24.8).

Therefore, because they are not seen in the Śruti and because the Smṛtis lack authority when in conflict with direct Śruti, the stages of life for those of perpetual chastity (ūrdhvaretas) do not exist. 1.16.
Now, it might be argued: there is an explicit scriptural statement (śruti) among the Vājasaneyins:
"Seeking this world alone, mendicants renounce their homes" [BAU 4.4.22];

and likewise, "Therefore, a Brahmin, having become disillusioned with scholarship, should seek to abide in childlike innocence; and having become disillusioned with both childlike innocence and scholarship, he then becomes a sage" [BAU 3.5.1]. 1.17.
And he demonstrates the proper conduct:

"Indeed, the ancient knowers did not desire offspring, saying, 'What shall we do with offspring, we for whom this Self is the world? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22). And they did not offer the Agnihotra sacrifice. (1.18)

To this it is replied: Is renunciation (*pārivrājya*) enjoined as a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), or is it for the sake of another performance, like marriage and other such acts? If it were a human goal, it would either be for the sake of heaven—according to the principle that "it would be heaven" (PMS 4.3.7.15)—or for the sake of something else. It cannot be for the sake of heaven, because that would contradict the context of liberation (*apavarga*). For indeed, everywhere renunciation is enjoined specifically within the context of liberation; therefore, some connection must be stated with that very context of liberation. Yet even that cannot be stated, because scripture declares that liberation results from knowledge alone.

"Knowing it thus, one goes beyond death; there is no other path for going. "By knowledge alone does one ascend to that place where desires have been cast away; neither sacrificial gifts nor the asceticism of the ignorant reach there" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 10.5.4.16). 1.19.
Now, it may be thought that [this] is enjoined as an auxiliary to the practice of knowledge.

This is not so. Since the practice of knowledge is possible even for householders, the injunction for other stages of life (āśramas) need not be postulated for that purpose. Even if such an injunction were postulated, it would not necessitate the attainment of a different stage of life; rather, it would merely enjoin a certain vow called *pārivrājya* for householders themselves, similar to the vow of one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*). And this is understood to be a duty consisting of the renunciation of attachments, which does not contradict an already active householder’s life. Furthermore, there is no inclusion of those duties seen in the Smṛtis that contradict the Śruti. Nor is the word *pārivrājya* itself well-known elsewhere as denoting a distinct stage of life, for that would entail the consequence of its being non-Vedic (*aśrauta*). Thus, this Śruti text merely reiterates the *pārivrājya* well-known from the Smṛtis for the sake of praising knowledge—showing how great is this knowledge, by the power of which those who abandon even prescribed ritual acts do not incur sin. (1.20)

Therefore, some teachers maintain that there is no such thing as a stage of life (āśrama) called wandering mendicancy (pārivrājya), because—unlike the Agnihotra and other rites—it lacks the specific Vedic duties of the householder stage which cannot exist for them; and because begging for alms and similar acts, like the twilight prayers (saṃdhyāvandana), are merely forms of customary conduct (ācāra) intended for the sake of fulfilling the duties of a stage of life, and thus cannot themselves constitute a stage of life. 1.21.

To this it is replied: there exists an uncommon dharma called *jñānayoga*. For, after introducing the rites beginning with truth and ending with mental discipline (*mānasa*), the scripture enjoins renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) by stating: "Therefore, they say that renunciation (*nyāsa*) is superior to these austerities" (MNU 538). Thus, having prescribed renunciation through the Śruti, [it continues:]

"One should unite oneself" (MNU 540)—this prescribes the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*), which is denoted by the term "deposition" (*nyāsa*). The yoga of knowledge consists in the practice of knowledge alone. Indeed, this is not possible for householders, because they must also perform the *agnihotra* and other such duties; therefore, for them, there is only the yoga of action (*karmayoga*). The yoga of action consists in the practice of the combination of knowledge and action, from which liberation follows. For wandering mendicants (*parivrājakas*), however, liberation comes through the yoga of knowledge alone. Therefore, since these [householders] lack [the exclusive practice of] action, the text shows the accomplishment of action by means of another [method].

For one who knows thus, the section beginning with "The self is the sacrifice" (MNU 543) is prescribed as something to be performed day after day even by a wandering mendicant; it is not merely a matter of praise, because it conveys a new injunction (*apūrvatva*). 1.22.

But surely even for wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*) there are rituals such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyāvandana*)? True; because these are their established custom, they serve merely as duties of their stage of life (*āśrama-dharma*) and not as means for liberation. For liberation, however, there is only the yoga of knowledge (*jñāna-yoga*). The twilight worship and other rites are for the sake of that [knowledge]. Indeed, one who has neglected the twilight worship has no qualification for it, for "one who neglects the twilight worship is eternally impure and unfit for all ritual acts."
This is because of the traditional teaching:
"The Vedas do not purify one who is devoid of right conduct," and also:

"The repetition of mantras, austerity, wandering for alms, and so forth, are included within the restraints (yama) and observances (niyama). Furthermore, that the restraints, observances, and other such practices constitute limbs of yoga is established by all the scriptures. Therefore, these too are included within the yoga of knowledge alone. (1.23)
Therefore, it is established that the yoga of knowledge belongs to wandering mendicants, while the yoga of action belongs to householders. And likewise:
"Neither by ritual action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone have some attained immortality" (MNU 227).
Thus, immortality is heard in scripture as being attained through the very renunciation of action.
Those ascetics of purified being, whose purpose is well-ascertained through the wisdom of Vedānta, by means of the yoga of renunciation,
[attain the goal] in the world of Brahman at the time of their final end.
"And thus: 'All are completely liberated from the supreme death' (MNU 229–30). Likewise, the Blessed Vāsudeva said:
'By the yoga of knowledge for the Sāṃkhyas, and by the yoga of action for the Yogins' (BhG 3.3). || 1.24 ||

Thus, because this unique dharma exists, there is indeed an āśrama called wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*) that is based on the Śruti. Furthermore, the authority of the Smṛtis is established because they are rooted in it. This dharma is not possible for householders, since it is heard everywhere in the texts that [the mendicant] "should practice the life of begging" and must renounce all property. Therefore, it is proven that wandering mendicancy is indeed a distinct stage of life. 1.25
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Rule for Wandering Asceticism," in the *Yatidharmasaṃuccaya* composed by Yādavaprakāśa. 1.26.
The second chapter:

Determining the Stage of Eligibility for Wandering Asceticism. Now, the stage of eligibility is considered. (2.1) One view is that wandering asceticism (*pārivrājya*) follows only after the forest-dweller stage (*vanavāsa*), and not directly from the student stage (*brahmacarya*). (2.2) And so says the Śruti:
"Having brought dear wealth to the teacher, do not cut off the thread of progeny," thus [it is said].
Likewise: "A Brāhmaṇa, indeed, when being born... (TS 6.3.10.5);
and "Procreation is the foundation; spreading the thread of offspring well, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors" (MNU 525). || 2.4 ||
And so Manu says:
"Having discharged the three debts, one should direct the mind toward liberation;
but he who pursues liberation without having discharged them goes downward" (MDh 6.35). 2.5.

Yājñavalkya said: "One who has studied the Vedas, performed recitations, has sons, given food, maintains the sacred fires, and performs sacrifices according to his ability—only such a person may set his mind on liberation, and not otherwise. (YDh 3.57) || 2.6 ||
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"After residing in the forest, one who has reached advanced age may, according to his own desire, enter the life of a wandering mendicant. (2.7)
Medhātithi said:
"One who is dispassionate toward the bonds of sons, wife, house, fields, cattle, gold, and so forth, as well as toward human enjoyments and those divine ones revealed in the Vedas. (2.8)
By the study of the Vedas, by sacrifice, and by austerity, one becomes free from impurity;
through practice over many successive births, one’s self becomes purified and the senses are conquered.

"Awakened by the Itihāsas, the Purāṇas, and the Śruti, one strives for the supreme state; through such striving, he becomes a *yati*. This is the supreme accomplishment of that *yati*, and not of anyone else. (2.10)
Some, however, say that one may adopt the life of a wandering mendicant at will, whether from the stage of studentship, from the household, or from the forest. 2.11.
And so says the Jābāli-śruti:

"Having completed the stage of studentship (brahmacarya), one should become a householder; having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller; having been a forest-dweller, one should renounce. Or else, otherwise, one may renounce directly from studentship, or from the home, or from the forest. [JU 64] || 2.12 ||
Yama said: A learned Brāhmaṇa who has fulfilled his Vedic vows should take refuge in liberation, remaining equal toward all beings, both stationary and moving. (2.13)

"A householder who has fathered a son, who has conquered himself and mastered his senses, who is free from longing for all desires and has accomplished what was to be done, should go forth as a wandering mendicant; or one dwelling in the forest, having performed rigorous austerities, should take recourse to the supreme path. (2.14)

In this regard, if a student (*brahmacārī*) should go forth [into the life of a wandering mendicant], he should do so only after having completed his vows; if a householder (*gṛhastha*), only after having fathered a son and performed the sacrifices, because it has been stated previously that "having withdrawn those fires into his heart"; and if a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), only after having performed arduous penance (*taptatapā*). This is understood to be the case. This same principle should be applied hereafter as well. It is precisely with reference to this subject that the Mānava statement begins, "Having discharged the three debts," and so forth. (2.15) Some say: "Whether a student or a householder, one who has lost his wife may become a forest-dweller."
"Having known the supreme Brahman correctly, one should renounce all attachments and wander as a mendicant. (2.16)
In this regard, it is understood that for a householder whose wife has died, renunciation may be undertaken even before the birth of a son, provided there is detachment. Bṛhaspati says:

"Having seen that worldly existence is indeed essence-less, one who is established in supreme detachment should go forth into homelessness, desiring to see the essential [truth], even without having performed marriage. (2.18)
"Another, whose lineage has already flourished, having performed various sacrifices, or one whose body is half-paralyzed, or another from the forest—such a person may go forth. (2.19)
"The wife is half the body," based on the observation that "half of the body falls for him whose wife drinks liquor" (VaDh 21.15).
And because of the Vedic revelation: "The wife is indeed half of one's own self" (TS 6.1.8.5). Śaṅkha says:
"Having thus spent his time in the forest, the twice-born man shall become a resident of the Brahma-āśrama."
Through the knowledge of various Upaniṣads, he attained proficiency in dispassion. || 2.21 ||
Having withdrawn the collection of his senses far from sense-objects, delighting in the Self alone, he cast aside his adversaries with his mind. (2.22)
Having repeatedly attained self-mastery through the practice of yoga, with his bonds firmly severed,
his mind withdrawn from all attachments, he is a celibate student of excellent vows.

"If a householder is endowed with these qualities, O Prajāpati, having performed the sacrifice according to the rule and given the gift of all his possessions as the sacrificial fee, and having internalized the sacred fires within himself, the twice-born man shall become one belonging to the stage of the Brahma-āśrama. (2.24)

Thus, while some *śruti* and *smṛti* texts enjoin renunciation (*pārivrājya*) from the very stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*), others do so only after the discharge of debts and similar duties. When such a contradiction exists, some say: "The *śruti* and *smṛti* texts concerning rising from studentship refer to those who are ineligible for ritual acts, such as the blind, the lame, and so forth. Likewise, Likhita said:
"When dispassion arises in one—brought about by the gods and attained through merit accumulated over hundreds of millions of births—and when even craving for Brahman becomes stable... (2.26).

Having studied the true meaning of the Vedas and being unable [to fulfill] the life of a householder, he should renounce from the stage of studentship; and when worn out, from the house, and even from the forest. (2.27)
"One who is free from disease and young should dwell in the householder's stage with diligence;
however, one who is blind, lame, afflicted with leprosy, or old should take recourse to silence. (2.28)

But others say: Why should there not be a reversal in both the Śruti and Smṛti? Why could one who is not dispassionate, being unable to practice the life of a wandering mendicant (pārivrājya), not remain a householder? For it is not possible for one who is not dispassionate to practice the life of a wandering mendicant. Thus says Dakṣa: "All those whose nature is dominated by *sattva* are likewise overcome by sense-objects;
what then can be said of human beings here who are of inferior nature? (2.29–2.30)
Therefore, one whose passions have been ripened should exercise restraint;
for another is unable to do so, since he is carried away by the objects of the senses. (2.31)
"Many twice-born ones live by relying on the emblem of the triple staff;
for he who does not know Brahman is not considered worthy of the triple staff. (2.32)
Likhita said:
"The king shall employ as a slave that twice-born man who, having performed a total renunciation, should resort to a relapse; likewise, he shall brand him with the mark of a dog's foot. (2.33)
Therefore, having first examined one's purity of intention over a long period of time, and knowing that the mind does not waver from dharma, one should then renounce. (2.34)

Yama said: "One who has turned away from sensual desire and the like, who is tranquil and devoted solely to Brahman—he alone is qualified for renunciation; any other is merely intent on a livelihood. (2.35)

Nor is it correct to say that the scriptural injunction regarding rising from one's seat does not apply to those who have not been initiated, because for them there is a separate injunction later on, beginning with the words:
"Whether he be observing vows or not observing vows, whether he be a *snātaka* or not a *snātaka*, whether he be a student (*sārinaka*) or otherwise" (JU 64).
The elder Jābāli said:

"Whether one has taken vows or not, whether one is a graduate (snātaka) or not, whether one maintains the domestic fire (āvasathya) or not, whether one maintains the sacred fire (agnihotra) or not—having fetched fire from a village," and so forth. (2.37)

Furthermore, as for what was said—"The blind, the lame, the leper, and the elderly should take recourse to silence"—that too is not contradictory, because the words "blind" and so forth have been explained otherwise. Thus says Medhātithi: [2.38]... Indeed, thus says Medhātithi.
He who, upon seeing a woman newly born, one sixteen years of age,
and one a hundred years old, remains free from any change of state, is a eunuch.
He who travels no more than a yojana for the sake of alms or for the discharge of excrement and urine—he is always as if lame. (2.40)
Whether standing or walking, he whose sight does not reach far—
having been freed from fear for the duration of four ages— is called a blind wandering mendicant.
"He who, having heard speech that is beneficial or harmful, pleasant to the mind or bringing grief, does not listen as if he were deaf, is proclaimed to be truly deaf. (2.42)

Furthermore, a blind person has no entitlement to the life of a wandering mendicant (*pārivrājya*), because of the injunction of the Dharma: "One should set down one's foot purified by sight" (MDh 6.46). Nor does a lame person or one afflicted with leprosy have such an entitlement.
Wandering among sacred fords and temples of the gods,
he should travel by the paths indicated by the sun and move upon the earth like an insect.

Because of the prescription of such duties [as these], [the renunciation of a eunuch is not permitted]. (2.44) Since celibacy (*brahmacarya*) is prescribed, there is no wandering life (*pārivrājya*) for a eunuch. For celibacy is the avoidance of sexual intercourse. Indeed, there is no avoidance of sexual intercourse for a eunuch, because for one who is like a pillar, there is no possibility of engaging in sexual intercourse. Avoidance is a vow (*vrata*) only with respect to that which has been attained. (4.45) Therefore, the scriptural injunction regarding debts refers to one who is not dispassionate; however, for the dispassionate person, there is only the wandering life. (2.46) And so says Bṛhaspati: "One who has not yet married may go forth [into the life of a mendicant], having resorted to supreme dispassion. (2.47)
Kratu said:

"Whether he be a student, a householder, one whose wife has died, or a forest-dweller, having fully realized the Supreme Brahman and abandoned all attachments, he should go forth as a wandering mendicant. (2.48)
Śaṅkha said:

"One whose self is withdrawn from all attachments, even if he is a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) observing excellent vows—if he is endowed with these qualities, he belongs to Prajāpati, whether he be a householder or otherwise. (2.49)

"Having performed the sacrifice according to the rules and having given all his possessions as the sacrificial fee, a twice-born man, having consigned the sacred fires into himself, shall become a member of the brahmacarya stage. (2.50)
Dattātreya said:
"The triple staff is the Vaiṣṇava mark, the means of liberation for Brahmins;
it is the extinction of all duties—such is the teaching of the Vedas."
"This was previously declared by the Self-Existent One for those who are dispassionate toward dwelling in a household. (2.51)

The teachers maintain that for the *upakurvāṇa* student, there is an option according to his own desire among the four stages of life (*āśrama*). And so says Vasiṣṭha: "There are four stages of life: the student (*brahmacārin*), the householder (*gṛhastha*), the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*), and the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*). Having studied one Veda, two Vedas, or all the Vedas, and having completed his period of studentship, he may enter whichever of these he desires. [VaDh 7.1–3] 2.53.
And Āpastamba says:
"Having understood the ritual acts, one may undertake whichever one desires" (ĀpDh 2.21.5).
The Blessed Vyāsa said:
Having duly acquired knowledge through service to the teacher, the twice-born man, permitted by his teacher, should perform the ceremonial bath after giving him a cow as a sacrificial fee. (2.55)

"Whether it be the lifelong student stage, that of the sage, or even the state of the wandering mendicant—whatever stage of life a Brahmin desires, he should dwell in that very one with self-restraint. (2.56)
Gautama said:
"Some state that there is an option regarding his stage of life (āśrama). [GDh 3.1] || 2.57 ||

As for what was said regarding "having discharged the three debts," that too—being established by the Śruti and Smṛti as prescribing renunciation from the stage of studentship itself for one who is dispassionate—is restricted to a person possessed of passion, or it pertains to one who has already fulfilled the purpose of discharging his debts. (2.58)

Therefore, for one who is dispassionate, the state of wandering mendicancy (pārivrājya) is established whether from the stage of studentship (brahmacarya), from the householder’s life (gṛha), or from the forest-dweller’s life (vana). And so says Bṛhaspati: "He who is attached to the Supreme Self and detached from that which is not the Supreme Self, being completely liberated from all desires, he is worthy to consume alms."
Renunciation is prescribed even for the sick by Aṅgiras:
"Exhausted from dwelling in the forest, one should go forth according to the prescribed rule;
a twice-born man, whether afflicted by disease or free from passion, who knows Brahman, should renounce. (2.61)
A wise man should go forth from the life of a celibate student, or he should go forth from the home;
or he should go forth from the forest—whether he be afflicted by illness or distressed by suffering. (2.62)
When a terrible crisis has arisen, such as being in the domain of thieves, tigers, and the like, the sage Aṅgiras declared that renunciation is for one who is terrified by fear. (2.63)
And likewise Śātātapa says:
"He who declares, 'I have renounced,' even when his life-breaths are at his throat, shall obtain a fruit equal to that of a thousand sacrifices. (2.64)
Dattātreya said:
"This dharma of bearing the mark of Viṣṇu belongs to those born from the mouth;
this dharma does not exist for those born from the arms or those born from the thighs. (2.65)
Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Determination of the Ten Stages for Those Qualified for Wandering Asceticism," in the Yatidharmasamuccaya. 2.66.

The third chapter: Determination of the Mark (liṅga). Now the mark is defined. It is of two kinds: external and bodily. Therein, the bodily consists of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), being shaven-headed, or wearing only a tuft of hair (*śikhā*). The external consists of the staff (*daṇḍa*), water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), and so forth. The external mark is called "measure" (*mātrā*). 3.1.
In this regard, the physical requirements are stated. Vasiṣṭha says:
"Wearing the sacred thread and holding a water-pot in his hand" (VaDh 10.31); and "shaven-headed, free from pride, free from anger, and without possessions" (VaDh 10.6). || 3.2 ||
Yama said: "He should always sleep on the bare ground and dwell in an unstable residence; he should be constantly in the forest, keep his head shaved, and practice for knowledge with his mind. (3.3)
Paiṭhīnasi said:
"The sage is without a fixed abode, shaven-headed, free from the sense of 'mine,' and without possessions. (3.4)
Bodhāyana says: "Having gone to the forest, he should have his hair tied in a topknot or be shaven. (BDh 2.11.17–18) || 3.5 ||

Kratu said: Having praised the Swan with three hymns dedicated to Viṣṇu and Puruṣa, one who has shaved his head or wears a topknot, clad in saffron robes and carrying a bowl and staff, shall depart from his home. (3.6)
Sumantu said: "A sage is one who is shaven-headed and free from possessions. (3.7)
Gautama says: "Either shaven-headed or with a topknot. (GDh 3.21) || 3.8 ||

Therefore, there is an option regarding whether one should be shaven-headed or wear a topknot; however, the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) is obligatory for all. Thus, Atri, referring specifically to the state of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*), said:
"The sacred thread has three deities and consists of the essence of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
Those Brahmins who, living by means of logic, abandon it out of delusion [fall from their status]."
"They have fallen away from the paths to heaven and liberation; of this there is no doubt. (3.10)

Āhośanā says: "By the abandonment of the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*), the student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and even the wandering mendicant fall; therefore, one should not abandon it. (3.11)
Now the external marks are described. Dakṣa says:
"A student is characterized by the girdle, deerskin, staff, and so forth;
a householder by the sacrificial post, the Vedas, and so forth; and a forest-dweller by [the growth of] nails and hair."
The triple staff and the ascetic—these are the distinct characteristics. || 3.12 ||
Bṛhaspati said:

"Having thus performed the renunciation (saṃnyāsa), one should take up the triple staff (tridaṇḍa) together with the purifier (pavitra), as well as a bowl and a water-pot, reaching as high as the hair. (3.13)
Śaṅkha and Likhita have stated:

"Having abandoned all undertakings, one should be shaven-headed, wear saffron robes, subsist on alms, and concern oneself only with the trident, the water-pot, and the tuft of hair used as a strainer. (3.14)
Āṅgiras said:
I shall describe the insignia of the ascetic (yati) by which he is recognized:
the sacred thread (brahmasūtra), the triple staff (tridaṇḍa), and the garment for warding off insects. (3.15)
"The sling, the bowl, the grass mat, the loincloth, and the waistband—whosoever possesses these marks is a renunciant (yati), and no other is a renunciant. (3.16)
A *bṛsī* is a tortoise-seat. Devala says:

"The saffron robe, the shaven head, the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*), the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), the alms-bowl (*pātra*), the purifier (*pavitra*), the sandals (*pādukā*), the seat (*āsana*), and the patched cloak (*kanthā*)—these are the requisites. (3.17)
Gālava said:

Now, the wandering mendicant (parivrājaka), whether bearing the [ascetic] marks or shaven-headed or with a topknot, must always wear the sacred thread (yajñopavīta) and a garment of saffron-colored rags; he may wear a cloth for the purpose of covering his loins, but no upper garment. He shall carry a triple staff (tridaṇḍa), a water-strainer (jalapavitra), a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), an alms-bowl (kapāla), and a patched cloak (kanthā). || 3.18 ||
Likhita said:
He should wear only saffron-colored garments, or cotton clothing, or a patched robe; or likewise, bark, wool, silk, or cloth made of hemp. (3.19)
A carrying-net, a bowl with its protective cover, joined with a tripod, fastened with a water-strainer, a triple staff, and a round seat. (3.20)
"Whether walking or sitting, being pure, he should always carry his topknot, the sacred thread, and a water-pot for the sake of purification. (3.21)
Yama said: A needle, a thimble, a triple-staff, sandals, a water-pot,
a rope, a sling, a begging bowl, and a seat.
"A patched garment, a rag, a staff—possessing only these few requisites. (3.22)
Āhośanā says: The vessel, that armor, the sling, the triple staff with its purifier,
the seat, the waist-thread, the loincloth, and the waist-band.
"Having taken up the sacrificial thread and a patched garment, he should abandon the other. (3.23)
Kratu said:
One should always carry twenty, ten, or five [articles]:
a patched garment, a needle, a deerskin, an umbrella, a water-strainer, a water-pot, and a seat. (3.24)

The alms-bowl, the carrying-net, the rosary, the clay-digging tool, the sandals, the garment for covering the private parts, the three-legged stool, the wooden shoes, the staff, the eyelashes, the yoga-band, and the outer robe— these are recorded as the twenty items known as the "measures" (mātrā). 3.25.

Among these approximately twenty items, five are permanent: namely, the sacred thread (*upavīta*), the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*), the water-purifier (*pavitra*), the bowl (*pātraka*), and the loincloth and waist-cloth (*kaupīna-kaṭivastra*). Thus says Viṣṇu:
"The sacred thread, the triple staff, the bowl, the water-purifier, the loincloth, and the waist-cloth must not be abandoned for as long as one lives. (3.27)

By the very mention of the bowl (*pātra*), there is also the inclusion of the net-bag (*śikyaka*), the waist-band (*vakra*), and the triple-staff (*triviṣṭabdha*), which are its constituent parts. As for the ten items mentioned in the Smṛti, beginning with "the needle (*sūcī*) and the thimble (*pippalaka*)," the number ten is reached by counting the needle and the thimble as one; here, *pippala* refers to the thread (*sūtra*). (3.28)

The wandering mendicant (*parivrāj*) is of two kinds: one is devoted to the practice of knowledge and desires to ascend to yoga; the other has already ascended to yoga, is a seer of reality (*tattvadarśin*), possesses unmanifest signs, follows unmanifest conduct, and though not insane, behaves like one who is insane. (3.29) And thus, the twofold nature is shown by means of a ritual injunction: "In the forenoon the yogi should wander about; but the one possessing perfect knowledge [should do so] in the afternoon. (3.30)
In this regard, with reference to right knowledge, Kratu himself said:
"Virtue, conduct, learning, wisdom, dispassion—these are the characteristics of dharma. What fruit can there be for one who possesses these in their full measure? (3.31)

"One should perform meditation, purification, austerity, worship, breath control, recitation, praise, the twilight rituals, begging for alms, and attendance [upon the deity] until the end of life. (3.32)

Because of the injunction that "five [elements] are eternal" and because of the rule regarding alms-gathering, even those possessing perfect knowledge must certainly maintain the five elements alone. (3.33)

Now, the characteristics of these items, beginning with the sacred thread (*upavīta*), are stated; first, among them, is the characteristic of the *yajñopavīta*. With reference specifically to the state of wandering mendicancy (*pārivrājya*), Dattātreya and Atri both said: "Three threads, twisted downwards, and again three times three twisted upwards;
it should be made of cotton or woven cloth, and likewise there should be one upper garment. (3.35)
With three threads wound downwards and three wound upwards, it is tripled; this is known as the Brahmasūtra, the sacred thread, made of cotton with nine new strands. (3.36)
"The compendium of the nine sūtras is the means for the liberation of the twice-born;
without it, one would immediately be excluded from all dharmas. (3.37)
The characteristics of the staff are now described. Kapila says:

"One should carry a bamboo staff that is straight, as long as the nose, and measured by the span of one's fingers, or one should carry staffs [of various lengths] commensurate with one's own height. Furthermore, they cite this:
"Where auspicious sprouts are seen emerging from the leaves..."
One should know that to be the first section; the remainder here is called the middle.

They say that for an ascetic, the staff is to be avoided at the third, fifth, seventh, ninth, and likewise the eleventh joints; and in all cases, two finger-breadths below the joint and from above, [the staff must not touch the body]. (3.40)
This is not even contradictory for householders. Dattātreya said:

"The triple staffs should be made of bamboo, as thick as a finger, reaching up to the head, with their bark intact, free from blemishes, pleasant to look at, and having joints that are even and well-proportioned."
[He should choose those] with six, eight, or ten joints, free from female organs and without sores. (3.41)
The ascetic [should carry] triple staffs made of bamboo, each as long as his hair and with even knots. (3.42)
"One should carry" refers to the elder Dakṣa:
"The wise man should carry the triple staff (tridaṇḍa) while standing upright, along with the water-strainer (udapavitraka). (3.43)
Hārīta: Having divided the triple staff into five parts,
one should wrap it with a cord made of black cow-hair for four finger-breadths, starting from the upper third.
Equipped with three streams of knots and purified by water above, one should receive it in the right hand, as given by the Guru, accompanied by the mantra. (3.45)
"Purified by water" means cleansed with water. [He should be] one whose skill has increased. One should bind it with a cord at the tip, the base, and the middle of the triple staff.
Having left two parts from the tip, and right there [at the middle], four finger-breadths [from the base]. (3.46)
One should bind [the penis] with a cowherd’s rope, or else with a fivefold binding;
one should make the binding with a cord alone and divide it again into five parts. (3.47)
In the *Tattvasāgara-saṃhitā* of the *Śrīpāñcarātra*,
one should meditate upon Parameṣṭhin at the upper tip of the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*),
Puruṣātman as the second [tip], and Viśvātman at the middle. (3.48)
The ascetic should meditate upon the fourth as the person of cessation (nivṛttipuruṣa), the fifth as the universal self (sarvātmā),
and the triple staff (tridaṇḍa) as a whole as the form of Viṣṇu.
Hārīta says: A renunciant should always carry the form of Viṣṇu known as the triple staff (tridaṇḍa). 3.50.

Śaunaka said: The staff of knowledge (*jñānadaṇḍa*) should be short; the staff of the self (*ātmadaṇḍa*) should be of medium length; and the staff of Viṣṇu (*viṣṇudaṇḍa*) should be long. An ascetic (*yati*) should carry these three staffs. (3.51)
Pracetās says:
The ascetic himself should carry the sacred thread and the triple staff like a topknot;
otherwise, he should have them carried by another, for [otherwise] he would become liable to penance. (3.52)
One should consecrate the triple staff with the *Puruṣasūkta* alone;
one should perform a hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) with the seven *Ṛg* verses dedicated to Viṣṇu.
During bathing, when necessary duties must be performed, while eating, during the practice of recitation,
during Vedic study, and even while sleeping, one should restrain oneself with a staff.
The ascetic should always carry a single triple staff made of bamboo, as well as a loincloth, a waist-cloth, and other such items for the purpose of wearing them. (3.55)
If an ascetic should void urine or feces while carrying his triple staff, he must perform the rite of sipping water (ācamana) for the sake of purification together with that staff. 3.56.
The elder Jābāli said:
"Having poured out a full handful of water and having taken up a staff or staves," and so forth. (3.57)
Baudhāyana says:
"From this point forward, he shall not wear white garments; he may carry either a single staff or a triple staff.
Yājñavalkya said:
"Or such a single staff may be used, provided it is devoid of cow-hair. (3.59)

Therefore, there is an option regarding the staffs. Because it requires greater effort and is seen more frequently among the many [practitioners], the triple-staff (tridaṇḍya) is indeed praised over the single-staff (ekadaṇḍya). Thus said the Blessed Vyāsa:
"The wearing of the triple-staff is praised, as well as dwelling in solitude; a light diet and lack of exertion are the means of liberation for ascetics. || 3.60-3.61 ||

Because there is no difference in the measure of the staff, other measures and duties such as the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyāvandana*) and so forth do not differ. However, in some cases, when the triple-staff (*tridaṇḍa*) is lost, a single-staff (*ekadaṇḍa*) is prescribed. Atri and Jābāla state:
"If the water-purifier (*jalapavitra*) or the triple-staff is lost through negligence, one should take up a single bamboo staff, or even a middle-sized one made of *pālāśa* wood. (3.63)
"Even in the absence of a *brahmapatra*, one may take a clump of *kuśa* grass;
having taken it, one may wander about until another [vessel] is obtained. (3.64)
Hārīta said:
"If the water-strainer or the triple staff is lost through negligence,
one should indeed carry a single bamboo staff, or alternatively, a middle-sized staff made of *pālāśa* wood."
Having taken them, he should wander about until a triple staff (tridaṇḍaka) has been obtained.
"One should always seek it with effort, being vigilant and composed. Once the triple staff has been obtained, one should hold it above, purified by water. (3.66)
Medhātithi says: "As long as there are not three staffs, one should wander with a single one; even then, however, having attached a cloth to its tip for the sake of purifying water. (3.67)
Jamadagni:
One should not fasten a loincloth or a waist-wrap upon the triple staff;
he who, out of delusion, should make such a binding, treats the triple staff with contempt. (3.68)
If the triple staff is accidentally joined with another staff,
the mendicant should wash it with earth and water and perform three breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma).

In the Kali age, a water-pot (kuṇḍikā) should not be carried. And so says Devala: "In the ages beginning with Dvāpara, an ascetic should eat from an alms-bowl; in the Kali age, he should not eat from his own vessel, nor should he carry a water-pot. (3.70)
Medhātithi states the characteristics of the water-strainer (*jalapavitra*):
"It should be hairless, white, untouched, and twelve finger-breadths in length on both sides.
"Untouched" means not previously used.
It should be twice or even three times that size, or likewise eight finger-breadths on all sides.
One should know that a water-purifier (*jalapavitraka*) is either a span long or subtle, made of cotton, free from blemishes, and not produced by a *caṇḍāla* or similar outcaste. (3.72)
Āṅgiras said: "For ascetics, these three white things should always be present: the sacred thread, the teeth, and likewise the means for warding off living beings. (3.73)
Āttri declared the vessels:
those made of clay, wood, gourd, bamboo, woven fiber, stone, grass, linen, and likewise leaf-cups. (3.74)
One of these should be accepted according to one's own capacity;
if, out of greed, one accepts from another recipient, one should perform ten breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).
Kratu said:
"One should take vessels made of bamboo, wood, stone, gourd, grass, or leaves, as well as earthenware and linen vessels, according to one's own capacity. (3.76)
Manu says: "Gourds, wooden vessels, those made of clay, or those of bamboo—these, Manu, the son of the Self-existent, has declared to be the vessels for an ascetic. (MDh 6.54) || 3.77 ||
Hārīta states the characteristics of the loop (śikya):
"Whether made of linen, or of kuśa grass thread, or of cotton thread— strung together with these very materials, the loop should be fashioned in the shape of a lotus."
"The characteristic of a *śikyaka* [water-strainer] consists of either six or five fistfuls. (3.78)
He himself stated the characteristics of the seat:
"The seat of the ascetic is declared to be circular, made of wood, and one cubit in size; it was fashioned by the sages of old for the sake of purification and for use as a seat. (3.79)
Kapila stated the characteristics regarding digging: there is no fault in taking earth by digging it to a depth of only four finger-breadths. || 3.80 ||
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Determination of the Mark," in the *Yatidharmasamuccaya*.

Those who do not belong to an āśrama must perform four *kṛcchra* penances; those who belong to an āśrama must perform one *kṛcchra*. In this way, fitness for renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) is attained. Having made a formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) on the twelfth lunar day or the full moon, and having performed the shaving of the head, one performs first the *deva-śrāddha*, second the *ṛṣi-śrāddha*, third the *divya-śrāddha*, fourth the *pitrya*, fifth the *mātṛka*, sixth the *mānuṣa*, seventh the *bhautika*, and eighth that for oneself. 4.2.
Thus spoke the Blessed Vṛddhavasiṣṭha; "on the full moon day," and so forth, is the same [as before]. Śaunaka said:

"Having performed the *nāndīmukha* rite on the preceding day, one should feed the Brahmins. Then, having caused them to pronounce 'an auspicious day,' 'well-being,' and 'prosperity,' one should have one's hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved. 4.4.
Regarding this, the Blessed One Jāmadagnya also said:
"One should have the hair of the head, the beard, the body hair, and the nails shaved. (4.5)
Śaunaka said:
"Then, having bathed according to the rule, one should give away all one's possessions, excluding the materials for the fire-oblation and other such items. (4.6)
Bodhāyana says:
"The staffs, the sling, the water-pot, the water-strainer, and the vessel—these are the items.
Vasiṣṭha says: A wise man should accept these six things—a triple staff, a seat, a patched garment, a sling, an alms-bowl, and a water-pot—and should renounce all other possessions. 4.8.
"One should perform the renunciation of material possessions; purification from impurity is thus ordained.
Without the renunciation of children and wealth, one should certainly not undertake the life of a wandering mendicant. || 4.9 ||

Kātyāyana says: Having set aside the triple staff, the water-strainer, the sling, the bowl, the loincloth, and the ochre garment in a place free from living beings, one who does not maintain a sacred fire should produce a fire [for the cremation]. 4.10.
Baudhāyana says: For those who do not maintain the sacred fires, the production of the fires is according to the rule for a single fire. 4.11.
Śaunaka said:

Then, having placed the staff and other items nearby, one should first perform the *brahmāñjali* mentally and recite [the following] in a temple, in a village, at the boundary of a village, on a riverbank, or in a sacred place:
"Salutation to Brahmā; salutation to Indra; salutation to Sūrya; salutation to the Self."

Then, having touched water and formed a handful of *darbha* grass, he should mutter the beginning of the Vedas. Then, having consumed a handful of barley meal (*saktu*), he performs the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*). Then he should consecrate the region of his navel with the mantras:

"Svāhā to the Self! Svāhā to the Inner Self! Svāhā to Prajāpati! Then, having consumed the threefold mixture of milk, curd, and ghee, and having sipped water, he shall fast; or alternatively, he may consume water and perform recitation (*japa*).
Oṃ bhūḥ, I enter the Sāvitrī: *tat savitur vareṇyam*. Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I enter the Sāvitrī: *bhargo devasya dhīmahi*. Oṃ suvaḥ, I enter the Sāvitrī: *dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt*.
Oṃ bhūḥ, I enter the Sāvitrī: *tat savitur vareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi*. Oṃ bhuvaḥ, I enter the Sāvitrī: *dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt*.
Oṃ suvaḥ, I enter the Sāvitrī: *tat savitur vareṇyaṃ bhargo devasya dhīmahi, dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt*.
"Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ, I enter the Sāvitrī: 'We meditate upon that excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ; may he impel our thoughts.

Having thus led himself to another stage of life (*āśrama*), he becomes one with Brahman—so it is known. Moreover, they quote: 'Having gone from stage to stage, having offered oblations and conquered his senses...'"
Exhausted by begging for alms and offerings, he later becomes a mendicant.
That very monk [is one who acts] for the sake of infinity. 4.12.
Śaunaka said:

Then, after sunset, having melted the clarified butter (*ājya*), purified it, and taken four portions into the ladle (*sruk*), he offers a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) into the kindled fire with "Oṃ Svāhā. Then, having performed the evening fire-rite (*agnikārya*), he spreads grass to the north of the fire, places the vessels upon them, and to the south of the fire, having spread *darbha* grass in the place of the Brahman priest and laid down a black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*) over it, he remains awake for that night. Then, rising during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, having bathed according to the rules, he performs the morning fire-rite. Then, having muttered the *vyāhṛtis* while standing within the water, he should mutter the hymn beginning with "tarat sa mandī. Then, having satisfied the Brahmins with food and caused them to pronounce "Auspicious day!", "Well-being!", and "Success!", he kindles the fire and offers an oblation of clarified butter.
"Swāhā to the out-breath! Swāhā to the in-breath! Swāhā to the diffused breath! Swāhā to the upward breath! Swāhā to the equalizing breath!"

Then he offers fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge with each verse of the Puruṣasūkta. Having recited the Puruṣasūkta, he spreads out the Praṇītā vessel and performs the offering for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. He performs the Jaya and subsequent offerings, ending with the Sviṣṭakṛt, according to his desire. Then, having given a vessel of clarified butter, gold, and a cow to the teacher, he should give other things as well according to his faith. Then he should worship the teacher with the mantra, "May they sprinkle me. Thereafter, with the mantra, "O Agni, that body of yours which is worthy of sacrifice," he should internalize the fires within himself. Then, standing either in front of the fire or within the water, facing eastward, he pours out a full handful of water with the formula, "Fearlessness to all beings from me, Svāhā!"—reciting "Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Suvaḥ, I have renounced [the world] by me" three times in a low voice, three times in a medium tone, and three times aloud. Thus ends section 4.13.
In the same way, Bodhāyana also, having recited from "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ, I have renounced" up to "he pours out water," says:
"The sage who wanders about after granting fearlessness to all beings, for him there shall never be any fear from any being" (BDh 2.17.27–30). 4.14.
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says: Having uttered the words "I have renounced" three times with the proper modulation of the voice,
[he purifies] thirty ancestors, thirty descendants, and thirty more beyond them.
By the very act of renunciation, one immediately saves one's ancestors from hell.
For upon seeing a twice-born man who has renounced the world, the sun moves from its place;
having pierced my orb, he attains the supreme Brahman.
But for the dispassionate Brahmin who desires the stage of renunciation,
even if he dies anywhere at all, he shall not be born again.
He himself says: "One who has not maintained the sacred fires, or one whose wife is deceased, may perform renunciation according to this rule. (4.18)

Now Śaunaka says: Then, with the verse "A youth, well-attired," he takes a saffron-colored garment. With the verse "O friend, protect me," he takes a triple staff (tridaṇḍa). With the verse "That auspiciousness we choose," he takes the sacred thread (yajñopavīta). With the verse "That which is beyond this darkness," he takes a sling (śikya). With "Om," he takes a vessel. With the verse "By which purifier the gods [purified]," he takes a water-strainer. With the verse "By which the gods rose upward toward the light," he takes a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu). || 4.19 ||
"The vessel [should be offered] with the seven vyāhṛtis," says Kātyāyana; Vasiṣṭha [says the same].

Taking up the sacred thread (*upavīta*) with the mantra "The sacrificial thread" (*yajñopavītam*), and having performed the ritual worship (*upasthāna*) of the five components beginning with the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*) using the mantras "The swan dwelling in purity" (*haṃsaḥ śuciṣat*), "That lofty one" (*udutyam*), "The bright eye" (*citram tac cakṣuḥ*), and "Obeisance to Mitra" (*namo mitrasya*); then, having dismissed the fire with the two verses beginning "The kindled one" (*samiddham*); having gone to the boundary of the village; he should take up the triple staff with the mantra "Bound in three ways, the bull bellows" (*tridhā baddho vṛṣabho roravīti*). Having recited the four purifiers (*pavitras*) and the triad [of mantras], and having walked three steps with the mantra "He strode out three steps" (*trīṇi padā vicakrame*); having performed the worship with "That is the supreme step of Viṣṇu" (*tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam*), he should mutter "Self-existent" (*svayaṃbhūr*). Having granted fearlessness to all living beings—fish and others in the water, and beasts, wild animals, reptiles, and so forth on land—he should avoid taking flowers, roots, or fruits, cutting down trees, honey, meat, untruth, giving, and receiving gifts, and other such things. Thus ends section 4.21.
Kātyāyana said:

Having abandoned his own village and kinsmen, and having reached another village, he should be devoted to recitation and meditation. He should subsist on alms obtained either by begging or unasked. He should avoid desire, anger, passion, hatred, and the like. Living in this manner for as long as life lasts, he attains Brahman and is not born again. (4.22)
Śaunaka said:

Then, without looking back and restraining his speech, he should set out toward the eastern or northern direction. By means of tranquility, self-control, and so forth, he should perform hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*). He should constantly practice the *praṇava*. 4.23.
Thus ends the ritual for renunciation according to Śaunaka (4.24). Kapila said:

But one who is without a sacred fire—whether shaven-headed or wearing a topknot—and having fasted for a day and night, bathes and offers oblations into the waters with his hand, saying: "The waters indeed are all the deities; I offer this to all the deities, svāhā! Having risen above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, I offer this, svāhā! Having whispered three times "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, I have renounced," three times in a medium voice, and three times aloud—for it is known that the gods are based on the triple truth—he pours a full handful of water onto the ground, saying: "Fearlessness to all beings from me, svāhā! Then, taking a staff or staves, a water-strainer, a water-pot, a sling, and a bowl, he should abandon his son, friends, enemies, and kinsmen, as well as the presence of the sacred fire. (4.25)
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha said:

But one who has maintained the sacred fires (āhitāgni), having risen in the morning, should offer a Vaiśvānarī oblation of rice or barley, or a Pāthīkṛti, or a Tantumatī. Then, having gone to the Āhavanīya fire, he should sacrifice the sacrificial vessels with the mantra: "To the heavenly world, svāhā! Having consigned the fire into himself with the mantra: "This is thy womb, seasonable," and having gone to the Dakṣiṇāgni fire, he should sacrifice the mortar and pestle with the mantra: "This is Agni Purīṣya. Having consigned the fire into himself with the mantra: "This is thine," and having gone to the Gārhapatya fire, he should sacrifice the two kindling woods (araṇi) with the mantra: "This is Agni Gṛhapati. Having consigned the fire into himself with the mantra: "This is thine," and standing in the middle of the altar, he should mutter the hymn: "The Puruṣa of a thousand heads. Having worshipped [the waters] with the mantra: "Born from the waters," and having worshipped himself with the mantra: "I know," he should perform the offering of funeral cakes (piṇḍa) to the ancestors. "In the eastern direction, may the ancestors together with Indra be satisfied. Having worshipped with the mantra: "The protector Indra," he should perform the offering of funeral cakes to the ancestors. "In the southeastern direction, may the ancestors together with Agni be satisfied. Having worshipped with the mantra: "Agni is the head," he should perform the offering of funeral cakes to the ancestors. "In the southern direction, may the ancestors together with Yama be satisfied. Having worshipped with the mantra: "Thou art Yama," he should perform the offering of funeral cakes to the ancestors. "In the southwestern direction, may the ancestors together with Nirṛti be satisfied. Having worshipped with the mantra: "This is for thee, O Nirṛti," he should perform the offering of funeral cakes to the ancestors. "In the western direction, may the ancestors together with Varuṇa be satisfied. Having worshipped with the mantra: "For wide indeed is King Varuṇa," he should perform the offering of funeral cakes to the ancestors. "In the northwestern direction, may the ancestors together with Vāyu be satisfied. Having worshipped with the mantra: "O Vāyu, a hundred," he should perform the offering of funeral cakes to the ancestors. "In the northern direction, may the ancestors together with Soma be satisfied. Having worshipped with the mantra: "King Soma," he should perform the offering of funeral cakes to the ancestors. "In the northeastern direction, may the ancestors together with Īśāna be satisfied. Having worshipped with the mantra: "Īśāna," he should perform the offering of funeral cakes to the ancestors. "In the upward direction, may the ancestors together with Brahmā be satisfied. Having worshipped with the mantra: "Brahman was born," he should perform the offering of funeral cakes to the ancestors. "In the downward direction, may the ancestors together with the serpents be satisfied. Having worshipped with the mantra: "Homage be to the serpents," he should perform the offering of funeral cakes to the ancestors. (4.26)

Having offered the rice-ball (piṇḍa) and said, "May the kinsmen rejoice," one should take a hundred darbha grass blades and follow the procedure stated by Śaunaka, beginning with the formula, "From now on, you are the sacrificial cord (yajñopavīta)," and so forth. || 4.27 ||
Kapila states a specific rule for one who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*):

"If an *āhitāgni* has duly performed the *prājāpatya* sacrifice with his entire property as the sacrificial fee, he should consign the fires into himself with the mantra, 'This is your womb, fit for the season. Standing in the middle of the altar, having meditated upon the divine Nārāyaṇa—Viṣṇu, the wearer of yellow garments, bearing the conch, discus, and mace, adorned with a crown, armlets, and earrings, and full of grace—he should, with the permission of his guru, utter the *praiṣa* mantra. (4.28)
The son of Jamadagni said:
"A twice-born man, having performed the twelve-day rite known as the *Ṛta*, and having duly heard the meaning of the Vedas, may renounce his worldly life free from debt. (4.29)
Having shaved off his hair and beard at a sacred body of water,
he observes a fast while restraining his speech and remains awake through the night on the festival day.

Having performed the sacrifice to Prajāpati, in which all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee, and having consigned the sacred fires into oneself with the verse, "O Agni, those [fires] of yours... (RV 8.44.16).
The best of the twice-born should stand within the sacrificial altar reciting "I am the tree";
for the Veda is indeed the tree of Brahman, and it leads one to the state of Brahman.
One should instruct a son or a disciple, saying, "Speak the truth.
One should never seek alms by means of such instructions or proclamations.
Saying "Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ, I have renounced," he recites it three times in a whisper, three times in a medium voice, and three times aloud.
"For the gods are indeed true in three ways," so say those who discourse on Brahman. || 4.34 ||
"A mendicant should carry the triple staff made of bamboo, which consists of three parts:
the wise one [should restrain] the mental, the verbal, and the physical. (4.35)
With the mantra "Agni is the deity, Gāyatrī is the metre," the twice-born mendicant should take a vessel made of gourd or wood;
he should take a water-strainer with the verse "Prājāpatya.
Purified by that, the sage, equipped with the strainer, should drink the water.
He who offers the "fearless palms" with the words, "Svāhā to all beings," shall never experience fear from any being. (4.37)
Having gone from the village toward the eastern or northern direction while maintaining silence,
one should perform an ablution according to the rules and practice six breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma).

Then he offers the sacrificial thread into the water with the mantra, "bhūḥ svāhā. He takes up the triple staff with the mantra, "sakhā me gopāya. In the *Pariśiṣṭa*, there is a statement regarding the rule for the disposal of the previous sacrificial thread. 4.39.
Now, renunciation in times of distress is described. Regarding this, Jābāli says:
"If one should be afflicted by illness, he may renounce either by word or even by mind;
this is the path of the Brahmins, which has been followed here. (JU 68–69) 4.41.
Aṅgiras says: "For those who are afflicted by illness, there is no specific rule nor indeed any ritual action;
for the sick, renunciation (saṃnyāsa) is ordained as consisting merely of a formal injunction. (4.42)
Likhita said:
"But he who meets death through tigers, fire, robbers, snakes, and the like, or he who,
afflicted by a great disease, is about to die— "
At that very moment, one should perform renunciation, whether according to the prescribed rule or even without it.
Even one whose life-breath is situated in the throat, if they should say "I have renounced," by that act their ancestors are delivered and they themselves stand upon the path of liberation. (4.44)
The twice-born man who has renounced all and is freed from the risk of life,
yet returns again, and those who carry on worldly dealings with him—
all of them are outcastes by their actions; no atonement for them is seen.
Having renounced and crossed over calamity, he should then approach a guru;
having received the mantras and taken up the triple staff and other requisites, he should practice yoga. (4.46)
When their destruction has occurred again, having himself taken them up with the mantra, "Go to the ocean, svāhā! he should cast the lost items into the water;
and he should train in the duties of an ascetic according to the words of the written [scripture]. || 4.47 ||

For those who have fallen into adversity, a threefold renunciation has been taught, as it is said that it may be performed either according to the rule or even contrary to the rule. If one is somehow able to act, one should perform it according to the rule. If one is unable, one should utter the mere formal dismissal with the words, "I have renounced. If one is unable even for that, one should effect the abandonment of attachment through the mind alone. Such is the procedure for renunciation in times of distress. 4.48
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Procedure for Renunciation," in the *Yatidharmasamuccaya*. 4.49.
The fifth book:
The Procedure for Primary Duties.
Now, the primary duties of ascetics (yatis) are stated. Regarding this, Uśanas says:

The student (brahmacārin) is of two kinds: the temporary (upakurvāṇa) and likewise the lifelong (naiṣṭhika). The forest-dweller (vānaprastha) is also recorded as being of two types: one who remains with his wife and one who has renounced his wife. || 5.2 ||

There are two kinds of renunciants: the monk-renunciant (*bhikṣu-saṃnyāsī*) and likewise the Vedic renunciant (*veda-saṃnyāsika*). Householders are divided into many types, such as the *śālīna* and others. (5.3)
Manu has declared that there are exactly two divisions among the four stages of life. Now hear about the one among them who is a mendicant renunciant (bhikṣu-saṃnyāsī). 5.4.

A twice-born man, detached from enjoyments both here and in the hereafter, should go forth into the religious life after performing the Vaiśvānarī sacrifice, in which all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee. (5.5)
Thus, a twofold division of the wandering mendicant (parivrājaka) has been accepted. However, some describe a fourfold classification:
"The mendicants are of four kinds: the kuṭīcaka, the bahūdaka, the haṃsa, and the paramahaṃsa; each subsequent one is superior to the preceding. || 5.6–5.7 ||

Some say that even this is established by the *Pāñcarātra* and established by the *Sāṃkhya*, but not established by the Veda (5.8). Āpastamba refutes this position: "Some [teach] liberation from everything: having abandoned both truth and falsehood, pleasure and pain, as well as these Vedas and this world and the next, one should seek the Self. When it is realized, there is the attainment of security. That is contradicted by the scriptures. If there were the attainment of security upon realization, one would not experience suffering even here [in this life]. By this, the other [state] is explained" [ĀpDh 2.21.12–17] (5.9).
"Āhātrins, some with topknots as heard of, and some shaven-headed mendicants;
Brahmins are of four kinds of mendicants, and all are indeed triple-staffed (tridaṇḍins). (5.10)
Parāśara said:

In this regard, there are four kinds of wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*): the *kuṭīcaka*, the *bahūdaka*, the *haṃsa*, and the *paramahaṃsa*. Among them, those called *kuṭīcakas* have their huts built by sons and others; having abandoned desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy, they perform renunciation according to the rules. Wearing the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*), the water-strainer (*jalapavitra*), and ochre robes, they are devoted to bathing, purification, sipping water (*ācamana*), recitation (*japa*), study of the Vedas (*svādhyāya*), celibacy, and meditation. At the time of begging for alms, they consume only enough food for sustenance from their sons and others, and dwelling constantly in that very hut, they liberate themselves. Those called *bahūdakas* wear the triple staff, the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), the eyelash-strainer (*pakṣmapavitra*), the sling (*śikyaka*), and ochre robes. Understanding the meaning of the Vedānta, they wander for alms among Brahmins of virtuous conduct and liberate themselves. Those called *haṃsas* carry the triple staff, the water-strainer, the sling, and the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). Subsisting on cow urine and cow dung, they perform vows such as fasting for one night, three nights, a month, or a fortnight, as well as the *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, *sāntapana*, *mahāsāntapana*, *parāka*, and *tulāpuruṣa* penances. Dwelling in holy regions abounding in cattle and twice-born men, they liberate themselves. Those called *paramahaṃsas* carry the triple staff, the water-strainer, the sling, and the sacred thread, and wear both an inner and an outer garment. They stay for only one night in a village and five nights in cities, holy places, or lodgings. At the time of begging, having made a bowl out of withered leaves, they take alms only from the family of a Brahmin and eat exactly eight morsels. Devoted to the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*), they dwell constantly at the foot of a tree and liberate themselves.
In this regard, Manu speaks concerning those who have renounced the Vedas:
"This dharma has been taught for other ascetics of restrained self;
now learn the yoga of action for those who have renounced the Vedas" (MDh 6.86). 5.12.
In certain regions, three verses are recited at this point: "Having discharged the three debts... [and so forth].
"The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the mendicant—these four distinct stages of life originate from the householder. (5.13)
All these, when practiced in succession according to the scriptures, lead a Brahmin who acts as prescribed to the supreme goal. (5.14)
And among all these, according to the injunctions of Vedic revelation,
the householder is said to be the best, for he indeed supports these other three.
Just as all rivers and streams find their resting place in the ocean, even so do all those in the various stages of life find their support in the householder. 5.16
Moreover, this tenfold duty must always be practiced with effort by the twice-born belonging to these four stages of life. (5.17)
Fortitude, forbearance, self-restraint, non-stealing, purity, control of the senses, modesty, knowledge, truthfulness, and freedom from anger—this tenfold set is the characteristic of dharma. 5.18
Those Brahmins who thoroughly study the ten signs of Dharma and, having studied them, live according to them, attain the supreme goal. (5.19)
For a twice-born man who practices the Dharma characterized by the ten marks and has heard the Vedāntas according to the injunctions, may renounce his worldly life free from debt. (5.20)
"Having renounced all actions and cast off the defects of action, being self-restrained and practicing the Veda, he may dwell happily under the sovereignty of his sons. (5.21)

"In this very same way, some say there is the *kuṭīcaka*. The mention of "signs" (*cihna*) in the phrase "the ten signs of dharma" is for the purpose of indicating their subordinate status with respect to the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-dharma*). Therefore, the intended meaning is that all those belonging to the stages of life, while performing their respective duties, must be endowed with these ten qualities beginning with fortitude (*dhṛti*). (5.22)
In that regard, the duty of the hermitage for renunciants who are monks is stated. Kratu said:
"Sāṃkhya, Yoga, devotion to Hari, vigilance, and dispassion—this is the essence; therefore, the remaining duty of the hermitage is so called. (5.23)

This is what is meant: *Sāṃkhya* is the knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*). *Yoga* is either eight-limbed (*aṣṭāṅga*) or six-limbed (*ṣaḍaṅga*). Devotion to Hari (*harer bhaktiḥ*) is the worship of the Lord (*īśvara-upāsana*), that is, affection for the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). *Apramāda* is constant wakefulness. *Virāgatā* is the absence of attachment toward sense objects. Thus said Bṛhaspati:
"He who is attached to the Supreme Self and detached from that which is not the Supreme Self, being completely liberated from all desires, he is fit to subsist on alms. (5.24–25)

"This is the essence; the rest is subsidiary" (5.26). This alone is the primary duty (*pradhāna-dharma*) of the stage of life (*āśrama*). However, "subsidiary duty" (*śeṣa-dharma*)—characterized by the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā-vandana*) and so forth—is merely a duty belonging to the stage of life itself; it is simply the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the *āśrama*. One should be established in that [primary duty], being established in the *āśrama* itself, and not merely established in the duties of the *āśrama*. Ritual activities such as the twilight devotions, having attained the status of being auxiliary members (*aṅga*) of the duties of the *āśrama*, are not themselves the duties of the *āśrama*. Thus Dakṣa says: "One who is devoid of the twilight devotions is eternally impure and unfit for all ritual acts."
Whatever other action one performs, one shall not partake in its fruit. || 5.27 ||
In this regard, Sāṃkhya is being described. Yama said:

"One who knows the twenty-five principles, regardless of which stage of life he is devoted to, and who understands primordial nature (prakṛti) and its transformations (vikāra), is liberated from suffering. (5.28)
The mind, the intellect, the ego, ether, air, fire, water, and earth—these are the eight primary natures (prakṛtis); the other sixteen are the transformations (vikāras). 5.29.
The ear, eye, tongue, nose, and skin; as well as volition;
and sound, form, taste, touch, smell, speech, hands, the anus, the generative organ, and the feet—these are recorded as the sixteen modifications (vikāras). (5.30)
Volition consists of the functions of the internal organs.
The wise call this the twenty-fourfold knowledge;
the twenty-fifth is the unmanifest, and the twenty-sixth is the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama).
Having known this, however, the ascetics with tranquil intellects are liberated. || 5.31 ||
Soundless, tasteless, touchless, formless, devoid of smell, free from suffering, supremely blissful, and pure—that is the supreme abode of Viṣṇu. 5.32.
"Unborn, stainless, tranquil, unmanifest, knowledge, imperishable, without beginning or end—Brahman is that supreme state of Viṣṇu. (5.33)
Bṛhaspati said: This is that supreme being from which all beings repeatedly emerge and into which they enter, just as vessels [arise from and return to] the earth. (5.34)
This is that supreme light; others are like its sparks, scattered among the sun, the moon, fire, lightning, the stars, the planets, and so forth. (5.35)
This is that supreme bliss, whereas other droplets of happiness are those which the meritorious— Brahmās, Indras, ancestors, and humans— drink.
The Lord abides as all things through the state of both multiplicity and unity;
yet this is supreme unity, the highest existence, and the ultimate goal.
Having begun thus, it concludes at the end:
"He who knows Brahman in this way is liberated from saṃsāra. (5.38)
Śaunaka said: A wise man should recognize these five as the great elements (mahābhūtas): earth, water, fire, air, and space. 5.39.
One should know that the ear, the eye, the sense of touch, the tongue, and the nose—these five alone are the organs of perception within this body. (5.40)
The mind, the intellect, the self, and likewise the unmanifest—these four are said to be superior to the senses. Thus they have been described. (5.41)
A wise person should always recognize these five objects of the senses: sound, form, touch, taste, and likewise smell. (5.42)
The hands, the feet, the generative organ, the tongue, and likewise the anus—these are the five organs of action always present in this body. (5.43)
These twenty-four principles have indeed been described;
having realized the self as the twenty-fifth principle, which is devoid of them, one is liberated.
Knowing which, the ascetics whose intellects are at peace are liberated—this is that supreme secret, this is that highest imperishable. 5.45

"Soundless, tasteless, touchless," and so forth—this is precisely the reading in the Yājñavalkya-smṛti. In this same way, elsewhere in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, in the Mānava-dharmaśāstra and other such works, as well as in the Vedānta texts, the knowledge of reality denoted by the word "Sāṃkhya" is to be sought. 5.46.
Now, the yoga of the reality of knowledge (jñānatattva) is described. It is said to have eight limbs in the Pātañjala [Yogaśāstra].

The eight limbs are restraint (*yama*), observance (*niyama*), posture (*āsana*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and absorption (*samādhi*). Among these, non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness are the restraints. Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord are the observances. Posture is that which is steady and comfortable. Breath control is the cessation of the movement of the vital breath. Withdrawal of the senses is the imitation by the senses of the nature of the mind itself when they are not in contact with their respective objects. Concentration is the binding of the mind to a particular place. Meditation is the one-pointed flow of cognition toward that object. Absorption is that same state when it manifests only the object and is, as it were, devoid of its own form.

Among these eight limbs, withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and the others are the essential limbs (*svarūpāṅga*), like the hands and other members of Devadatta; the others are limbs by virtue of being instrumental means (*sādhanatvena*). In the event of a conflict between an internal and an external limb, the internal limbs alone must be maintained. || 5.48 ||

And so the Blessed Vyāsa said: "The wise man should always strive for the restraints (yamas), even at the expense of the other [observances]; for one who fails to practice the restraints while merely devoting himself to the observances (niyamas) falls. (5.49)
These limbs are explained in various ways in the Smṛtis. Among them, first is the sacrifice (kratu).
Having stated, "Or by the limbs of yoga, such as restraint (yama) and the rest," he says:
Fortitude, forbearance, self-control, non-stealing, purity, restraint of the senses, modesty, learning, truthfulness, and freedom from anger—this is the characteristic of dharma. 5.50.

Non-violence, equanimity, non-stealing, patience, self-restraint, tranquility, and so forth; contentment, freedom from malice, absence of deceit, and lack of enmity—these are remembered as the *yamas*. (5.51)

Discrimination, hypocrisy, indolence, attachment, the fruit of action, fear, possession, and the sense of "mine"—these, as well as renunciation and marriage, are recorded as the stages of life. (5.52)
The renunciation of these is what is meant by "renunciation.
The conquests of desire, passion, duality, sleep, delusion, hunger, evil thoughts, hatred, egoism, and greed are known as self-restraints (saṃyama). (5.53)
Humility, virtuous conduct, faith, yoga, right behavior, learning, ritual action, equanimity, gentleness, steadfastness, and supreme dispassion—these are the higher restraints (yamāḥ). || 5.54 ||
They know that silence consists of non-seeking, lack of volitional thought, non-touching, and non-seeing; it is meditation, clarity, sweetness, and self-restraint. (5.55)
Śaunaka said: Ten vows have indeed been prescribed for all ascetics:
non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness. (5.56)
Freedom from anger, service to the teacher, purity, avoidance of misconduct, and the avoidance of negligence in the activities of speech, mind, and body—thus [it is said]. (5.57)

Baudhāyana says: Now, these are the observances (vratas): non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, avoidance of sexual intercourse, and renunciation. There are five secondary observances (upavratas) as well: freedom from anger, service to the teacher, vigilance, purity, and purity of food. [BDh 2.18.2–3] || 5.58 ||
Yama said: Now King Yama, the son of Aditi, declared the prescribed duties for the self-purified ascetics who have renounced the Vedas. 5.59
Non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, celibacy, austerity, sacred learning, non-stealing, and fidelity—dharma is traditionally said to be tenfold. (5.60)
Austerity is tenfold because it is divided according to the distinctions of speech, mind, and body.
Contentment, service to the teacher, vigilance, forbearance, compassion, silence, purity of food, and cleanliness are the eight vows. (5.61)

Surely, non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) is also differentiated according to the types of violence (*hiṃsā*).
