And violence is of ten kinds: namely, causing agitation, causing distress, causing pain, drawing blood, backbiting, depriving of happiness, transgression, restriction, forbidding what is beneficial, and killing. (5.62) Furthermore, Vṛddha-Jābāli speaks of other less well-known varieties: "The killer, the one who consents, the butcher, the buyer and seller, the preparer, the server, and the eater—these eight are slayers. (5.63)
"Vāyu has spoken the truth;
'An untruth joined with righteousness does no harm,' so say the wise.
Nevertheless, that must not be said, for even such a consequence would be terrible. (5.64)
And he himself has stated non-stealing:
"A mendicant who desires righteousness must not engage in false speech, nor should he ever commit theft, even when fallen into distress. (5.65)
Bṛhaspati has declared the breach of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) to consist of:
remembering, speaking of, playing with, looking at, secret conversation, intention, determination, and even the actual performance of the act. (5.66)
The wise declare this to be sexual union with its eight components; celibacy is the opposite of this, and it likewise possesses these same eight characteristics. (5.67)
The author of the *Aparigraha* says:
One should not speak conditioned speech; one should act like a fool or like one who is mute.
One should not accumulate wealth, nor even a measure of food intended for another time. (5.68)
Purity will be explained further on by Garga [see 6.5]. Regarding self-study (*svādhyāya*), Yama says:
"A mendicant (*yati*) who is weary from meditation should always pass the time with recitation;
when weary from recitation, he should meditate again, and when weary from meditation, he should recite again. (5.70)
The four *pākayajña* sacrifices, even when accompanied by the *vidhiyajña*, are all not worth a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*). (5.71)

"Compared to a ritual sacrifice performed according to the rules, the sacrifice of recitation is ten times superior; that which is whispered is a hundredfold more effective, and the mental is declared to be a thousandfold. (5.72)
Manu:

"One should constantly recite the Veda pertaining to sacrifice (*adhiyajña*), as well as that pertaining to the deities (*ādhidaivika*), that pertaining to the self (*ādhyātmika*), and whatever is declared in the Vedānta. (MDh 6.83) By "declared in the Vedānta," the *praṇava* is meant. Āpastamba:
"Releasing his speech only during the private recitation of the Veda," so says [Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 2.21.10].

Bodhāyana states: "One should mutter the mantras of the Agnihotra in the evening and the morning. This is the rule for one who, having been an Agnihotrin, goes forth as a wandering ascetic. || 5.75 ||

Kapila has declared devotion to the Lord (īśvarapraṇidhāna) to consist of: morning ablutions, silent recitation, silence, constant habituation to solitude, prostration, fasting, and likewise devotion toward Viṣṇu as well as toward the teacher. (5.76)
Faith, contact with Brahman, delight in breath-control, and the worship of Viṣṇu at the three divisions of the day are the supreme means for liberation. 5.77
Atri says:

"One should perform worship at the three periods of the day for Viṣṇu and for the gods who have him as their self, including salutations, offerings, and so forth; but not for anyone else whatsoever. (5.78)
Kratu said:
"The Lord, the Blessed Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self, the Great Unborn, the sole ruler of all that is moving and unmoving, is the supreme goal of ascetics. (5.79)
Furthermore, he himself said:
"If one who has taken refuge in another sign of Viṣṇu meditates upon or worships that other, his goal is not attained even in hundreds of millions of kalpas. (5.80)
Moreover, he himself said:
"One should perform worship with the Puruṣasūkta and praise with hymns from the secret portions of the Vedas;
one should meditate on the single syllable 'Om' as the sacrifice, and likewise recite it."
The Trika and the Puruṣasūkta, along with the Catuṣka, [are accomplished] through breath-restraints (prāṇasaṃyama). || 5.81 ||
The "triad" consists of the *praṇava*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *gāyatrī*. These same three, together with the *śiras*, constitute the "tetrad. Regarding the seat (*āsana*), Śaṅkha says:
"In an empty house, a temple, a cave, or a mountain glen—wherever the intellect finds delight, there one should sit with a tranquil mind. (5.82)
Having assumed a steady posture according to the path taught in the Yoga scriptures, one should constantly practice yoga, especially during the junctions of the day (saṃdhyās). || 5.83 ||
Viśvāmitra said:
Then, on a delightful site free from depressions and elevations, one should arrange layers of kuśa grass, deerskins, and fine cloths, each placed upon the other. 5.84.
Having assumed the lotus posture (padmāsana) right there, one should keep the limbs even;
then, being composed, one should perform breath-control (prāṇāyāma) for as long as time permits.

Śaṅkha states the definitions of breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), and meditation (dhyāna): "By means of breath controls one should burn away defects; by means of concentrations, sins; by withdrawal of the senses, attachments; and by meditation, qualities that do not belong to the Lord. (5.86)
One should recite the Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras three times while restraining the breath; that is called prāṇāyāma. (5.87)
Indeed, the restraint of the senses is proclaimed as withdrawal (pratyāhāra);
the restraint of the mind is designated as concentration (dhāraṇā) by those who know it. (5.88)
Through the yoga of meditation upon Brahman, there is the vision of the God of gods;
meditation has been declared, and I shall now explain the auspicious yoga of meditation. 5.89
Dhyāna is samādhi; indeed, the practice of dhyāna is dhyāna itself. Thus it is said: "All deities reside in the heart; the vital breaths (prāṇas) are established in the heart;
the luminaries and the sun are in the heart; everything is established in the heart. (5.90)
Making one's own body the lower friction-stick and the *praṇava* the upper friction-stick, through the practice of the churning of meditation, one shall behold Viṣṇu abiding in the heart. (5.91)
The intention is that one should meditate on Brahman by means of the syllable *oṃ*, having abandoned other objects such as sound and the rest. And so says the Śruti:
"With 'Om,' one should yoke the Self. (5.92) Likewise:
"Release other words," having said this, he says:
"Meditate on the Self as 'Om' alone. (MuU 2.2.6)
"One should not meditate on many sounds" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.21). And Yama said: "Two Brahmans are to be known: the Brahman of Sound and that which is the Supreme Brahman."
One who is proficient in the Brahman of sound attains the supreme Brahman.
The *śabdabrahman* is the *praṇava*. Yama is the conch. The moon is situated in the center of the sun; in its center is the fire;
in the center of the splendor is the *tattva*; and in the center of the *tattva* resides the Imperishable One (*acyuta*). (5.95)
Viśvāmitra said: As long as the mind remains tranquil, one should restrain the consciousness and meditate upon a blazing solar disc in the center of the heart. (5.96)
In its center, one should contemplate the god Acyuta— the Moon, the Fire, and the Great Brahman with a lofty crest—
within the lotus of the heart, for the sake of pacifying all obstacles.
One should recollect [the deity] resembling pure crystal, with four arms;
thereafter, unwearied, one should meditate upon the partless Brahman preceded by Brahmā. 5.98.
The meaning is that [the name] begins with "Brahman" and begins with the "Praṇava," namely "Nārāyaṇa.
It is the entire reality, the essence of all things, known as Viṣṇu, the supreme state;
it is stainless, free from affliction, and should be repeatedly established within one's own mind. (5.99)
That Brahman is indeed myself, the supreme Self that pervades all;
having cast off attachment to sense objects and having restrained the mind within the heart. (5.100)
When one perceives that very supreme state within the disposition of one's own mind,
one should again take up that awakened understanding within the self, the Lord.
The sage should not fall into despondency; he must indeed restrain the mind.
It should be restrained within the heart only until it has reached its dissolution. 5.102
"This is both knowledge and meditation; all other extensive treatises are merely superfluous.
When the senses have been restrained and the mind is free from vibration, the pure Self shines forth in the form of awakening, undisturbed. (5.103)

Having written this and having reflected upon the meanings of the Purāṇas and the Vedāntas, one should remain established in devotion and always meditate upon Viṣṇu in the heart, whether with form or as the formless. 5.104.
But this, which is the vision of the Self through yoga among all dharmas, is supreme; one should oppose everything else and abandon it, except for what is indispensable. (5.105)

Bṛhaspati said: Forbearance is a sacred ford, self-control is a sacred ford, restraint of the senses is a sacred ford, compassion toward all beings is a sacred ford, and meditation is the unsurpassed sacred ford. (5.106)
These are the five sacred fords (tīrthas), while truth is always the sixth;
they abide everywhere within the body, and one should perform one's ablutions in them.
A person is not liberated from sins by bathing at Puṣkara, nor at the Gaṅgā, nor in Kurujāṅgala, as one is liberated by bathing in the Kṣamā and other such [virtues]. 5.108
Wherever a man whose collection of senses is restrained may dwell,
there is Kurukṣetra, Naimiṣa, and likewise Puṣkara.
For those people who speak with partiality, saying "this is a sacred ford" and "that is not," the journey to sacred fords and its respective fruit are prescribed.
For one who knows that "all is Brahman," there is nothing whatsoever that is not a sacred ford;
he abides in Brahman alone throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
That alone is the supreme dharma; all others are but its droplets.
Sacrifice, charity, austerity, and the Vedas exist in the form of sacred fords.
Kratu praises yoga and its constituent limbs—prāṇāyāma, pratyāhāra, dhāraṇā, dhyāna, and samādhi:
"When the cosmic egg is filled with jewels and offered to those who know the Vedas, that fruit is seen to be perishable; but the remembrance of Viṣṇu even once is not. (5.113)
Those who stand amidst the five fires or in the midst of water, and those who dwell in the open air inhaling smoke—
these are not worth even a sixteenth part of one established in breath control (prāṇāyāma).

Through subsisting on bark, leaves, flowers, vegetables, water, fruits, roots, and air for twelve years, there is purification of the principles (tattva-śuddhi); through withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), it occurs in one year.
One who desires the welfare of the body, senses, mind, and vital breaths may remain steady;
however, in the concentration of yoga, it is difficult for those of unrefined self to remain steady.
It is possible to remain for even a moment in fire, in snow, in battle, in Vedic study, in austerity, or in a vow;
but it is not at all possible to remain for even an instant in a place that destroys one's merit.

In this world, those people who endure leprosy, fever, and poison-induced diseases, and who remain steadfast through yoga despite these afflictions that are difficult to bear in the world, [attain success]. (5.118)
For the yogin who has abandoned all bonds, who is pure, established in samādhi,
and who is like the stainless sky— that is indeed the ultimate state, the goal of Viṣṇu.
Those whose splendors are like those of the sun, moon, and fire, and who are as pure as clear crystal,
cross to the further shore of darkness when Hari is gratified by the limbs of yoga.
The fire of yoga burns away all defects born of mind, speech, and body arising from ignorance and negligence, just as a flame consumes a heap of cotton.
Endowed with devotion, one should always behold Hari by means of the lamp of yoga. (5.121)
Hārīta has stated that the culmination of yoga is as follows: "Meditation is said to last only so long as the bliss of self-attainment [is not reached];
thereafter, one should perform the actions prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti. (5.122)
Bṛhaspati has stated that for one who is unable to perform meditation on the partless [Brahman], meditation should be practiced as follows:
"One who is unable to perform meditation upon the formless Brahman alone should, having been purified by breath control (prāṇāyāma), practice meditation on its embodied form. (5.123)
One should recite the Gāyatrī together with the Vyahṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras three times while restraining the breath; that is called Prāṇāyāma. (5.124)

One should burn away the defects arising from mind, speech, and body by means of breath-control (prāṇāyāma); one should abandon attachments through withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), and ungodly qualities through meditation (dhyāna). 5.125.
Just as the accumulated impurity of metallic ores is cast off when they are being smelted, so too is the defect produced by the senses consumed by breath control (prāṇāyāma). 5.126
One should practice the retention, obstruction, and release of the breath three times each;
by meditating upon Brahmā, Keśava, and Śambhu, one shall be liberated from bondage. (5.127)
One should meditate on the Grandfather (Brahmā) as red, Viṣṇu as having the luster of a blue lotus,
and Śambhu as white, three-eyed, and the savior from the ocean of worldly existence.
The ascetic who thus constantly remains devoted to the practice of yoga, having attained the entirety of dispassion, goes to the supreme goal. (5.129)
Vāsudeva is the supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self, who consists of the universe;
these forms of his indeed differ in three ways according to their designations.
One should daily contemplate with devotion Nārāyaṇa, the source of the universe, Hari, the Lord of all worlds, the cause of all causes. (5.131)
He holds the conch and the discus, is gentle, has four arms, and wears a crown;
his chest bears the Śrīvatsa mark and the Kaustubha gem, and he is adorned with divine jewels.
Clad in yellow garments, with noble limbs and a face resembling the serene moon,
he was dark-complexioned, lotus-eyed, and wore shimmering makara-shaped earrings.
It immediately destroys all torment like a rising monsoon cloud;
it consists entirely of splendor, is meritorious, and is a refuge for those seeking shelter.
"One should meditatively contemplate the lotus-eyed Nārāyaṇa, who is free from ailment, with the mind through the sixteen proper services with great effort. (5.135)
Dattātreya said:
"The Blessed One, Puruṣottama, is worshipped with eighteen types of offerings by those seeking liberation, both in the heart, in the fire, and likewise in the sun. (5.136)
Worship with *palāśa* leaves and lotus flowers is recommended for Hari.
Having thus worshipped Nārāyaṇa, the Lord of Gods, without weariness... (5.137)
The yogi, composed through the syllable Om, should contemplate that form;
or, as appropriate, he should constantly hold it with form in his mind. (5.138)
The Person, whose color is like the sun, with eyes resembling lotuses,
holding a conch, a discus, and a mace in his hands, and clad in bright yellow garments.
Adorned with a crown, beautiful armlets, bracelets, and other ornaments,
the Lord of Śrī has the Śrīvatsa mark upon his chest, and his breast is resplendent with the Kaustubha gem.
Or one may meditate on Hṛṣīkeśa as dark-complexioned, the lotus-eyed, the infallible Acyuta, seated or indeed standing within the pericarp of the heart-lotus. (5.141)
In this way, one should contemplate the God, the Great Lord of all worlds, the destroyer of all afflictions, who abides as both cause and effect. (5.142)
Śaṅkha states the fruit of the practice of yoga:
"The yogi, firmly established in all the Yoga-śāstras and Vedāntas, should always contemplate Brahman through those various specific attributes. (5.143)
Without becoming weary again and again, he attains that firm light—
the gentle, blissful, non-dual state which has been revealed many times.
Having attained it through identification with that, he reaches supreme liberation.
Yājñavalkya said:
Among the acts of sacrifice, conduct, self-restraint, non-violence, charity, and the study of sacred texts, this indeed is the supreme dharma: that one perceives the Self through yoga. (5.145)
Viśvāmitra said:
"For one who meditates in this manner, that yogi established in Brahman, the non-dual supreme Brahman—the bliss of Sāṃkhya—shines forth. (5.146)
Liberation has been declared for the wise through the reality that has been revealed;
it is not obtained by anyone else who is devoid of yoga and devoid of spiritual action. (5.147)
Therefore, action must be performed day by day at the proper time;
and that action, joined with knowledge, must be performed by those who desire liberation. 5.148
Bṛhaspati said:
For one who contemplates in this way, the latent impression of ignorance departs, and the rising of the lamp of knowledge occurs, just as darkness vanishes at the rising of the sun. (5.149)
One should effect the purification of the impure mind by means of all this;
but when that [mind] has become stainless, there is absorption into Brahman, and not otherwise. (5.150)
Medhātithi describes the nature of liberation:
"The liberated one attains the Supreme, just as rivers reach the ocean;
having become that which is called 'That' and being absorbed in That, he is not born again in this world" (5.151).
For he is indeed the Self of all that pertains to the elements and the divine, as well as of the sacrifice and that which pertains to the inner self. 5.152
He is Brahmā, he is Śiva, Viṣṇu, Śakra; he is the Lord of Day, Yama, Hutāśa, Nirṛti, Vāyu, and Īśāna, the sovereign of all beings.

"The Vedas, the sacrifices, as well as the gods, the sacrificial animals, the priestly fees and so forth, faith and the rest, the oblation, time, ritual action, the agent, fortitude, and the injunction— he is the soul of all, the Lord of all beings, and the abode of all. (5.154)
Regarding Sāṃkhya-yoga and its fruit, Kratu said:

"One should purify the organs of action along with the mind and the intellect through knowledge; one should purify one's mental state through purification itself, and [discern] knowledge and ignorance by the word of the guru. (5.155)
The queen is the intellect (buddhi), the minister is the quality (guṇa), and the doorkeeper is the mind (manas);
one should appoint the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) as the commander-in-chief by virtue of its self-conceit. (5.156)
The lords of ten villages, without their own volition, [perceive] that great city composed of the five elements and joined with the three coverings. 5.157
Seated upon the throne of the sovereignty of yoga, the person stands like a king;
having known everything, he beholds the inequality of the qualities (guṇas) like a witness. (5.158)
Free from conceptualization, imagination, thought, fear, and distraction, [he perceives] the connection, as well as the meanings and properties based on place, genus, and quality. (5.159)
"Having abandoned all states of being, one should contemplate 'I am the Real.
Having become always alone by day and night, one should reflect upon this in the mind.
Then, through the destruction of passion, the Self enters into the Supreme at that very moment. (5.160)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Rule for Primary Duties," in the *Yatidharmasamuccaya*. 5.161.
The Sixth Book: The Daily and Nocturnal Duties.

Now, the daily and nocturnal duties of ascetics (*yatins*) are being described. Regarding this, whatever has not been explicitly stated but is required should be understood from the rules for religious students (*brahmacārins*).

"And this is not in conflict with others," because of this permission [GDh 3.10]. Even there, if it is unavailable, it should be taken from the duties of a householder. And so says the venerable Vyāsa:
"Those duties of all the stages of life which are not mutually contradictory..."
"May they all attain commonality with respect to all stages of life. (6.2)
Viśvāmitra said:

Having risen at the time of dawn and performed purification according to the rules, he should then, without sloth, rinse his teeth with a tooth-stick and perform the ceremonial sipping of water (ācamana), avoiding the forbidden lunar days. 6.3.
Having performed his bath, he should mutter [the prayers] until the sun is seen;
"Arise, O Brahman," and so forth, is declared to be the mantra for rising.
Garga says:

Now we shall explain the rules for the purification, restraint, cleanliness, and atonement of the monks. First among these is the purification after urination. Having applied three applications of clay to fill [the crevices], one should wash the penis with four [applications of clay], the left hand with twelve, and both hands with eight applications of clay. Having thus performed the purification of the penis and urine as prescribed, one should thereafter perform the purification of the anus. One handful of clay should be applied first, a second and a third each half the size of the previous. Having thus performed the purification of the anus with twenty applications of clay according to the stated sequence, one should wash the left hand with double that amount (forty), and both hands with twenty-eight. Having washed the feet with three applications of clay and having sipped water (ācamana) and performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), one should sip water again.

If one performs purification with sand in the absence of clay, one should perform it twice as much. A healthy monk must not neglect purification; by neglecting purification, a transgression occurs. To remove that transgression, he should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and then sip water again. 6.6.
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, one should meditate daily upon the Supreme Self in the heart with the mantra: "Vasu, Aṇu, Vibhu. (6.7)
Then, having performed the necessary duties and first taking up earth,
he should perform fourfold purification according to what is prescribed for a householder;
thereafter, taking [the earth], he should enter the water with his clothes on.
Devala says:
One should cleanse the four signs [of the anus] using three finger-joints of the fingers;
when it is filled with earth, that is remembered as the single prescribed measure of earth.
The left hand [should be washed] with twelve [applications of clay], and both hands joined together with eight;
thereafter, one should perform the purification of the anus with twenty applications of clay to the anus.
The first handful should be given, and the subsequent ones half that size;
there are forty [grains] in the left hand, and twenty-eight in both hands together.
And if there is sand on one foot, he should wash it three times; if on both feet, twice as many times.
Having sipped water twice, or having sipped water thrice, he should again perform the sipping of water for the vital breaths. (6.12)
He himself says:
"One should always take earth before voiding feces or urine;
but having finished, one should enter the water while still wearing one's clothes. (6.13)
Jamadagni said:
"The purification for the day is one thing, and that prescribed for the night is another;
it is otherwise when afflictions such as illness and the like occur, as has been stated. (6.14)
Half of the purification prescribed for the day is ordained for the night; for one who is ill, it shall be half of that, and for one traveling on a road, half of that again. (6.15)
Devala says:

Whether it be one, two, or three [restraints], a practitioner of yoga should perform breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) upon urinating or defecating, taking into account the place, time, and other such factors. 6.16.
He himself says: "In meditation, in the worship of the deity, in eating, in cleaning the teeth, in necessary duties, and in bathing—in these six instances, silence is prescribed. (6.17)
The wind;
one whose head is covered up to the ears; while traveling in a vehicle on water;
standing with unwashed feet; speaking; or even having one's topknot untied.
Without the sacred thread, even one who has sipped water for purification remains impure. (6.18)
Devala says: After purging, vomiting, voiding feces or urine, or at the two junctions of day and night (saṃdhyā),
one should bathe and then perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) while looking toward the sun.
Prāṇāyāmas performed at night are prescribed with a single *praṇava*; at midday, they are performed with one [recitation]. A mendicant established in the *kāṣṭha* stage should not rinse his mouth.
Garga says:
A student and an ascetic shall not purify their internal organ (the mind).
By purifying the internal organ, those two should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (6.21)
Then, having performed the cleaning of the teeth, one should perform the bath. Kratu said:

"The ascetic, the yogi, the celibate student, the centenarian, the speaker of truth, the observer of vows, the virtuous woman, and the person of a charitable disposition—these are always pure when they have bathed. (6.22)
One should not perform the preliminary purification nor bathe; rather, the Brahma-bath is prescribed.

For the elderly and the infirm, one may use warm water, or the limbs of Yoga beginning with Yama, or the Varuna-bath using mantras containing the word "water"; this the ascetic (yati) should always perform.
Dakṣa said:
When the time of dawn has arrived, having performed purification according to the rules, one should then perform the ritual bath preceded by the cleaning of the teeth. (6.24)
The body is utterly impure, endowed with nine openings;
it flows [with secretions] day and night. Morning bathing is its purification. (6.25)
Bathing at dawn, whether before the morning twilight, during it, or after the sun has risen,
is equal to the Prājāpatya penance and destroys all sins.
The Brahmin who, having risen in the morning, performs the twilight ritual bath, removes the sins committed during seven lifetimes within three years. (6.27)
One should meditate upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa during rites such as ritual bathing;
for indeed, the Śruti declares that he is the expiation for every evil deed.
For the virtuous person devoted to bathing, there are ten qualities: beauty, splendor, strength, purity,
longevity, health, and freedom from greed.
The destruction of bad dreams, asceticism, and intelligence. 6.29.

Kapila says: One who is unable to perform the morning bath should wash the area below the navel and, having made his body pure by wiping it with a water-soaked cloth, put on an inner garment and perform the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*). He should always bathe either before or after midday. Then, having sipped water (*ācamya*) and performed three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), he should sip water again. 6.30.
Viśvāmitra says: If one is unable to perform the morning bath, one should perform the Kāpila bath;
if one is incapable even of that, one should perform the mantra-bath. (6.31)
Aṅgiras:
When the time for bathing has arrived, one should cause half of the garment to be worn;
however, at the time of recitation, half of it should be a cloth for wrapping around the waist.

In this manner, one should perform the bath during the three libations (*savana*). The mantras for the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*) are recited with the three verses beginning "ava te heḍa," "ud uttamam," and "dadhikrāvṇo akāriṣam," as well as "āpo hi ṣṭhā. Furthermore, the four verses beginning "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ" and the *Pavamāna-anuvāka* are prescribed for the sprinkling. (6.33)
Now, the sipping of water with mantras (*mantrācamana*). Regarding that, Kratu says:
"Having sipped water with the four [verses], and having sprinkled oneself with the *drupada* and the *aghamarṣaṇa* [hymns] using purified water, one should satiate the ancestors and the gods. (6.34)
The meaning of this is that one should drink water four times with the mantra consisting of exactly four [parts]. Manu says:
"They say that the Gāyatrī, joined with ten *praṇavas*, preceded by the seven *vyāhṛtis*, and accompanied by the *śiras*, is the destroyer of sin. (6.35)
This is the fourfold section containing the secret of the Veda: the *praṇava*, the *vyāhṛtis*, and the *gāyatrī* together with the *śiras*; some say the fourfold consists of these alone. Devala says:
"With this very verse consisting of three feet, along with the *sāghamarṣaṇa* hymn, having sprinkled his limbs with handfuls of water, Viṣṇu should be satiated with the twelve names. (6.36)
A pure ascetic should first perform the libation with twelve names, preceded by the *praṇava* and ending with *namaḥ*, using his right hand for each mantra. (6.37)
"Oṃ, obeisance to Keśava," and so forth. Now follows the libation for the deities and the libation for the ancestors.
Having drawn up water to the depth of a cow's horn, one should satisfy the gods with cupped hands;
thereafter, one should satisfy the ancestors as before, with well-formed cupped hands. (6.38)

The paternal [ancestors] should be offered with the *devatīrtha* [finger-position] while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītin*); at the end, one should utter "mahar" or "namaḥ," and then pronounce "tarpayāmi. || 6.39 ||

*Oṃ bhūs, I satiate. Oṃ bhuvas, I satiate. Oṃ suvas, I satiate. Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvas-mahar-namas, I satiate.* *Oṃ bhūḥ svadhā. Oṃ bhuvaḥ svadhā. Oṃ suvaḥ svadhā. Oṃ bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvas-mahar-namaḥ svadhā.* This [rite] ends with *svadhā*. Having completed the bath and performed three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), one should perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) as before, beginning with the ritual sipping of water (*mantrācamana*). In these five acts, beginning with the sipping of water, the water-strainer (*jalapavitra*) must be employed. If one performs the sipping of water, the sprinkling (*mārjana*), the libations (*tarpaṇa*), the worship of the sun (*ādityopasthāna*), the filling of the water-pot (*kuṇḍikāpūraṇa*), and the recitation of the *Sāvitrī* while a water-strainer is available, yet does so without it, then all of that becomes fruitless for him.
[It] occurs. 6.41. Medhātithi says:

"He should perform with that [water] the sipping (ācamana), as well as the sprinkling (mārjana), the libation (tarpaṇa), the worship of the thousand-rayed one (the sun), and the filling of the water-pot (kuṇḍikā). 6.42.
Gālava said:
That ascetic who does not perform daily cleansing, sipping water, and libations with water-purified [mantras], nor even the worship of the Sun;
All that is fruitless for him; he must then perform an expiation.
Atri: When flowing streams have been drawn out and in clear lakes, water need not be strained with a cloth; it is pure, according to the Śruti. (6.44)
Hārīta says:
Having bathed and sipped water according to the rule, standing or even sitting,
he should hold a water-strainer and a rosary of beads in both hands.

In the same way, having performed the twilight devotion (saṃdhyā) according to the rules from sunrise until the purification made of cow-hair that destroys evil deeds, accompanied by the triple recitation (trikajapya). || 6.46 ||
Having worshipped the Sun with the three verses beginning with "mitrasya carṣaṇīdhṛtaḥ," one should perform worship in the morning and evening with the five verses addressed to Varuṇa.
That ascetic, devoted to the Supreme Self, should offer the *arghya* oblation to Lohitārka three times a day,
and he should also offer it after having eaten.
The service after eating is performed with the *udvaya* mantra during the time for alms;
at sunrise, one should offer the *arghya* with the *sāvitrī* while composed in mind.
When the sun has reached the middle of its course, one should cause the *arghya* to be offered at the conclusion of the recitation.
Devala said:
One should perform the ritual attendance of the Sun at the three junctions of the day;
thereafter, one should circumambulate him and bow with the knees and the head. (6.50)
One should not utter one's own name; one should bow to the Sun.
Then, having performed the libation as before, one should recite [the mantra] properly with a concentrated mind. Thus [ends verse 6.51].
Baudhāyana:
One should worship the evening twilight with verses addressed to Varuṇa, and the morning twilight with verses addressed to Mitra. Śaunaka: [as above].

Having risen from sleep, he should reflect [upon his duties]. Then, having performed the necessary rites, being pure and having sipped water (ācamana), and having first brushed his teeth, he should bathe according to the rules at dawn. Having purified himself with the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā* while reciting the appropriate mantras, facing eastward, he should scatter water upward with the *gāyatrī* mantra. Holding *darbha* grass in his hand, he should practice the *gāyatrī* while standing until sunrise. Then, he should conclude the remainder of the day with recitation (*japa*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and hymns of praise (*stuti*). || 6.53 ||

Kapila says: Having placed his feet firmly on the ground, he should perform his recitation (*japa*), eating, and worship. Then, standing or sitting facing the east with *pavitra* grass in hand, he should recite the three-fold mantra according to his ability, either with the beads of a rosary or with his fingers. At the three junctions of the day (*trisandhya*), he should perform three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*). For purification from the unintentional killing of living beings, he should perform sipping of water (*ācamana*), sprinkling (*mārjana*), libations (*tarpaṇa*), filling the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), and so forth, using water as a *pavitra*. He should perform the ritual attendance upon the Sun (*ādityopasthāna*) with his hands cupped full of water. Thus ends section 6.54.
Having thus performed the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*), one should then practice the yoga previously described. Viśvāmitra says:
"Having performed his bath, he should recite [the mantra] until the sun is seen;
then, in a pleasant, windless place free from depressions and elevations..."

...and so forth (6.55). Having thus performed *yoga* and having accomplished the aforementioned duties for that sacrifice of knowledge (*vidvadyajña*), he should then desist from that *yoga*, perform silent recitation (*japa*), and, if he is one who dwells for only one night in a village, proceed to another village. Regarding this, Śaṅkha says:

"Having meditated slowly and gradually upon the bliss of self-realization as long as possible, one should desist from *yoga* and perform the recitation of the *praṇava* as well as the study of the sacred texts (*svādhyāya*)."
He should dwell elsewhere, moving from village to village; such is the rule. 6.56.
If he does not go to another village, then he should remain seated performing praise, recitation, meditation, and so forth. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati says:
"Having risen before dawn, having performed his necessary duties, and being pure, he should practice the Gāyatrī until the sun is seen. (6.57)
One should spend some portion of the day with breath-control exercises, recitations, meditations, hymns of praise, and with Purāṇas and Vedic texts. 6.58
Thus ends the section on the morning duties. 6.59.
Now the midday ritual is described. Regarding this, Śaunaka says:

"Then, having bathed according to the rules and sipped water (ācamana), having purified himself with the three verses beginning 'āpo hi ṣṭhā mayo bhuvaḥ,' having gone into the water and performed sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) with the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn, having emerged and wrung out his garment, having performed purification of the shanks with earth and water, and having put on another clean loincloth and outer garment, and having sipped water again, he takes a water-purifier (jalapavitra) with the words 'Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar' and offers libations, saying: 'Oṃ bhūḥ, I offer libation. (6.60)

As before, up to the point where he has his hands joined in reverence (as in 6.38). Then, with the two verses "ud u tyaṃ" and "citram," he worships the Āditya. Having performed six breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), he should mutter the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times. Thus says Baudhāyana.

He worships the Āditya with the two verses beginning "ud u tyam citram. "Oṃ" is the Brahman; indeed, this light which shines yonder is the Brahman. This which shines yonder is the Veda; this which shines yonder is that which is to be known (*vedya*). In this very way he satisfies his own self; he pays homage to the self. The self is the Brahman; the self is the light. Then he should repeat the Sāvitrī a thousand times, a hundred times, or an unlimited number of times. Taking the water-purifier with the words "oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ suvar," he takes up water. (BDh 2.17.39–42) || 6.62 ||

Hārīta says: Having bathed and sipped water according to the rule, one should indeed satisfy [the ancestors] with water purified by a strainer, and having done so, one should bow to the Sun while reciting the mantra. (6.63)

The *Kratu*, the hymn "ud u tyaṃ citram," that eye which is wondrous and auspicious in its resolve, the *Puruṣasūkta*, and the Vaiṣṇava hymns— a mendicant, having bathed, should recite these in front of the sun. (6.64)
In the morning and in the evening, he should worship the Sun with mantras addressed to Mitra and Varuṇa;
having eaten in a village during the day, he should wander for alms while reciting the Haṃsa-mantra.
Having purified oneself with the *pāvamānī* and *aghamarṣaṇa* verses, each recited three times in their respective genders,
one should mutter the *gāyatrī* one hundred and eight times using well-purified water.
Viśvāmitra said:
Then, having bathed at midday and being composed, the wise man should recite the Sāvitrī and perform some Vedic chanting. (6.67)
Having recited the Vaiṣṇava, Pāvamāna, Vāruṇa, Raudra, Saura, and Upaniṣadic mantras for the sake of his own purification,
and having performed meditation according to the rule, he should then go about for alms. (6.68)
Hārīta says: Seated, facing east, and observing silence, one should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).
Having recited the Gāyatrī according to one's ability, one should meditate upon the Supreme State.
Then, for the sake of his own constant sustenance, he should practice wandering for alms.
Devala says:
A renunciant (yati), facing the east, should mutter the mantras of the Ṛgveda and other Vedas, as well as the *stokas*;
for there is no time when these are unfit for study, since they are considered his obligatory duty (*nityakarman*). 6.70.
Then one should perform worship of Hari according to the Vedic injunctions;
or, in the absence of Vedic mantras, according to that proclaimed in the Pañcarātra.

Manu: "Whatever living beings a mendicant kills by day or by night unintentionally, for the sake of purification from those acts, he should bathe and perform six breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). (MDh 6.69)

"How should one perform worship? [The answer is: It should be performed with water, either fetched by oneself or brought by others, because there is a prescription for penance regarding the plucking of fruits and flowers [for such purposes], using the *Puruṣasūkta*, the secrets of the Vedas, and other mantras. (6.73) Āpastamba:

"While continuing his private Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), or even ceasing his speech, having obtained his livelihood for sustaining life in the village, he should live without sacrificial fires and without concern for the world beyond. A garment that has been discarded is prescribed for him; some say he may be completely free from all possessions. (6.74)
Manu says:
One should recite the Veda pertaining to sacrifice and that pertaining to the deities.
He should constantly contemplate that which is internal and that which is declared in the Vedāntas;
he should reflect upon conjunction and disjunction, as well as the means of disjunction, and the essential natures of the individual soul (jīva), the Lord (īśvara), and primordial matter (pradhāna).
Having reached midday, one should spend the day with the study of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas and the perfection of meditation; this very rule applies at midday as well.

At the conclusion of the ritual acts of bathing, having offered the *arghya* as prescribed, and having performed the worship with the two [hymns] beginning with "ud u tyaṃ" and "citram," he should then recite [the following]. || 6.78 ||
Thus ends the midday bath. 6.79.
Now, the practice of begging for alms is described. Regarding this, Uśanas says:

"The *mādhūkaraka* (like gathering honey), the *asaṃkḷpta* (unprepared), the *prākpraṇīta* (previously set out), the *ayācita* (unsolicited), and the *tātkālikopapanna* (obtained at that very moment)—alms are traditionally held to be of these five kinds. (6.80)
Having gone to three, five, or seven houses that are free from mental attachment, whatever is collected like honey is known as *mādhūkara*. (6.81)
The sage Uśanas, the Blessed One, has stated that whatever was requested by those endowed with devotion prior to rising from bed is called *prākpraṇīta*. 6.82.
Manu has declared that one should eat that alms-food which was invited before the effort to wander for alms began, and which was not specifically requested. 6.83.

Furthermore, regarding that which was prescribed by the Brāhmaṇa for the purpose of alms-offering during attendance, it is said to be "for that time only"; and that too should be consumed by one who seeks liberation. (6.84)
"Siddham" (accomplished) is food brought by devotees to the monastery; the sages who long for liberation say that such food is truly "upapanna" (attained). 6.85.
For these five kinds of alms are considered equal to drinking the Soma juice;
by subsisting on any one of them here, one may attain purity. (6.86)
Viśvāmitra said:
"The wise know these [other means of subsistence] to be substitutes for alms-gathering when the practice of collecting from many houses (mādhūkarī) is not possible.
However, one who is capable of practicing the mādhūkarī way and yet performs these [substitutes] incurs sin. (6.87)

Prohibitions such as "not eating from a single person's meal," "honey," and "meat" must be understood as applying specifically to one who is capable of following the *mādhūkarika* mode of life, because they form a single syntactical unit with that rule (see 10.59). However, even for one who is capable, eating from a single person's meal is not forbidden if it is for the sake of showing favor. Thus says Medhātithi:

"One should not eat from a single person's meal, nor the food of a Śūdra, nor even in large quantities. Only if he is incapable or for the sake of showing favor may a Brahmin eat from a single person's meal. (6.89)
Kātyāyana says:
A renunciant should subsist on almsfood, whether it has been specifically requested or not. 6.90.
Aṅgiras: For those who are ill, for ascetics, for the elderly, and for those suffering from chronic diseases, no sin arises from the fault of eating food provided by a single person. 6.91.
Baudhāyana says:
"He should eat only as much as is necessary for sustenance. (BDh 2.18.12) Kapila says:
A renunciant should eat excellent food that is not merely conventional or intended for the moment; he should avoid the food of the deceased (pretas). Thus [ends verse] 6.93.
Yama says:
A renunciant (yati) may gather alms like a bee even from the household of an outcaste;
however, he must never eat food from a single source, even if that person is equal to Bṛhaspati.
There is nothing superior to the Brahmins, nor anything higher than Vāsudeva;
there is nothing higher than the system of castes and stages of life, and no scripture equal to the Vedas.
There is no purity equal to living on alms, and no austerity greater than fasting. (6.95)
That alms-food which is collected from many houses like honey is the destroyer of great sins;
therefore, one should subsist on that alone, using a pure vessel that is free from cracks. || 6.96 ||
Now, the rules for the *mādhūkaradharma* (the practice of collecting alms like honey from flowers). Regarding this, Manu has stated the proper time:

"A renunciant (*yati*) should always go for alms when the smoke has ceased, when the pestle is laid aside, when the embers are extinguished, when people have finished their meals, and when the removal of the dishes has been completed" (MDh 6.56).
The ritual act: the yogin who possesses perfect knowledge should wander in the forenoon, but in the afternoon; by begging at midday, the mendicant indeed incurs sin. (6.98)

After fifteen *ghaṭikās*, for three and three-quarter *ghaṭikās* it is midday; this is because of the indicative mark [in scripture] stating, "that which is posterior to *saṅgava* and prior to midday. (6.99) Kapila says:
"One who is extremely hungry should not wait for even the slightest [portion of] grain. (6.100)
Regarding the rule for the place of begging, Bodhāyana states:
"Now, concerning the practice of begging for alms: one should seek alms from Brāhmaṇas of the Śālīna and Yāyāvara classes after the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice has been performed. [BDh 2.18.4] Viṣṇu says:
He should beg for alms from householders and from the houses of wandering ascetics;
however, this first mode of livelihood is taught here as the most excellent. (6.102)
From this point forward, the ascetic should seek alms among householders who maintain the sacred fires—among those who are faithful, self-controlled, learned in the Vedas, and high-souled. (6.103)
Henceforth, for those who are not Śūdras and who are neither corrupt nor outcaste,
this practice of begging alms is proclaimed to be of three kinds.
Medhātithi:
He should practice that mendicancy among Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas.
Even there, if it is not possible, he should take from those in the subsequent order. 6.105.
But if there is a total absence of all [these], one who does not eat for three meals may accept alms even from a Śūdra; for life must be preserved by means of begging. (6.106)
Life is the cause for the stability of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
for those who destroy it, what is not destroyed? And for those who protect it, what is not protected? (6.107)

One should perform a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), or fifty, or even twenty-five, for the sake of purification after begging from Śūdras, Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, or in times of distress; for if this is done out of ignorance, half of this penance serves for purification. (6.108)
Sacrifice is [the true rite]; there is no concern for the performance of rituals, conduct, purity or impurity, auspiciousness or inauspiciousness.
When seeking alms from a Madhūkarī, one should not inquire about [the giver's] character, behavior, learning, or lineage.
But when the alms have fallen into the bowl, both purity and impurity are destroyed. || 5.109 ||
Vṛddhajābāli says:
One should not examine the caste [of the giver], nor should one inquire about the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness [of the food];
once alms have fallen into the vessel, one should not consider purity or impurity. (5.110)
Or the reading may be *vinaśyati*. Atri says:

One should not beg from the family of one's own kinsmen. Having obtained alms from the house of a pupil, an adversary, a kinsman, a lord, a deceased person, or a house in which there is a birth-impurity, one should not accept them. One should avoid food prepared for oneself and that which causes harm to others. (5.111)
Kapila says: Well-worn out, emaciated, diseased, tranquil, and with impaired senses, he should practice begging for alms from disciples, kinsmen, sons, brothers, and friends. (9.112)
Through the tactile characteristics of external objects such as horses, beds, seats, and so forth;
and through officiating at sacrifices, teaching, expounding, and the possession of garments and vessels. (9.113)
A renunciant would become defiled by performing acts of sexual intercourse, looking upon it, or even forming a thought of it;
therefore, he should seek alms from his own son, whether staying in a house or in the forest. (9.114)
He himself says:
"Worn out, extremely emaciated, diseased, a hundred years old, with impaired senses—he should practice begging for alms from disciples, kinsmen, sons, brothers, and friends. (9.115)
Humpbacks, dwarfs, those with cataracts, the maimed, the lame, the blind, and the diseased would not be defiled by the faults of begging, were it not for the king who provides protection. (9.116)
Vasiṣṭha states the number of houses:
he should wander for alms at seven houses where no preparations have been made, when the smoke has ceased and the pestle is laid aside, clothed in a single garment or an antelope skin.
Devala says:
Or, in the absence of those previously mentioned, he may wander through the entire village, restraining his speech and remaining pure, while avoiding those who are accused of crimes. 9.118.
Having deliberated upon both the miserly Vedic scholar and the liberal usurer, the gods ordained that their food is equal. 9.119
Regarding them, Prajāpati said: "Do not make the unequal equal;
that which is purified by faith belongs to the generous man, while the other is struck down by lack of faith. (9.120)
A wise man should not accept food that is being served up, food whose consumption is forbidden, food that provokes disease, or food that has been rejected by another. 9.121.
Atri:
Now I shall describe the complete rule for begging alms, as well as those things that must always be avoided;
by not doing which an ascetic falls quickly, but by doing which he is liberated. (9.122)

One should subsist by the honey-making way (mādhūkara) and never perform other [means of livelihood]; all those others are censurable modes of life, except for that which is blameless through consultation. 9.123.
One should eat blameless food that is like honey gathered from many flowers—unprepared, obtained by chance—with a mind entirely free from desire. (9.124)

A monk should always go for alms at six, three, seven, or eight houses; this practice of gathering from door to door (mādhūkaraka) is the best, though he may go beyond that according to his desire. 9.125
He should collect alms endowed with all flavors— such as grain, lac, oil-cake, vegetables, sour gruel, milk, curd, and so forth— while avoiding any injury to living beings.

Whatever is not contrary to one's vow, that may be eaten by him. One should always eat what is wholesome and moderate, which is digested with ease. The ascetic should avoid that food by which the bodily constituents are provoked. 9.127.
A household beset by family distress and overcome by greed afflicts one even as it provides food; therefore, one should avoid such a home. 9.128.
If either deceit or wretchedness is observed anywhere in a house, the mendicant should avoid that house, just as one avoids an oblation pecked at by crows. 9.129
A renunciant should avoid food prepared by a woman in her courses, food served by a twice-born man at the command of a Śūdra, or food placed upon a limb of a living being or upon iron. (9.130)
One should avoid such alms as were previously intended for the sake of ancestors, or for the sake of gods, or for some other purpose, as well as those that cause distress to others. (9.131)
A mendicant should not eat in a house where no offspring have been born for either a woman or a man; if he eats there, he should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. 9.132.

It has been seen [as defiled] by those who have killed a fetus, by heretics, by those afflicted with leprosy and the like, by a woman in her courses, by dogs, eunuchs, crows, and Caṇḍālas, or by others who are outcasts and dwellers in huts for the dead. (9.133)
Seeing these, he should not beg for alms; if he begs, he should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
He should not even converse with them, except when asking for directions out of fear. (9.134)
One should avoid all those who have committed great sins (mahāpātakin) and those who are outcasts (patita), in all legal dealings and especially when it concerns the matter of food. (9.135)

In the Kṛta age, one should abandon the country; in the Tretā, the village; in the Dvāpara, the family; but in the Kali age, the ascetic should wander for alms, having abandoned the corrupt performer [of rituals]. 9.136.
The doer, the one who consents, the one who impels, and the one who approves—these all become partakers of the fruit, whether it be merit or likewise sin. (9.137)
Whether it be of one's own lineage or a different lineage, as long as there is birth-impurity (sūtaka) in a house,
the ground is not purified until that period has passed ten days.
In that state, one never performs any ritual action for the ancestors, the gods, or others;
a mendicant should not beg for alms, and if he should beg, he must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
A monk should not seek alms from the family of his relatives, nor ever from the house of a lord, nor should he ever desire alms from disciples, kinsmen, friends, and so forth. (9.140)
The ancestors do not eat the food of the husband of a *vṛṣalī*, nor do they eat that of one conquered by his wife; an ascetic should avoid such food. (9.141)
The specific duty (*svadharma*) of the social classes (*varṇas*) and the stages of life (*āśramas*) is designated as "heroic" (*vīra*).
Those who engage in that [duty] are proclaimed as heroes;
but one should abandon as a slayer of heroes (*vīraghna*) anyone who violates that dharma. (9.142)
Then [he should avoid] a naked girl, one who is pregnant, as well as one who is soiled, intoxicated, joyful, angry, or intent on eating food. (9.143)

And likewise those who harm the fetus or the husband, a wanton woman, one who acts according to her own lust, one who lacks heroic kin, one afflicted with leprosy, a blind woman, a remarried woman, and one who is artificial (kṛtrimā). || 9.144 ||
With disheveled hair, sitting at ease, full of passion and filled with wonder—deceitful, wretched, ill-behaved, weary, and afflicted by disease. (9.145)

A mendicant should not accept alms from one who is shameless, a carpenter’s wife, one who is exhausted, a female servant, one who is impotent, one who is very harsh, or one who is nursing an infant at her breast. (9.146)
Kapila says:

One should not enter a house that is in distress due to family troubles or where there is obstruction. One should not beg for alms from one who is asleep, intoxicated, inattentive, delighted, distressed, sitting at ease, pregnant, diseased, absorbed in her husband, full of passion, intent on eating food, or whose breasts are occupied by a child. One should neither beg for nor accept alms offered by a woman in her menses, those placed in the hand of a naked bride, those given with contempt, or those brought by a maiden. 9.147.
One should avoid meat that has been salted before one's eyes, honey, the milk of a cow that has recently calved, and the food of fools, those accused of crimes, outcasts, and eunuchs. (9.148)
One should never beg from an unsteady woman, a wanton woman, one afflicted with leprosy, those who have harmed their fetus or husband, a maiden, a nurse, a remarried woman, or a naked woman. (9.149)
Vṛddha-Jābāli says:
Only two types of ascetics are worthy of being fed—the forest-dweller and the householder;
the food of others who bear sectarian marks is not to be eaten. (9.150)

Now, regarding the practice of begging for alms: concerning this, Śaunaka says—“Then, having washed the vessel with water using a rope made of cow-hair while reciting the seven vyāhṛtis, and having worshipped the sun with the mantra ‘The swan dwelling in purity’ (RV 4.40.5), one should go forth, restrained in speech and with a tranquil mind. (9.151)
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

"The alms-vessels may be made of wood, gourd, split bamboo, or clay—one of each. Having scrubbed it with a rope of cow-hair or with a hand wet with water, he should go about begging alms from Brahmins of virtuous conduct.
Atri says:
Having taken the vessel with the left hand and the triple staff in the right hand, one should perform the worship of the Sun, meditating upon the oneness of oneself [with the deity]. (6.153)
With a concentrated mind, meditating upon the deity, one should mutter the Virajas mantra—that Puruṣa known as Viṣṇu who resides within the sun and within the heart. (6.154)
Thus I am the god Nārāyaṇa, the Puruṣa who is the witness of the world;
having thus meditated upon the Self by means of the self as the Puruṣa, the creator of the universe.
Then, having performed a circumambulation, one should pay homage to the Dispeller of Darkness;
having paid homage, one should again mount one's sandals upon the ground.
A monk may wander for the sake of purification, but he should not discard his footwear;
likewise, without a water-pot and alms-food, he is defiled by his sandals. (6.157)
Holding his sandals, the mendicant should walk while remembering Hari:
"Viṣṇu is my horizontal, downward, and upward direction; Vaikuṇṭha is my intermediate and cardinal directions. (6.158)
May Rāma protect me from all sides, as well as Keśava, the wielder of the bow and the discus;
may Govinda, the drinker of Soma and the consumer of sacrificial offerings to gods and ancestors, protect me.
Viṣṇu, whose seat is Tārkṣya, who is Ananta, the wielder of the discus, and the one who assumed the form of Vāmana—he who is omnipresent, subtle, the eternal Supreme Self. (6.160)

May that Mādhava— who is devoid of qualities, partless, the bearer of a white form, and imperishable; who is without beginning or end— protect me in the midst of the white Ocean of Milk, which is eternally infinite and adorned with the jewels upon his hoods.
May He whose banner is Garuḍa, possessing all weapons and all powers, protect me— my body, both inside and out, from the soles of my feet to the crown of my head.
May that Mādhava, the Supreme Lord whose very self is everything, protect me—he from whose navel-lotus was born Brahmā, the Lord who effects creation. (6.163)
Meditating in this manner, he should wander about wearing a single garment and with the sacred thread over his left shoulder;
for clothing was created by Brahmā for the successful accomplishment of all duties.
It is proclaimed that in the absence of clothing, all ritual acts are fruitless. (6.164)
Devala says:

Having established himself in the state whose nature is Brahman, having performed salutation with the words "Obeisance to Brahman," having muttered the *virajas* mantra, having circumambulated [the fire] with the words "By Truth," and having muttered "Those paths of yours," he should wander forth as a mendicant, restraining his speech. 6.165.
Yama says: He should always wander for alms that are pure, being silent and clean in the evening;
wearing a single garment or even naked, walking slowly, with his gaze fixed on the tip of his nose.
He should wander alone for alms, single-minded and free from greed;
he who is without fire and without a fixed dwelling should not seek the purpose of mere physical gratification. (6.167)
Medhātithi: Having wrapped one garment around [the body] from above the knees to below the navel, and having put on a second as an undergarment, he should then [worship] the Sun. (6.168)
Then, having attended to his needs, he should go from house to house for alms, carrying his bowl and staff;
he should stand at the doorway within sight of the householder, and, seeking alms, keep his face cast downwards. (6.169)
Restraining his speech, with a perfectly serene mind, whether sleeping or even during the day,
he should remain silent for a period equal to the time it takes to milk a cow, at a time when no visible activity occurs.
If he is not invited, he may go to another house even after seeing it; however, once a promise has been made, he should wait until the alms have been given. (6.171)

Intent on his purpose, placing his footsteps purified by his vision, silent, wise, and tranquil, wearing but one garment and using but one vessel, he should wander without attachment like one who is asleep. (6.172)

Or at the times of the four, six, or eight [meals], the ascetic may subsist by means of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, or he may seek alms from five or seven houses of those who perform religious rites. (6.173)

One should beg for alms once, having first addressed the householder, standing with face cast downwards; one should wait for the time it takes to milk a cow, and having departed, one should not return again. (6.174)
Baudhāyana says:
[The formula] beginning with "bhavat" and ending with "pracodayāt" [should be used]; one should wait for the milking of the cow.
Devala says: [the same].
At the time of begging for alms, ascetics must always carry a parasol;
however, this is required when it is raining, and not merely from the heat of the sun.
Atri:
A renunciant should always wander alone, possessing only one garment and one alms-bowl;
he should go for alms only once a day, and never at the lowest (final) part of the day. 6.177.
While wandering, the ascetic should not look upward, nor sideways, nor into the distance;
a mendicant should walk looking at the surface of the earth only as far as a yoke’s length. 6.178.
Desiring alms, an ascetic should not peer into the interior of a house through a gap in the door;
he should not make a proclamation there, nor should he strike upon the door. (6.179)
Having passed by a house previously, he should not enter it again; having entered [another], and having taken alms, he should perform thirty breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma). 6.180.
At the time of begging for alms, one should not wander from house to house by deviating to the left or right;
having avoided censurable transgressions, one should perform a hundred breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma).

One should take refuge in a dwelling that was not previously intended for oneself and has opened of its own accord, according to the divisions of place and time, and also in consideration of one's own capacity. (6.182)
When another monk has not yet arrived, he should enter a house for the sake of alms; having entered, he should eat his begged food with a mind free from trembling. (6.183)
Whether standing in the presence of his wife or even in the fire-sanctuary,
he should hold the bowl with his left hand and the triple staff with his right.
One should beg for alms, beginning with the syllable *praṇava* (Om) and preceded by the word "bhavat" (O noble one), saying, "Give me alms.
Having made this request for the sake of alms, a capable person should never sit down anywhere.
And one should not ask for any other object out of greed for satisfaction;
having received alms purified by sight and placed in the hand of the donor. (6.186)

The ascetic, having placed the triple staff upon his right shoulder with his hand, and having lifted the bowl-armor with his right hand, should place the bowl in his left hand; it should never be held in the right hand. (6.187)
It is written:
Even when dying, one should not eat the food of a single person, nor even that of a Niṣāda;
one should subsist on honey-gathered food (mādhūkara), for that brings about purity of being.

He should not be rejected in one place and then enter another house at the time of begging for alms, nor should he go from one house to another; furthermore, he must never accept alms that have been prepared for someone else or intended for another purpose. (6.189)
Kāśyapa.

He should stand motionless with his feet even, separated by a distance of four finger-breadths. He should not feel disgust toward anything—excluding wood, stone, or clay—thinking it impure; rather, regarding it as pure, he should take it up. He should never look at the circle of his own face. He should look with his eyes only a hand’s breadth ahead, and likewise gaze forward only the distance of a yoke. He should not repeatedly look to the sides or behind him. He should enter through open doors and not enter through side-entrances. He should neither strike nor shout at a door. He should not exit hastily, nor should he linger for long. (6.190)
Devala says:
If an obstacle should arise anywhere when one has entered a village for the sake of alms, he should not seek alms again after having gone outside the village. (6.191)
Jamadagni: A mendicant should always avoid that house where alms are not obtained for five days or seven nights, treating it like the house of a Caṇḍāla. (6.192)
On those days, the mendicant should depart without expectations from the householder;
he departs taking with him all [the merit of] Vedic study, burnt offerings, and gifts. (6.193)
He himself says:
"A renunciant should not take alms beyond the mere amount required for food;
however, one who takes cooked food by improper means deserves punishment like that of a thief. (6.194)
Vṛddha-Jābāli says:
One should eat from a single vessel; this is declared to be the highest vow.
There is no fault in using two vessels, however, for one who is incapable due to being afflicted by disease. (6.195)
Though capable and free from illness, he who does not eat from a single vessel, being greedy for more bowls, that evil-minded man falls into hell. (6.196)
But that monk who, out of greed and pride, desires to fill his bowl—while the giver attains heaven, the consumer partakes of sin. (6.197)
But when a renunciant who has been invited goes out to beg for alms, if he should harbor greed therein, he falls without a doubt. (6.198)
If one should say "give, give" regarding salt, condiments, or the like, that alms-food is equal to beef; having eaten it, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (6.199)
If one of small intelligence does not accept whatever is being given when it is placed in the hand of his wife, he is born among the wombs of crows.
Kapila said:
Having begged for alms, he should not remain there for long; if told "no," he should turn away with a mind free from resentment; he should not seek to fill a single bowl. (6.201)
Bharadvāja says: Having murmured the mantra, "O full ladle, fly away," he should turn back, saying again, "Homage. 6.202.
Now follows the rule for eating. Regarding this, Śaunaka says:

Having returned from there, having placed his vessel in a clean place, having washed his feet, sipped water (ācamana), and performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), he should sip water again; then, having sprinkled the alms-food with water while saying "Oṃ," and having consecrated it with the Gāyatrī mantra, he should offer it as an oblation to Viṣṇu with the verse, "Viṣṇu strode across this. With the two verses, "Upwards that [sun]" and "The wonderful [light]," he should offer it to Āditya; with "Brahman was born first," to Brahmā; and with "Salutation to the beings," he should offer it to the beings. Then he should consume the remainder like medicine. 6.203.
Baudhāyana says:

Then, having returned from his alms-round, he should set down his bowl in a clean place, wash his hands and feet, and perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*). He should first offer it to the Sun with the verses "Upwards that" (*ud u tyam*) and "The bright" (*citram*). He should offer it to Brahmā with "The Brahman born" (*brahma jajñānam*), to Viṣṇu with "This Viṣṇu" (*idaṃ viṣṇuḥ*), and to the elemental beings (*bhūta*) with "Salutation to the beings" (*bhūtebhyo namaḥ*); so it is known. From the time of the laying of the fires (*ādhāna*) onwards, the fires themselves become the sacrificer. His out-breath (*prāṇa*) is the Gārhapatya fire; his in-breath (*apāna*) is the Anvāhāryapacana fire; his diffused breath (*vyāna*) is the Āhavanīya fire; and his common and upward breaths (*samāna* and *udāna*) are the Sabhya and Āvasathya fires. These five are indeed situated within the self; he offers them into the self alone. It is known that this is the sacrifice to the self (*ātmayajña*), centered in the self, established in the self, which leads the self to security. Having first offered it with compassion to all beings and having sprinkled the remainder with water, he should consume it like medicinal herbs. (6.204) [BDh 2.18.7–10]
Yama says: One should not eat from an alms-bowl, nor should one perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) from a bowl;
in the Kṛta, Tretā, and Dvāpara ages, a renunciant (yati) may eat from a bowl.
In the Kali age, one should not eat from an improper vessel, nor should one carry a water-pot. || 6.205 ||
Bharadvāja:

Having obtained whatever vessel made of withered leaves has fallen, he should eat from that; never from a metallic vessel. Having eaten from a metallic vessel, one should perform the *prājāpatya* penance. Having gone to the edge of a village, a secluded forest, a pond, a secluded riverbank, or to lotus-pools, he should consume that food. Having performed the washing at a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*), he should set down the vessel while keeping it covered. Having washed his feet with three applications of clay and likewise washed his hands, and having sipped water (*ācamana*), he should perform six breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*). Having recited the *anna-sūkta* (the hymn for food) with the *praṇava* and the *gāyatrī*, and having meditated upon the nature of the Supreme Self, he sips water with the mantra "This is the under-layer of nectar" (*amṛtopastaraṇam asi*) and offers the oblation to the vital breaths (*prāṇāhuti*). During the meal, if anything—such as a fine hair or a fly—has fallen into it, he removes a morsel's worth of that food, washes his hand, and then continues eating. If a hair becomes stuck in his mouth, he should spit it out immediately; having rinsed his mouth with twelve mouthfuls of water, he continues eating.

Bṛhaspati: Having well-guarded his speech, mind, and eyes, having kept his private parts concealed, and having performed his daily rites, he should bring back well-guarded alms and partake of his meal with careful restraint. (6.207)
While eating, one should never touch food with the left hand;
nor should one touch one's feet, head, or genitals, nor should one touch the food with one's feet. (6.208)
There is nothing other than medicine, nor likewise a tooth-stick, that a mendicant should consume outside of mealtime. (6.209)
Viṣṇu says: He should eat alms-food, or young barley, or milk, or ghee; or well-cooked fruits and roots, or vegetables, oil-cakes, or parched grain flour. (6.210)
Thus, these indeed are the forms of food for yogins that bring about accomplishment;
one should employ them day after day with supreme meditative concentration. (6.211)
Having drunk water once silently, the ascetic, composed and facing the east while eating, should take the first mouthful with the formula: "To Prāṇa. (6.212)
The second [syllable] should be for apāna, then the next for vyāna;
the fourth should be for udāna, and the fifth for samāna. (6.213)
Having thus offered the oblations of breath, he should eat the remainder while restraining his speech;
then, having sipped water once more and performed the ritual rinsing (ācamana), he should touch his heart.
Yama said:

"In a house where the smoke has ceased and the pestle lies still, when the sacrificial rites have been completed, and which is neither crowded with those who live like dogs nor filled with ascetics. (6.215)
A mendicant should not beg for alms from anyone who has not yet eaten;
he should take only as much as is necessary merely to sustain life.
He should eat whatever is obtained, and never eat according to his own desire. (6.216)
As many mouthfuls as one eats of alms-food that is pure by its source, sprinkled with water, and offered as an oblation, for so many sacrifices is he equal to. (6.217)
Sprinkled with the *praṇava* itself, it is offered into the internal fires within the five vital breaths (*prāṇa*, etc. individually, accompanied by the utterances of *svāhā*. (6.218)
Prāṇa is the eye, the sun, and heaven; vyāna is the ear, the night, and the moon;
apāna is speech, the mind, and fire; samāna is the waters, the intellect, and the thunderbolt. || 6.219 ||
May the udāna wind and space be satisfied by the food offered with concentration; by giving to these and eating himself, he attains satisfaction and is released from the three debts. (6.220)
"Eating alms-food is prescribed everywhere; eating after having washed [the bowl] is also taught. Thus said Saṃvarta:
"Having collected eight, five, or seven alms-bits, that sage, being well-composed, should wash all of them with water and eat. (6.221)

Kapila said: Now, having returned from the village, he should eat his alms-food once, mixing it with water from a single vessel; he should not converse at all with anyone, nor should he ask for anything other than medicine. Living in this manner for as long as he lives, the mendicant becomes liberated. 6.222.

This should be understood in the event of suspicion of a fault: "The sacrifice: one should sprinkle the alms-food with sets of four [mantras] and offer the oblation with those same signs; one should give something to Viṣṇu, Brahmā, the Sun, and the spirits, or to a petitioner. (6.223)

Having turned the lotus upward, by means of inhalation and the other breath-controls (prāṇāyāma) starting with prāṇa, one offers food into the Brahma-fire located at the distance of a span; thus one is liberated from impurities.
While eating, one should not relish the six flavors, nor should one proclaim them;
being equal toward honor and dishonor, one should neither rejoice nor feel aversion. (6.225)
He himself says:
"One should not leave food uneaten, nor eat too much, nor find fault [with it], nor take more than one's share;
one should not revile cows, Brahmins, the sun, the moon, fire, the wind, or water. (6.226)

Kapila says: Whatever food, even if stale, is not contrary to his vow, he may accept it if he desires to nourish himself. Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), he should sip water again; having washed the place or the vessel two or three times, and having placed the food upon the ritual diagram (yantra), he should sprinkle it with the *praṇava* and consecrate the alms-food with the three [syllables]. He should honor even a single mouthful with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ. He should not eat anything without first offering it. It is also praised to have a disposition for sharing with those who ask, such as by giving the sacrificial portion to the spirits (*bhūtabali*).
The sages live happily, subsisting on the practice of alms;
free from malice toward all beings, they are like six-legged bees among the deer.

"Having meditated, 'May Soma alone eat the food,' whoever eats food, he eats nectar. With 'Svāhā to Prāṇa,' he eats food in Prāṇa; with 'Svāhā to Apāna,' he eats food in Apāna; with 'Svāhā to Vyāna,' he eats food in Vyāna; with 'Svāhā to Udāna,' he eats food in Udāna; with 'Svāhā to Samāna,' he eats food in Samāna. Whoever eats food, he is Agni; whatever food is eaten, that is all Soma. Having washed the vessel, one should receive it consecrated by the three [mantras]. By eating thus, one is released from evil. (6.229)
Viśvāmitra says:
A renunciant should offer [the food] to the fourth [ascetic] in the case of the *mādhūkara* [gathering] as before;
but in the other four cases, the renunciant should not dismiss that [food]. (6.230)
With the two verses beginning "Upwards that bright one," he should offer [the oblation] to Āditya;
having recited "The Brahman was born first," he should offer food to Brahmā;
and with "This [Viṣṇu]," he should then offer it to Viṣṇu. (6.231)
Then, having offered the fourth oblation to all beings,
one should give a mouthful [of food] to the Sun and the other deities in due order.
He who, having collected food from others, abandons that food day after day, would incur the fault of that [act]; such an ascetic must perform penance.
Moreover, from where could there be a gift for him, and from where could there be a fruit for it?
Both the giver and the recipient would surely go to hell after death. (6.234)
Hārīta says:
One should indeed pull off the armor with the right hand;
having placed the vessel in the left hand, one should press it against [the body] with the right. 6.235.
One should practice begging for alms only as long as there is suffering from hunger;
then, having desisted, the self-controlled one should set down that bowl and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Having covered [the mouth] with four fingers, being composed, one should offer a mouthful of food together with all its condiments into a separate vessel. (6.237)
Having offered food to the sun and other deities and spirits, and having sprinkled it with water, the ascetic,
restrained in speech, should eat from a leaf-cup or a bowl.
One should never eat from the leaves of the banyan, the arka, or the aśvattha, nor from the leaves of the kumbhī or the tinduka, nor from those of the kovidāra or the karañja.
One should never eat from a bronze vessel, even in times of distress;
for all those who eat from bronze vessels are said to be like the Palāśa trees, though they may be ascetics.
Whatever sin belongs to one who possesses bell-metal and likewise to a householder,
an ascetic who eats from a bell-metal vessel incurs all that guilt of both.
Yama says: Golden vessels and those made of black iron—these are unfit vessels for ascetics, whether for receiving alms or for eating. (6.242)
Having given alms in vessels of gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, or iron, there is no merit; having taken them [for oneself], one goes to hell. (6.243)
It is written: One should not eat from an alms-bowl, nor should one perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) from a bowl.
In the Kṛta, Tretā, and Dvāpara ages, an ascetic may be one who eats from a bowl. 6.244.
In the Kali age, he should not eat from a vessel, nor should he carry a water-pot;
he should eat from a leaf-cup, and never from the back of a leaf. (6.245)
In the absence of leaves from the *palāśa*, lotus, or plantain tree, one should indeed refrain from eating;
even when other vessels are unavailable, one must not eat from bronze or silver.
Nor on black iron, nor on gold, nor on copper; nor on a part of a living being, nor on the ground, nor on grasses such as *kuśa* and the like. (6.247)
One should eat from a *palāśa* leaf or, in times of distress, from the hollow of one's hand.
Having eaten from *palāśa* or lotus leaves, a householder must perform the *aindava* penance;
an ascetic (*yati*) and a forest-dweller (*vanastha*) likewise incur the fruit of the *aindava* penance for doing so.
Medhātithi: A mendicant eating from vessels made of gold, bell-metal, silver, copper, lotus-leaf, or stone does not incur sin; he incurs sin, however, through the act of possession. 6.249.

The view of Yama and Likhita is that vessels made of gold and other such materials should not be accepted by oneself for the purpose of begging or eating. However, the opinion of Medhātithi is that even if one accepts them oneself, one does not incur fault when eating from them during times of distress, provided they belong to another. Even in the absence of vessels belonging to others, one should eat from the hollow of the hand (*pāṇipātra*). One must not eat from bronze or similar vessels merely because leaves are unavailable; rather, according to Hārīta’s statement, "even in times of distress, never [from these]," this applies only when one has reached the state of being on the verge of death. (6.250) Atri describes the application of the *bali* offering:
One should not give the offering to one who does not ask for it, nor should one discard it at will;
