the wise man should either cast it into water or bury it in the ground. (6.251)
The sage declares the rule regarding the giving of alms-food and its disposal when an obstacle to eating has arisen:
"He who, having collected food from many sources (mādhūkara), gives it to Brāhmaṇas, goes to a terrible hell; and the one who eats it shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (6.252)
In cases of penance, vows, or misfortune, it is prescribed that alms be sought from the twice-born;
however, for others, such theft must be given away, but for ascetics, it is equal to performing sacrifices.
Śāṇḍilya says that an ascetic should eat only once a day:
"Having gone to a village in the evening and collected alms while remaining silent, he should eat exactly eight mouthfuls every single day. (6.254)
Vṛddha-Jābāli says:
One should never eat at night, nor should one eat again after having already eaten.
A renunciant who eats at night falls; of this there is no doubt. (6.255)
If an ascetic eats at night when the time of twilight has arrived, his attendance upon the deity,
his recitation, his breath-control, and likewise his offerings—
all these become fruitless for him, and an expiation is prescribed. (6.256)

Regarding eating twice a day, Vasiṣṭha says: "He should eat what he obtains at the house of a Brāhmaṇa, both morning and evening, excluding honey and meat, and he should not eat to satiety. (VaDh 10.24–25) This [rule] pertains to one who is incapable [of fasting]. 6.257.
Now follows the ritual to be performed after the meal. Regarding this, Śaunaka says:

Having consumed water and performed the ceremonial sipping (ācamana), having murmured, "Speech is in my mouth; breath is in my nose," and having sipped water again, he should worship the sun with the verse, "We have risen above the darkness" (*ud vayaṃ tamasas pari*). Then, having washed a vessel with cow-hair rope and water while reciting the seven *vyāhṛtis*, and having performed three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāmas*), he should mutter the *Gāyatrī* one hundred and eight times. He should spend the remaining time in recitation and meditation. Then, sitting for the evening twilight (*sāyaṃsaṃdhyā*) until the sun has set and the stars have appeared, he should perform the *Gāyatrī* recitation. Furthermore, he should meditate for as long as he is able; even when rising from sleep, he should meditate. (6.258)
Yama says:
For gold, silver, sacrificial vessels, and the bowls of ascetics, purification by water alone is prescribed. (6.259)
Having written [it], and having approached the Sun after eating, one should always recite the Purāṇas.
Through the purification of one's inner being, devotion to Hari arises from listening to the Purāṇas. (6.260)

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: One may have a single alms-bowl made of wood, gourd, split bamboo, or clay. Its cleansing is by scrubbing with a rope of cow-hair moistened with water; this purification must be performed daily. One should not sip water (ācamana) from it, nor throw it on the ground, nor let it be touched by impure things. Having eaten and sipped water, one should sip water again and sprinkle the utensils. A rope-sling or other such items may be used provided they are not prohibited. (6.261)

Śaṅkha says: Having eaten, having worshipped the sun, and having performed breath-control while seated, one should mutter the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times and then meditate again upon Nārāyaṇa. (6.262)

Having spent the remainder of the day with the recitation of Purāṇas and other texts, and having performed the evening twilight devotion (saṃdhyā), he should then practice yoga; likewise again at the end of his sleep.
Acting thus day by day, making meditation alone his primary focus even while performing ritual acts, he becomes fit for union with Brahman. (6.264)
Viśvāmitra said: "Having eaten, there is again the ritual of worship: 'We have risen above the darkness. I have declared to you the fivefold rule for a mendicant’s wandering for alms. (6.265)
The monk who conducts himself in this manner is a true ascetic and belongs to the spiritual order;
having performed the twilight devotions according to the rule, he should practice the rite of meditation. (6.266)
One worships at the morning twilight with verses beginning with "maitrī," at the midday twilight with those addressed to Sūrya, and in the evening with those whose deity is Varuṇa. (6.267)
This twilight which rests upon the rising [of the sun] is to be known as Sārasvatī;
that at midday is Śāṅkarī, and that in the afternoon is Vaiṣṇavī.
Thus, meditation should always be practiced by a wise Brahmin for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the sacrifice of recitation; this very meditation has been declared by me. (6.269)
Whoever performs the twilight devotions with the hair-strainers of cows, whatever evil deed has been committed by him is instantly destroyed. (6.270)
Seated upon darbha grass, with darbha grass in hand, facing eastward and well-composed, he should mutter the Sāvitrī mantra a thousand times, or even a hundred times. (6.271)
The three pure Great Utterances preceded by the syllable *oṃ*, together with the three-footed *gāyatrī*, should be known as the supreme state. (6.272)
One should always wear a sacred thread made of silk on the right hand;
especially while eating, one who does so is not defiled by defects in the food. (6.273)
Wearing the sacred thread, carrying the triple staff, possessing a topknot, seated on a mat, and wearing saffron robes, he should perform those rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti.
By constantly practicing yoga in this manner, the ascetic attains perfection; not otherwise. (6.274)
Medhātithi says:
A woman in her courses should herself wash the vessel with a rope made of cow-hair;
having eaten, she should do so with the Vyāhṛtis, or with the Gāyatrī, or with the Praṇava. (6.275)
Having performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), one should recite the Gāyatrī mantra one hundred and eight times;
if there is anything that must be said, one should speak only as much as is necessary.
Having spent the remainder of the day in meditation, he should then complete it with undistracted mind;
he should attend upon the twilight when the sun is red until the appearance of the stars. (6.277)
One should meditate again until one falls under the power of sleep;
having risen from sleep, one should meditate once more, and while standing, one should recite the prayers of the twilight.
Bharadvāja:

Having taken a handful of water with the mantra "Thou art the covering of immortality" (*amṛtāpidhānam asi*), he cleanses his teeth with the syllable *praṇava* (Oṃ). Having thrown the leftover food and the vessel into the water, sipped water for purification (*ācamana*), performed three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), and sipped water again, he should mutter "May speech be in my mouth" (*vāṅ ma āsan*) and purify himself with the hymn "O Waters, you are indeed... (*āpo hi ṣṭha*). He should perform the ritual salutation (*upasthāna*) with the hymn "Upward from the darkness... (*ud vayaṃ tamasas pari*). He should wash the vessel with the *praṇava*. He should mutter the *gāyatrī* one hundred and eight times. Taking a cow-hair brush, he should wipe the dry vessel with the *praṇava* alone. Having tied it up with the hymn "The quarters, the intermediate quarters... (*diśaḥ pradiśaḥ*), he should set it down with the *gāyatrī*. He should worship the red sun. By eating in this manner according to the prescribed rule, the mendicant attains the supreme goal. 6.279.
Now follows the evening twilight worship (*sāyaṃsaṃdhyopāsana*). Regarding this, Śaunaka says:

"The bathing and other rites should be performed in the same manner in the evening; having completed the entire ritual procedure, one should offer the water for honor (*arghya*) as before when the sun is turning red. (6.280)
Then, having performed the worship with the Vāruṇī verses, one should carry out the rites of the twilight devotions;
one should remain meditating until falling under the power of sleep.
If one awakens again, one should meditate once more, for thus one becomes fit for union with Brahman.
Regarding the place for keeping the night's clothing, Hārīta says:
"Having eaten, the ascetic should always wash his bowl with mantras;
that bowl of his does not become defiled, just like the *camasa* cup used in sacrifices. (6.282)
Then, having sipped water and restrained his breath, he should worship the Sun;
he should spend the remainder of the day with recitation, meditation, and the study of ancient histories.
Having performed the evening twilight rites, he should then pass the night in a temple or similar sacred place.
Śāṇḍilya says: Having abandoned the Veda, one should renounce all ritual actions indeed;
having built a hut outside the village, or even at the root of a tree, one should dwell there. (6.284)
Established in yoga, free from attachment, fearless, and pure, he should dwell in an empty house, a cave, a fire-sanctuary, or a temple. (6.285)
Vasiṣṭha has stated the prohibition of beds and similar items, as well as the use of a mat, sleeping on the bare ground, and the dwelling place:

"Clothed in a single garment or in an antelope skin, with his body covered by grass plucked by cows, he should always dwell as one who sleeps on the bare ground. At the edge of a village, in a temple, in an empty house, or at the root of a tree, he should live constantly in the forest, reciting his private Vedic study mentally; he should not wander about when domestic animals are in sight. (VaDh 10.9–16).
He says the same:
And he should not be satisfied with little; he should dwell in a village; he should be straightforward, free from deceit, and not fickle.
(6.287) [VaDh 10.25–27] Regarding the fitness and unfitness for residing in a common dwelling, Dakṣa said:
"A single mendicant is as described; two are traditionally considered a pair."
Three villages are declared to be a *grāma*; beyond that, it becomes like a city (*nagara*). || 6.288 ||
A city, a village, or even a pair [of attendants] should not be established by him;
for by undertaking these three, an ascetic falls away from his own duty. (6.289)
Talk of kings and the like, as well as talk among themselves concerning monks, affection, backbiting, and envy will arise from their close proximity. (6.290)
Those emaciated by austerities and recitations, those afflicted by disease, those worthy of dwellings, the elderly, those possessed by spirits, and others whose senses are impaired; 6.291.
A mendicant who is healthy and young is not worthy of a dwelling.
If a mendicant, while residing in a dwelling, indulges in sexual intercourse, he defiles that place and brings distress even to the elders. (6.292)
Kapila, however, approves of living together [with such people].

One should salute those who have arrived—teachers, elders, and ascetics—and regard them as if they were the four-armed [Viṣṇu]. It is also praised to be disposed toward sharing according to one's ability when there is need. One should dwell together with ascetics of similar character who do not cause agitation.

Śaunaka says: One should neither build nor cause to be built a shelter; one should enter only what has already been made. Then one should worship Brahman; one should lie down with the mind fixed on that alone. Having entered a temple of the gods free from reproach, one should pass the night however one may, remaining awake yet as if in deep sleep. Sitting down, then having sipped water (ācamana) and performed three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), one should sip water again. At night, one should sip water using a water-pot placed upon a piece of wood; during the day, from a flowing stream. One should not abandon a sacred place that is pleasing to one and possesses abundant water. One should not be greedy for various holy bathing-places (tīrtha). 6.294.
Wind; and water drawn up at the end of the night in a pure vessel according to the rule—if it has stood for a day and a night, it must be discarded, even if it is itself pure. (6.295)
Now, the duties to be performed by a householder when mendicants arrive for the purpose of receiving alms-food and so forth are described. Regarding this, the aged Jābāli says:

"Even a Brahmin who is a knower of the four Vedas, a performer of the Soma sacrifice, and a celebrant of a hundred rites—even from such a person, the ascetic is superior; the difference between them is like that between sesame seeds and husks. (6.296)
He who, upon seeing an ascetic, does not relinquish his seat or even his bed—that deluded soul, after death, is born among the animal wombs. (6.297)
Whether one is of evil conduct or of good conduct, one should not cause censure toward ascetics; for he who hates ascetics falls into hell. (6.298)
Dattātreya:
"The Brahmin who bears the form of the triple staff is Nārāyaṇa himself in person.
He who worships him with devotion has thereby worshipped Viṣṇu. (6.299)
Whether he possesses qualities or is devoid of them, whether he is senior in his vows or even a youth, a monk who is established in his own duty is to be honored by monks. (6.300)
With the eight-syllable mantra, which is essentially Nārāyaṇa,
one should daily pay homage with a spirit of devotion to the bearer of the triple staff, who is the very form of Viṣṇu.
The triple staff is indeed the Vaiṣṇava mark, the means to liberation for Brahmins;
it is the extinction of all dharmas—such is the teaching of the Vedas. (6.302)
The Dharma of the Three Vedas was destroyed by the heretics of Kaṇāda and Śākya;
formerly, the Three Vedas were protected by Viṣṇu, who bears the triple staff.
Jamadagni said:
"That fool who gives dry food cooked separately to an ascetic goes to hell because of that sinful deed. (6.304)
Both the ascetic and the student are the rightful owners of cooked food;
having eaten without first giving food to those two, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (6.305)
One should give water into the hand of the ascetic, then give alms, and again give water;
that alms is equal to Mount Meru, and that water is comparable to the ocean. (6.306)
Wherever an ascetic eats in someone’s house, there Hari himself eats;
wherever Hari eats in someone’s house, there he eats the three worlds. (6.307)
Whatever accumulated sin a householder has committed until the end of his life, an ascetic who has stayed for even a single night will completely burn it away. (6.308)
He who abandons one who is not cooking and instead feeds one who is cooking during rites for the gods or the ancestors, his labor is in vain. (6.309)
He who abandons a virtuous ascetic who is neither corrupt nor fallen gives away his own merit and takes upon himself the other’s demerit. (6.310)
Whether he is ill-behaved or well-behaved, whether he is a fool or even a scholar, O Yudhiṣṭhira, an ascetic is worthy of honor merely by virtue of his saffron robe and staff. (6.311)
Atri says:
A giver of alms should always give water into the right hand of the mendicant, and then,
while the left hand is held out, he should place the alms into his bowl.
Water was prepared for that offering for the sake of satisfying the ancestors and the gods; by giving that very food, it becomes accomplished. (6.313)
If one were to prepare alms-food and give it to a mendicant who is an embodiment of Viṣṇu, that would not be equal to giving away the entire earth. (6.314)
By giving an alms-bowl, a seat, a staff, a sling, and a water-strainer to a renunciant, one obtains the fruit of the gift of a cow. (6.315)
One should construct a hermitage pavilion for monks who are ill, or attend to them with wholesome foods and the like; such a person enjoys infinite fruit.
Vṛddha-Jābāli says:
Alms that have been set aside separately, smelled by cats or mice, or food that has been blown upon or fanned, or even dried food, shall be equal to honey and meat. (6.317)
Alms that have been kept overnight, as well as those prepared as an offering to a deity, cause no fault for one who accepts them; however, the giver shall go to hell. (6.318)
One should give water into the hand of the monk, give alms, and then again give water;
that alms is equal to mountains, and that water is like the ocean. The deities are satisfied by the alms given in this manner. (6.319)
Jābāli said:
"Whatever object a man anywhere takes from the hand of an ascetic,
that fool goes to hell because of that sinful deed."
Indeed, one who gives a triple staff, a water-purifier, an alms-bowl, and a seat to a renunciant shall obtain the fruit of giving a thousand cows. (6.321)
He who gives a suitable fourfold vessel to a triple-staffed ascetic, having filled it with sacrificial food (haviṣya), should offer himself as well. 6.322.
Even those most sinful beings who are being cooked in the places of hell,
he who delivers himself by his own self shall go to the supreme goal.
As many as are the ascetics' bowls and as much as is the food therein,
for that many thousands of years he is honored in the heavenly world.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "Daily Rites," in the Yatidharmasamuccaya. 6.325.
The seventh book is on Conduct; now, regarding conduct, Manu says:

He should be without fire and without a fixed dwelling; he may resort to a village only for the sake of food. Indifferent, free from accumulation, the sage should be endowed with the realization of the true nature of reality. (7.1) [MDh 6.43] An alms-bowl, the roots of trees, ragged clothing, and solitude—
And equanimity toward everything—this is the characteristic of one who is liberated. (7.2) One should not rejoice in death, nor should one rejoice in life;
one should simply await one’s time, just as a hired laborer awaits his wages. (7.3)
One should place one's foot down purified by sight; one should drink water purified by a cloth;
one should speak words purified by truth; and one should act with a mind that is pure. (7.4) [MDh 6.46] One should endure harsh words and should not despise anyone.
And one should not harbor enmity toward anyone on account of this body.
(7.5) One should not return anger to one who is angry; when reviled, one should speak kindly;
and one should not utter false speech scattered through the seven gates. (7.6)
Delighting in the inner self, seated, indifferent to worldly objects, and free from sensual desire,
he should wander about for the sake of happiness with only the Self as his companion, as if in heaven.
(7.7) Nor [should he seek livelihood] by means of portents or omens, nor by the science of astrology or bodily marks.
He should never seek alms by means of instruction or by preaching.
(7.8) [MDh 6.50] He should not approach a house crowded with ascetics, Brahmins, birds, dogs, or other mendicants. (7.9) [MDh 6.51]

One should, however, despise gains obtained through honor in every way; for even a liberated ascetic is bound by gains obtained through honor. (7.10) By consuming little food, by staying in solitude, and by sitting in a secluded place, one should restrain the senses when they are being carried away by sense-objects. (7.11)
Through the restraint of the senses, through the destruction of passion and hatred,
and through non-violence toward living beings, one becomes fit for immortality.
One should contemplate the destinies of men, which arise from the defects of their actions.
Falling into hell and undergoing torment in the abode of Yama;
separation from beloved ones and union with those who are unpleasant; being overcome by old age and being afflicted by diseases. (7.13–14)
The departure from this body, the subsequent conception in a womb,
the wanderings of this inner self through thousands of millions of births,
and the connection with suffering for embodied beings arising from unrighteousness— [these he perceives]. (MDh 6.63)
And he should contemplate the inexhaustible union with happiness that arises from the pursuit of dharma and artha;
furthermore, through yoga, he should perceive the subtlety of the Supreme Self and its manifestation within bodies, both high and low. (7.16–17)
Viṣṇu: These two—honor and dishonor—which cause pleasure and agitation to men, are the very opposites for a yogin and bring about his perfection. (7.18)
These two, honor and dishonor, are said to be poison and nectar;
therein, dishonor is the nectar, while honor is the supreme poison.
And furthermore: "Just as people despise him and speak ill of him, even so should the yogi conduct himself with discipline, not defiling the dharma of the virtuous. (7.20)
Furthermore, in that very same place: "One should practice that which is the essence, by which one may attain liberation;
for any other activity, though it be manifold, is indeed an obstacle to yoga. (7.21)
Having abandoned those actions performed for the sake of desire as well as those that are prohibited, one should constantly perform the obligatory duty.
Yama said:
"Whether one anoints his right arm with sandalwood paste or another hews at his left, one should regard them both as equal. (7.23)

In this way, his disposition toward both the pleasant and the unpleasant would always be such that he would conduct himself with equanimity toward everything, whether it be desirable or hateful. (7.24)
He is equal toward the virtuous and the wicked, and indeed equal toward enemy and friend;
he is the same in cold and heat, in pleasure and pain, and is free from all attachment.
He does not rejoice in honor nor does he become angry in dishonor;
he for whom passion and hatred are equal is a sage, free from longing for all things.
That man who, having heard, touched, seen, tasted, or smelled,
neither rejoices nor becomes dejected, should be known as one who has conquered his senses.
One should not be fickle with hands or feet, nor fickle with the eyes; one should also not be fickle with speech—this is the characteristic of a refined person. 7.28
Likewise:
From pure food obtained through pure means, which is free from any particular relish, pure *sattva* arises; from impure [food], it becomes defiled. (7.29)
A mass of flesh and blood, a collection of fat, marrow, and bones,
joined with nails and hair, and a mire of grease and the like.
Filled with urine and excrement, foul-smelling, bound by skin, the body is a vessel consisting of wind, a receptacle for impurities, and utterly devoid of essence. (7.31)
Resembling a painted wall, comparable to the foam of water, joined with the eternal and the non-eternal, it is a collection of passion and hatred. (7.32)
It has a single pillar, nine gates, three supporting beams, and consists of the five elements;
it is enclosed by a wall of pleasure, with the mind as its powerful master.
This city is crowded with the soldiers of the ten sense-faculties, infested by the wild beasts of disease, overrun by the objects of the senses, and presided over by consciousness. (7.34)
One should abandon this abode of the elements, which is possessed by old age and sorrow, a dwelling place for disease, afflicted, full of passion, and impermanent. (7.35)
Bathing, recitation, meditation, purity, and moderation in food—one who performs this pentad becomes liberated; not otherwise. (7.36)
One should constantly practice the habit of listening to the Purāṇas with devotion;
through listening to the Purāṇas, even a fool develops devotion. (7.37)
"Liberation comes through uninterrupted devotion; therefore, one should practice the Purāṇas.
Through that practice, the sage attains the state of the Supreme Brahman. (7.38)
Vasiṣṭha:
A wandering mendicant (parivrājaka) should set forth after granting fearlessness to all beings.
Furthermore, they cite this:
The sage who wanders having granted fearlessness to all beings never experiences fear from any being. But he who turns back without having granted fearlessness to all beings—
He destroys both those already born and those yet to be born, as well as his possessions, by accepting gifts.
(7.40) The single syllable is the supreme Brahman; breath control is the highest austerity;
begging is superior to fasting; and compassion excels giving. (7.41)
Likewise, later on:
"With unmanifested signs, with unmanifested conduct, though not insane, he should have the appearance of one who is insane.
And they also cite this:
Liberation is not for one who delights in the science of grammar, nor for one who delights in winning over the minds of the world,
nor for one who is intent on food and clothing.
Nor indeed for one who is fond of pleasant dwellings. (VaDh 10.18–20) One must not study, nor speak, nor listen in any way whatsoever.
Only when these have been previously perfected does one become an ascetic, and not otherwise. (7.43)
But having taken up the life of a wandering mendicant, he who does not abide by his own duty, the king shall brand him with the mark of a dog's foot and banish him from the realm. (7.44)
Later on:
"For the sake of gain and honor, exposition and the gathering of disciples—these and many other such elaborations belong to those wretched ascetics. (7.45)
Meditation, purity, begging for alms, and constant adherence to solitude—these are the four duties of a monk; a fifth does not exist. (7.46)
If one perceives here a second thing distinct from the self, then the scriptures are studied and the vastness of the texts is heard. (7.47)
Having established the sacred fire within himself, the twice-born man should become a wandering mendicant,
constantly devoted to the study of the Vedas and dedicated to the knowledge of the Self.
Having served all the stages of life, with anger conquered and senses subdued,
the twice-born who knows the meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras attains the world of Brahma;
for in all the stages of life, the rule ending only with death has been proclaimed.
Śātātapa says: "If an ascetic who has ascended to the lifelong vow of renunciation falls away from it, I see no expiation by which that self-destroyer might be purified. (7.50)
But he who, having taken up the life of a wandering mendicant, becomes a householder again,
is born as a worm in excrement for sixty thousand years.
He who, having previously made a vow here, does not carry out his renunciation, is consumed by false speech and sinks into blinding darkness. (7.52)
But he who, having become a renunciant, should again indulge in sexual intercourse, is born as a worm in excrement for sixty thousand years. (7.53)
In terrible, empty dwellings he becomes a most dreadful rat;
after a short time he is born from a womb, and for twelve births he shall be a dog.
For twenty years he is a glow-worm, for nine years a boar;
he is born as a tree devoid of flowers and fruit, covered all over with thorns.
Then, consumed by the forest fire, the lustful man becomes a withered stump;
thereafter, he remains unconscious for eight hundred and two years.
When a full thousand years have passed, he is born as a Brahmarākṣasa;
exhausted by hunger and thirst, a consumer of raw flesh and a drinker of blood,
he eventually attains liberation through the destruction of his lineage.
He who causes another to fall from renunciation, he who, being himself fallen, takes up renunciation, and he who creates obstacles to renunciation—these three are declared to be outcasts. || 7.58 ||
The Caṇḍālas known as Bindulas take the form of wandering mendicants;
their offspring born [to them] should be made to dwell together with the Caṇḍālas. (7.59)
Hārīta says: He who, having intentionally renounced according to the prescribed rule, should become a householder again,
is indeed one who has fallen from his high station (ārūḍhapatita) and is excluded from all religious duties.
He who, having abandoned the life of a wandering mendicant, becomes a householder again,
is born as a worm in excrement for sixty thousand years.
Thus, according to the supreme reading of the Śātātapa-smṛti:
"One who has fallen after having ascended [to the order of asceticism] shall destroy ten ancestors and ten descendants;
but a Brahmin ascetic who is properly established [in his vows] shall deliver those very same people. (7.62)
Therefore, with every effort, an ascetic should maintain the triple staff; by the observance of the duties of an ascetic, he shall not be born again in this world. (7.63)
Among all the stages of life, the bearer of the triple staff (tridaṇḍin) is indeed the one in the highest stage;
he alone should be honored with devotion by one who follows the true path.
The Brahmin who bears the form of the triple staff is Nārāyaṇa himself;
he who worships him with devotion has thereby worshipped Viṣṇu. (7.65)
One should daily pay homage with a spirit of devotion to him who bears the triple staff, who is the very form of Viṣṇu, and whose essence is Nārāyaṇa through the eight-syllable mantra.
Thus, O brahmins, has this eternal path of the righteous been described to you;
for when the terrible Kali age arrives, there will be others besides these who bear the insignia of the low.
They will all arise, illuminated by the fire of Gautama;
and in the Kali age, they will explain the entire meaning of the Vedas in a distorted manner.
Naked and disguised as Buddhists, they will revile the Veda;
those of small intelligence will recite the secret doctrines of the Vedas at night. (7.69)
Thinking, "We have been liberated," they will consume the food of Śūdras;
in that Kali age, they will even incite others who abide in their own dharma.
Many twice-born ones live by depending on a single bamboo;
yet, due to the abandonment of their duties, they fall into the terrible Raurava hell.
Therefore, a wise person should neither speak to them nor even look at them;
however, by looking at the sun, one is purified from the sight of them.
He who feeds a twice-born man at a śrāddha who is either naked or uninitiated offers semen, urine, and excrement to the ancestors. (7.73)
If, out of impulse or greed, a wise man has resorted to the single-staff order, he may again take up the triple-staff upon becoming disillusioned. (7.74)
Parāśara said: These two persons, having indeed pierced the solar orb, go [to the highest state]:
the wandering mendicant absorbed in yoga, and he who is slain facing the enemy in battle. (7.75)
Seeing that twice-born man who has renounced all worldly ties, the Sun moves from his station, thinking:
"Having pierced through my orb, this man shall attain the Supreme Brahman."
Kātyāyana says: One should avoid defects such as desire and anger for as long as one lives; by thus constantly practicing self-restraint, the ascetic attains Brahman. (7.77)
Uśanas said: Having abandoned attachment, conquered anger, eating light food, and mastered the senses, one should close the doors with the intellect and fix the mind in meditation. (7.78)
Vyāsa said:
One who knows all things and is free from attachment should diligently practice all that knowledge of the Self which was previously indicated by me in the past. (7.79)
One who contemplates the Self should diligently avoid worldly affairs;
with effort, one should study the various Upaniṣads, which are the cause of liberation. 7.80

Āpastamba: Now, regarding the wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*). He goes forth from this very stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*). For him they prescribe: "He should be without fire, without a fixed dwelling, without shelter, and without protection; a sage (*muni*) who has renounced even his Vedic recitation (*svādhyāya*), having obtained in the village only what is necessary for the maintenance of life, he should wander without regard for this world or the next. (ĀpDh 2.21.7–10) Bṛhaspati:
For those dwelling in the three stages of life, celibacy is absolute;
the householder alone is a practitioner of celibacy by virtue of his restriction to his own wife. (7.82)
Later on: "One should not [associate with] kinsmen, sons, friends, and so forth, even if they are esteemed among the twice-born;
even upon seeing them in another country, one should not dwell together with them."
In that case, the persistence of passion, hatred, and the like is inevitable.
Likewise:
A renunciant should not be a permanent resident at a sacred ford, nor should he be intent on fasting;
he should not have a habit of teaching, nor should he be devoted to exposition. (7.84)
Śaṅkha says:
Even if one person anoints his arm with sandalwood paste while another hacks at it,
one should not harbor thoughts of either as being either auspicious or inauspicious.
Beneficent toward all beings, friendly, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal. || 7.85 ||
He should not be one who delights in non-internal (worldly) treatises, nor should he be an astrologer;
furthermore, he should not, even for the sake of dharma, treat diseases, poisons, or vetālas. 7.86
One should not gather disciples, nor should one reveal one's own knowledge;
one should not speak refined speech, but should act like a child or as if mute. (7.87)
Later on: Having renounced even the duties of an ascetic and remaining constantly established in yoga for three years, he attains liberation after death. (7.88)
Therefore, one who desires sovereignty— that supreme station of Viṣṇu—
should reach the stage of absolute liberation (kaivalyāśrama) and practice it for even a single day, O twice-born.
Śaṅkha and Likhita say:

Subsisting on alms, having no desire for sharing, avoiding food from those who are accused or outcastes, and living on food that is not censured or defiled; content with only a loincloth and a covering; with his impurities fully ripened away, awaiting his time; ever disciplined, delighting in the Self, not habitually staying in one place, free from hypocrisy, deceit, and arrogance; never dwelling in a single village, he should wander about, having abandoned the faults of attachment. Skilled in the purpose of self-knowledge and discrimination, after the two months of the rainy season, he should have no desire to stay in one place; he should perform purification, rinsing, and other rites with water drawn [from a source]. 7.90.
Likewise: "He who endures the word-arrows discharged by the wicked and does not become angry, remaining instead well-pleased in his disposition—that self-control of his is born of wisdom. (7.91)
When one maintains with the intellect the pairs of opposites such as cold and heat, as well as those inflicted by wicked people, that is known as endurance (titikṣā) and forbearance (kṣamā). 7.92.
Toward beings whether dear or disliked, and in times of misfortune or prosperity, he was tranquil, having attained supreme wisdom, characterized by peace and self-control. (7.93)
He who, through austerity, knowledge, self-restraint, and sovereignty, is never provoked to anger even when struck by the sharp arrows of speech— that steadfast man is not deluded in this world.
The ascetic who practices the dharma of liberation here with a gentle disposition quickly abandons the bondage of existence and becomes fit for immortality.
In that very manner,
he should practice begging for alms from all four social orders, yet he should avoid those who have fallen from their status.
With his senses, speech, and eyes restrained, he should avoid each preceding order in preference for the next.
Vṛddha-Dakṣa says:
"The staff of speech, the staff of mind, and likewise the staff of action—one becomes a 'staff-bearer' (daṇḍin) by means of these staffs, but certainly not from carrying a bamboo rod. (7.97)
The restraint of speech is the practice of silence; the restraint of action is non-violence. But the restraint of the mind consists in the steady holding of the breath. (7.98)
Kapila: [He speaks.]

One should avoid pronouncing blessings of well-being (*svasti*). One should neither take refuge [in worldly things] nor cause others to do so; one may enter a place where refuge has already been taken. Then, one should worship Brahman. One should sleep with the mind fixed on that alone. Having entered a temple of the gods free from reproach, one should pass the night somehow or other, remaining awake even while in deep sleep. Sitting down, having sipped water (*ācamana*) and performed three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), one should sip water again. At night, one should sip water using a water-pot placed upon a wooden stand; during the day, from a flowing stream. One should not abandon a sacred place that is pleasing to the heart and abundant in water. One should not be greedy, nor intent upon the exposition of the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*. (7.99)
Later on.

One who cannot endure [the cold] should kindle a fire with fuel that has fallen of its own accord and is free of living beings. There is no fault in eating seeds, roots, and fruits that are devoid of life. One should not harm anything sentient or insentient for the sake of a minor purpose. There is no fault in collecting a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*), purifying grass (*pavitra*), a sling for carrying loads (*kusīda*), metallic vessels, and so forth. Even when provoked to anger, one should not become angry; even when gratified, one should not become pleased. One should desire neither death nor life. One should not discard an alms-bowl that has not been scorched. For the sake of purification, one should recite prayers while standing in water that is immediately available—even for a moment—rather than making it foul. Then, one should contemplate the Four-Armed [Lord]. One should not show partiality toward a single deity. One should abandon a nearby refuge that provides shelter. Upon seeing a beautiful woman, one should never gaze at her; one should close one's eyes. One should never utter "Oṃ" with a trembling voice. (7.100)
In the same way,
the withdrawal of all the senses, which brings about both seen and unseen results,
must be performed by the ascetic who is vigilant and desires ultimate happiness. (7.101)
For one who is habituated to singing the Gītās and devoted to breath control (prāṇāyāma), sins—even those committed in previous births—do not taint them at all. 7.102.
Sacrificial ritual;
a metallic vessel that destroys seeds; the emission of semen; white clothing;
sleeping during the day; and idle chatter—these are the six causes of downfall for ascetics. (7.103)
One should never accept long-standing articles such as accumulated stores,
nor grass, clay, wood, water, stones, leaves, roots, or fruits;
one should not take what has not been offered, nor should one hoard what has been offered.

Having accepted as a gift that which should not be accepted— female and male slaves, a house, a vehicle, cattle, land, grain, wealth, or liquids— one destroys two hundred generations of one's lineage.
Vṛddha-Jābāli says:
A self-controlled ascetic should not go to rites of hospitality, śrāddhas, or sacrifices; nor to divine processions, festivals, and the like; nor to any kind of worldly spectacles. (7.106)
Later on: "But that monk who is intent on giving and he who is a hoarder of robes and such—both of them, due to their dull-wittedness, fall into the Puti hell. (7.107)
Dattātreya said:
"That fool who, having received a Vaiṣṇava liṅga, abandons it, goes to a terrible, intense, and dreadful hell of great distress. (7.108)

Devala says: Being impartial toward friend and foe, being without possessions, practicing celibacy, engaging in auspicious conduct, refining one's character, and the avoidance of attachment to living beings, training, jewels, wealth, grain, and sensual objects, as well as envy, pride, deceit, delusion, joy, hostility, wonder, dispute, fear, and discursive thought—these are the duties of an ascetic. 7.109.
A mendicant should daily beg for food and medicine at the house of a virtuous householder, so that no remnant remains.
If an ascetic, out of delusion, keeps food or medicine for his own sake beyond what is required for that time, he falls into hell. (7.111)
One should accept the means for practicing dharma from those who are virtuous and active in it;
one should not accept anything, even out of negligence, from those who have turned away from it.
Garga says:
Having renounced all duties, one should take refuge in the duty of an ascetic;
one who has fallen away from the duty of an ascetic does not enjoy the fruit of dharma. (7.113)
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha says: One should avoid plucking flowers, roots, and fruits; cutting the tips [of plants]; and the giving or taking of honey and meat. 7.114.
Medhātithi: "The triple staff, the water-pot, the sling, the alms-bowl, the seat, and a garment for covering the privities—these six are his possessions. (7.115)
A renunciant should not accept these six things—immovable property, moving property, seeds, money, poison, or weapons—as he would urine or excrement. (7.116)
Alms-gathering, recitation, bathing, meditation, purification, and worship of the gods—these six must always be performed like the punishment of a king. (7.117)
One should avoid the knowledge of tastes, the doctrine of ritual action, astrology, buying and selling, and various crafts, just as one avoids the wives of others. 7.118.
One should not look at actors and the like, gambling, women, friends, nor food and drink, nor a woman in her courses—these six—as one would excrement. (7.119)
A mendicant should never dwell for any length of time in these six places: in a military camp, in a city, in a caravan, in a marketplace, in a cow-pen, or in a house. (7.120)
Traveling by night, using a vehicle, talk of women, greed, a bedstead, and white clothing— these are the six causes of downfall for ascetics.
A renunciant should never, even in his mind, contemplate these six: passion, hatred, intoxication, pride, hypocrisy, and malice toward others or oneself. (7.122)
A fixed seat, the loss of the alms-bowl, accumulation of possessions, gathering of disciples, sleeping by day, and idle chatter—these six are the bonds for an ascetic. (7.123)
A place beyond one day’s journey in a village, or beyond five days’ journey in a city—other than during the rainy season—is declared to be a faulty seat for staying. (7.124)
If there is not even the possession of a single one of the aforementioned mendicant’s vessels, that is called the "loss of the vessel" for a monk who subsists on alms. (7.125)
The acceptance of a second item, such as a bowl or a triple staff, for the purpose of use at another time—that too would be an accumulation of material goods. (7.126)
The gathering of disciples for the sake of service, gain, honor, or fame, and not out of compassion, is to be known as the "gathering of disciples" [in name only]. (7.127)
Knowledge is called day because it is luminous; ignorance is called night.
That negligence which occurs in the practice of knowledge is called sleeping during the day. (7.128)
Except for talk concerning the internal self, the journey for alms, praise of the gods, a request for favor, or inquiries about the road, any other speech is called idle chatter. (7.129)
One who is tongueless, impotent, lame, blind, deaf, and deluded—he is called a monk by virtue of these six qualities; of this there is no doubt. (7.130)
He who, even while eating, is not attached, thinking "this is delicious" or "this is not," and who regards "this is pungent" or "this is sweet"—him they call tongueless. (7.131)
He who, upon seeing a woman just born, one sixteen years of age,
and one a hundred years old, remains free from any change of feeling— he is a eunuch.
He whose wandering for alms and for the discharge of excrement and urine does not extend beyond a single yojana—he is always truly lame. (7.133)
Whether standing or walking, he whose sight does not reach far—
having been freed from fear for the duration of four ages— is called a blind wandering mendicant.
He who, having heard speech that is beneficial or harmful, pleasing to the mind or bringing sorrow, does not listen as if he were deaf—he is indeed called deaf. (7.135)
He who, while in the presence of others' property, remains indifferent with his senses unimpaired, yet behaves as if asleep—he too is called a deluded monk. (7.136)
Endowed with supreme faith and devoted solely to the Supreme Self,
one who knows the ten and six [principles] is liberated from both the gross and subtle bodies.
Jamadagni said:
"That foolish soul who uproots grain, trees, creepers, climbing plants, as well as stationary and moving beings, falls into hell. (7.138)

One who eats from a single house, one who accepts two invitations, one who lives on alms, and one who gathers food in three ways—these four are indeed fallen ascetics; of this there is no doubt. (7.139)
A renunciant, a student of sacred knowledge, and a widow should avoid betel, the application of unguents, and eating from a vessel of white copper. 7.140.
These two, liquor and betel-leaf, are indeed equal in their potency;
therefore, an ascetic should avoid betel-leaf with every effort. (7.141)
Śaunaka:

He should not proclaim his own virtues; even when threatened, he should not become angry; even when honored, he should not give way to joy. He should perform the three daily ablutions with a staff in hand. Likewise, he should not cross a river by leaping over it, nor should he swim across it with his arms. He should desire neither death nor life. He should not wander about at night, nor during the two twilights. He should avoid chewing betel. He should not seek oil massages or a second meal. He should not attend weddings, *śrāddha* ceremonies, sacrifices, divine processions, or festivals. Furthermore, he should avoid forming friendships with fellow forest-dwellers (*vānaprasthas*) or householders (*gṛhasthas*) when traveling in a caravan. (7.142)

Paiṭhīnasi says: "Being praised, he should not be pleased; being reviled, he should not become angry; he should conduct himself with equanimity, having attained both of these through knowledge and austerity. (7.143)
Satyakāma said:
"Having abandoned all dharmas, one should take refuge in the dharma of liberation (mokṣadharma).
One who has fallen away from the dharma of liberation undergoes the purificatory rites (saṃskāra). (7.144)
One should not stand upon ground that has not been inspected, nor should one travel by a path where the sun does not shine;
one should not harm any living beings through action, thought, or speech. (7.145)
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "Conduct," in the Yatidharmasamuccaya.
[Now begins] the eighth chapter.
The Procedure for Atonement regarding the Duties of the *liṅgin*.
Now, the duties of the *liṅgin*, beginning with shaving and including atonement, are described. Regarding this, Śaunaka states:
"One should have [the hair] shaved during the junctions of the seasons, excluding the tuft (*śikhā*); one should not have the body hairs shaved. (8.1)
Devala says:
The lunar day following the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight is known as the junction of the seasons (*ṛtusaṃdhi*); one should have the shaving of the head performed on that occasion.

It has been written: at all the junctions of the seasons, except for the interval between the Cāturmāsya festivals, a renunciant (yati) should shave his head on the full moon day, with the exception of the top-knot (śikhā). 8.3.
In the event of failure to obtain [the necessary materials], or when afflicted by disease, or during calamities such as those caused by kings or thieves,
one should perform the sowing from the full moon day until the fifth day of the dark fortnight.

The time of the junction between seasons (*ṛtusaṃdhikāla*) is to be understood as that day-and-night (*ahorātra*) which is the junction between the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight and the following first day (*pratipad*). The meaning is that one should perform the shaving (*vapana*) during that very day-and-night which constitutes the junction between the fifteenth day and the first day of the dark fortnight. || 8.5 ||
Devala: After the Cāturmāsya [observance], one should have the hair of the head and beard removed, but not the hair of the lower body. 8.6.
Manu:
Having had his hair, nails, and beard clipped, carrying a bowl, a staff, and a water-pot, he should wander constantly, self-restrained, without causing pain to any living beings. (MDh 6.52)
Devala says:

Whether it be total tonsure or the option of leaving a crest-lock, if one should destroy [the hair] through negligence, he is purified by the Prājāpatya penance; there is no doubt in this matter. || 8.8 ||
Gālava says: Having performed the shaving of hair from three locations and having performed a Prājāpatya penance, one should perform one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). 8.9.
Jamadagni says:
A renunciant who shaves his armpits, private parts, and so forth, shall perform an expiation;
having performed three *prājāpatya* penances and hundreds of breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*). || 8.10 ||
This is the penance for the simultaneous shaving of the armpits, the pubic region, and so forth. Medhātithi states:

"A monk should have his hair shaved during the seasonal transitions, excluding the armpits, the pubic region, and the tuft; he should never, at any time during the year, fail to observe the three-shaven (traimuṇḍya) rule. (8.11)
After shaving, having bathed with twelve applications of clay,
the ascetic should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and purify himself with the Vāruṇī verses.
Having bathed and emerged from the water, he should cleanse his shins with the remaining earth and water;
for a mendicant is rendered impure by the water dripping from his loincloth.
If one should void urine or feces, one should perform a twofold bath;
if one drinks or eats without having bathed for two muhūrtas, the penance is sixfold.
If a staff or other such object has been taken and is not destroyed, one should not abandon it;
if it is destroyed, one should throw it into water with the mantra: "Go to the ocean, svāhā! (8.15)
Having cast that away, he should take another with either the Gāyatrī or the Praṇava;
[he should take] the sacred thread with "That, may it be auspicious for us" (tac chaṃ yoḥ), and the water-pot with verses that do not contain specific deity-mantras (abliṅga).
He should suspend his water-pot, filled with water and attached by a cord, in the air at a height of one arrow-length; otherwise, the ascetic incurs fault. (8.17)
In the forest, he may go without a triple staff for a distance of three arrow-shots; he does not incur fault [thereby], whereas he incurs fault by walking from house to house in a village. (8.18)

Likewise: "If one should abandon the triple staff and other such items that have been properly taken up and are not yet ruined, one must stay overnight and perform hundreds of breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma). (8.19)
Gālava says:

For one who does not perform the ritual sipping (ācamana), libations (tarpaṇa), and worship (upasthāna) with a water-strainer (jalapavitra) that is available, all of that becomes fruitless. An expiation is prescribed for him: having performed three hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), he should mutter [the sacred syllables] three times three hundred. Having drunk water without a water-strainer, he should maintain ten breath-restraints. 8.20.
Atri:
If one drinks water that is tainted by smell, color, or taste, or is turbid, or defiled by hair, or drinks it without a cloth [filter], one should perform ten breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). 8.21.
In that regard, when streams have been drawn out and in clear lakes,
water purified by a cloth need not be used, for the Veda declares it to be pure.
Thus, this has already been answered by him previously [see 6.44]. || 8.22 ||
Gālava:

One should perform the taking up and the binding of the water-strainer (*jalapavitra*) with the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*). One must not separate the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*) from the water-strainer. If this occurs through negligence, one should sip water (*ācamana*), perform three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), and sip water again. However, during the time of bathing or eating, one must not separate the triple staff [from the body]. If this occurs through negligence, one should sip water, perform three breath-restraints, and sip water again. One should set down the triple staff with its head toward the east or north, reciting: "Thou art the station of Viṣṇu. If it falls to the ground, one should mutter: "Arise, O Lord of Prayer (*brahmaṇaspati*). Regarding other staffs, having touched them, one should wash them while reciting: "By the mind of Viṣṇu ye are purified," and perform three breath-restraints. If this is done through ignorance, one should wash them with the *praṇava* and repeat the *praṇava* ten times. (8.23)
Garga says:

Having rubbed the staff together and muttered the mantra "O Tree, with wide-reaching limbs," and having washed it while reciting "O you who are purified by the mind of Viṣṇu," he should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). If he has used it unknowingly, he should wash it with the syllable Om (praṇava) and repeat the Praṇava ten times. || 8.24 ||
Gālava:
"In the event of the friction between the water-pot and the vessel containing the sacred water, immediate renunciation [of the object] is prescribed. (8.25)
Atri: One should not rub the interior of a vessel with oil; if this is done through ignorance, one shall fall into impurity. 8.26.
He himself says:

having abandoned an undamaged or non-defective vessel, or items such as the triple staff (tridaṇḍa), one should fast for a day and night and recite the Gāyatrī mantra one hundred and eight times. Having used a broken vessel, one should observe three days of fasting. (8.27)
Jamadagni says:
In the case of a breach of purity, one should perform a hundred [repetitions]; likewise in the case of a breakage of a vessel.
However, when a vessel held by another is broken, one should observe three fasts.
Later on: "If a mendicant's vessel has been touched by pus, blood, or flesh, or likewise by feces, urine, semen, tears, or phlegm, he should discard it. (8.29)
Having touched a dog, a crow, a mouse, a cow, a camel, a jackal, or a monkey, as well as a Caṇḍāla or one who has fallen from his caste, one should discard the vessel held in the hand. 8.30.
If a mendicant's staff is touched by marrow, urine, or feces, or by semen, saliva, or blood, he should discard it; for anything else, it deserves purification. 8.31
Without a staff, he should not go even from house to house within a village;
likewise, he should perform breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) when traveling on a path in the forest. 8.32.

If he should go home or to the forest without having been punished, even for as little as three finger-joints [of debt], he should return to his nest and perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) each time. 8.33.
There must never be a separation from the triple staff, the seat, the bowl, and so forth; by being separated from them, the mendicant falls, and for that, an expiation is prescribed. (8.34)
But upon the loss of the triple staff, one should perform a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas);
for the loss of the water-pot, fifty; and for the loss of the alms-bowl, sixteen are prescribed.
Eight [verses] are to be known for the purifiers (pavitra), six are proclaimed for the carrying-pole (śikya), and four are to be known for the seat; this indeed is the rite of purification.

Satyakāma and Jābāla: Now we shall explain the penance for mendicants. If one goes having abandoned the alms-bowl within the distance of a *krośa*, he is subject to penance; having performed thirty *prāṇāyāmas*, he should recite [the sacred syllable] three hundred times three. If, having abandoned the triple staff or the bowl and seat, he goes to the far bank of a river flowing to the ocean, he should perform three fasts and practice a hundred *prāṇāyāmas*. (8.37)
Regarding what follows:

if one comes into contact with a woman or a Śūdra, one should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). If one comes into contact with a donkey or a camel, one should practice six breath-restraints. If one comes into contact with a dog, a pig, or a Caṇḍāla, one should maintain twelve breath-restraints. Having committed a transgression of prescribed rules, one should maintain twelve breath-restraints. (8.38)
The capable one:
Having abandoned his staff and alms-bowl, the ascetic should stay for only one night;
he should take up the staff with the mantra and abandon the alms-bowl. (8.39)
Atri: If one should ever drop a staff or even a vessel upon the ground, one should perform sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), or eight, six, or twelve. (8.40)
Devala said:
O great sage, when a staff or other such items have been defiled by excrement, carnivorous animals, and the like, tell me what should be done there so that purification may occur. (8.41)
Having carefully cleansed staves with twelve applications of clay and water, and having recited the Puruṣa Sūkta, one should purify them even with water;
but for others, O King of kings, immediate abandonment is prescribed. (8.42)

One should discard vessels, purifiers, and such items if they have been defiled by white remnants, tears, feces, urine, phlegm, a Śūdra, a cow, or fire; or if they have been touched by thieves and the like. (8.43)
Having received [the staff and other requisites] from the Śūdra and other castes in order, the ascetic shall perform one hundred, fifty, five, or even ten breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). (8.44)
Atri states: Sandals, an umbrella, clothing, and other such items used for the purpose of begging—
having accepted these from a Śūdra, one should perform a hundred [penances], and likewise half a hundred from a Vaiśya.
From a Kṣatriya, twenty-five [years], and from a low-caste Brāhmaṇa, ten indeed.
Vṛddha-Jābāli says:
Having set aside his triple staff and water-purifier, a mendicant within a house should recite the Puruṣasūkta and perform ten breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).
Devala says:
A householder who eats the food of others and a mendicant who neglects his alms-bowl is born among the animal species for ten thousand years.
In the absence of a bowl, a leaf-cup shall always serve as the mendicant’s bowl;
that bowl shall remain in use only so long as a primary one is not obtained. (8.48)
Kapila says: One who is incapable [of other duties] should maintain a needle, a nail-cutter, a water-vessel for purificatory water, and both an inner garment and an outer garment. 8.49.
Atri: Having abandoned the sacred thread, one should perform six *kṛcchra* penances together with the *gāyatrī*; then one should undergo initiation once again. 8.50.
Vṛddha-Jābāli says:
If a mendicant devoted to meditation should be devoid of the sacred thread (yajñopavīta), his ritual acts would be fruitless; therefore, an expiation is prescribed. 8.51.
One should perform six Prājāpatya penances accompanied by the Gāyatrī;
having undergone the rite of re-consecration, the sacred thread (yajñopavīta) must be worn once more. (8.52)
One should take up the triple staff and not allow for any delay;
thus one does not go to hell, but goes instead to a happy rebirth. (8.53)
This very [act] constitutes the expiation for those who have performed the wandering life (*pārivrājya*) consisting of the renunciation of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). Hārīta says:
"Whatever eating and other such acts are performed without the sacred thread, I shall declare to you the expiation sufficient for the pacification of that sin. (8.54)
But for those [deities], being pure and well-composed, he should perform their daily offerings of food and so forth, according to the prescribed rites, with five hundred breath-restraints (asuyama).
In this world, the sins of one who delights in the practice of yoga are destroyed;
therefore, becoming devoted to yoga, one should constantly meditate during the intervals between ritual actions.
He himself says:
"But if a lord of brahmins, out of ignorance, voids urine or excrement without his sacred thread, he should perform six breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma). (8.57)
One should always wear the sacred thread (yajñopavīta), except during necessary duties; while performing such necessary acts, one should cast it over the back in the nivīta fashion. (8.58)
Now, clothing is discussed. Regarding this, Gautama says:
"He shall wear a garment for the purpose of covering his private parts; some say it should be worn after washing one that has been discarded. Bṛhaspati says:
And for the purpose of covering his private parts, he should wear a worn-out garment; some, however, say that what has become soiled should be washed and discarded outside. 8.60.
Hārīta says:
One may take a garment for the loincloth, a patched cloak to ward off the cold, and also sandals; one should not make a collection of anything else. (8.61)
Jābāli says:

One should wear a garment made of cotton, or a cloth other than one made of bark; otherwise, one shall not be purified by the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), nor even by the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana).
He should wear only saffron-colored clothing, whether made of cotton or a patched garment.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"With the triple staff and the purifier (pavitra) in his hand, wearing garments of kuśa grass, bark, or rags, he may wear a woolen blanket for protection against the cold—some say so.

Although it is stated without qualification that [the garment] should be "ochre" (kāṣāya), it must nevertheless be dyed with the mineral substance known as red ochre (gairika). For Vṛddha-Jābāli makes this known by prohibiting a householder from assuming the outward signs of the wandering mendicant:
"He should not wear clothing dyed with minerals, nor should he carry a sling;
he should not carry the triple staff—these are the characteristics of a *snātaka*. (8.64)
Dattātreya says:
In the stage of liberation (mokṣāśrama), it is prescribed that a garment dyed with red ochre (gairika) should be worn;
the sacred thread (yajñopavīta), however, should be white and consist of nine strands.
Even when these measures have been prescribed, one must not form an attachment to them. And so Devala says:
"One who regards clay and gold as equal, who is unattached even toward his own kinsmen, and who remains impartial—" (8.66).
Manu says:
"Having emerged from attachment to the elements," (8.67).

Vasiṣṭha: He who has no attachment to a hut, nor to water, nor to clothing, nor to the three times of day (tripuṣkara), nor to a house, nor to a seat, nor to food—he indeed is a knower of liberation. (VaDh 10.23)
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Rule for Atonement regarding the Characteristics of the Mark," in the *Yatidharmasamuccaya*. 8.69.
The ninth chapter, "The Determination of Movement and Stationariness," now defines the movement and stationariness of ascetics (*yatins*). Regarding this, Gautama says:
One whose semen is drawn upward and who is firm in his conduct during the rainy season. (GDh 3.11–12) Medhātithi:
When the sun has risen, except at midday; and when the sun has not yet set.
But he is seen as one who should be homeless, free from attachment like the sun. 9.2
One should spend the night in a single spot within a temple or a fire-sanctuary;
elsewhere, due to the fear of death and great calamities. 9.3.
One should spend the four months of the rainy season outside the village;
even there, the two previously mentioned reasons for undertaking this practice remain unaltered.

In this regard, it is understood that one must dwell in one place during the rainy season, and otherwise one must not dwell there. Regarding this, Manu has stated that the benefit [of such a rule] is slight:
"He should generally wander for eight months—those of summer and winter—for the sake of compassion toward all living beings; he may dwell in one place during the rains. (9.5)
Regarding this, Kratu specifies the favor indicated by the word "mostly":
"In a village he may stay for one day, in a town for three, and in a city for five or seven;
during the rainy season he should remain in one place, but on the path he should travel as soon as the sun has risen. (9.6)
Having renounced [the fruits of action] in the Supreme Brahman, performing actions according to his ability,
he should be primarily intent on the practice of yoga, devoted to the recitation of mantras, and dedicated to forgiveness. (9.7)
One should wander to sacred fords and temples of the deities,
and one should perform penances such as the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* for the sake of one’s own purification.
Neither blind, nor diseased, nor lame, he should not stay anywhere for more than six nights;
if he is intent on dharma, he may stay in another land either for that duration or for all his life.
Starting from the month of Śrāvaṇa until the end of four months, all ascetics shall dwell together in one place; this is the settled rule. (9.10)
Devala says:
One should not dwell in one place for long, except during the rainy season. The "rainy season" consists of four months beginning with Śrāvaṇa; during that time, one should not travel. 9.11.
Gālava said:
During the rainy season, he should dwell in one place, either in an empty house or at the foot of a tree. 9.12.
Viśvāmitra says:
Even apart from the rainy seasons, he may indeed dwell in one place. 9.13.
Vṛddha-Manu says: "One who has increased in dharma may live even in one place until death; however, teachers maintain that he should be inclined to travel elsewhere. (9.14)
Regarding the manner and the location, Yama said:
"A sage should dwell for one night in a village and five nights in a town;
he may reside in one place during the four months of the rainy season. (9.15)
Living beings in the water, living beings on land, and hosts of living beings in the sky—
when the world is crowded with these multitudes of living beings, one may dwell together in one place during the rains.
The path of the sun has been pointed out; one should traverse the earth like an insect, possessing a wise mind and being well-composed, with no store for the morrow.
Having abandoned even the evacuation of feces and urine, he should not wander elsewhere at night, nor at midday, nor during the two twilights. 9.18.
One should always wander alone, liberated in soul and without companion;
for the path of one who is alone becomes level, whereas elsewhere one is overcome.
One should set down one's foot purified by vision; one should drink water purified by a cloth;
one should utter speech that is true and kind; and one should act for the welfare of all beings. (9.20)
Wearing but a single garment, eating but one meal a day, and using but a single bowl, the mendicant should wander alone through the village; that is the ancient vow of the seers.
He should always sleep on the bare ground and dwell in an uncertain residence;
being constantly in the forest, he should keep his head shaven and practice meditation with the mind.
One should not, even in thought, consider the place for alms, nor kings, kinsmen, sons, friends, and women, nor even stories of their favors. (9.23)
"Come," "Go," "Stay"—even such words of welcome for a friend, a sage devoted to liberation would not utter as a mark of honor. (9.24)
Day after day, one should indeed offer salutations to those ascetics who are advanced in their vows and who follow their own dharma, regarding them as the very form of Viṣṇu.
If there should be a renunciant who was previously ordained, or one equal in terms of his dharma, he should perform salutations, worship, and so forth for him, but not for anyone else. (9.26)
An ascetic should bow to aged ascetics who abide in their own duty and to the gods;
he should not bow to anyone belonging to another stage of life, even if that person is praiseworthy. 9.27.
One should not be satiated with food in the evening or in the morning, nor should one become attached to eating; one should never, out of desire, become attached to the objects of the senses. (9.28)
One may ask for the path and say "give alms"—these two things alone should be spoken; everything else is forbidden. (9.29)
Atri:
The wise man, adhering to the hidden dharma, remaining in the conduct of the ignorant, though unconfused, should move about in the form of a fool, practicing dharma without causing offense. 9.30
Kapila says: One should maintain one's existence in any way whatsoever, like an old man or a sick person. 9.31.
Bṛhaspati says: A wandering ascetic (yati) should never take provisions for a journey except in times of distress;
in times of distress, he may accept cooked food, but only as much as is required for a single day.
Jamadagni said:
Having voided urine or excrement in a forest, in a desolate place, or on a path infested with thieves and tigers, one who holds an object in his hand does not become defiled. (9.33)
Having placed that object on the ground and performed purification according to the rule,
he should take that object onto his lap, having sipped water, being self-controlled and pure.
Gālava says:
For traveling more than a yojana, one should perform twelve breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). || 9.35 ||

Now, the time for the Cāturmāsya is stated: beginning on the full moon of Āṣāḍha, the conclusion is on the full moon of Kārttika; or else, beginning on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, the conclusion is on the full moon of Mārgaśīrṣa. Others, however, say this: because of the seasonal injunction "he should be firm in his conduct during the rains," the completion of the vow occurs after two months. (9.36) Jābāli says: A mendicant should wander through the eight months of summer and winter;
for the sake of compassion toward all beings, he should dwell in one place during the rains. (9.37)

One should dwell in a village for the four months of the rainy season, endowed with faith and devotion; for by not causing disturbance to the established order, one shall attain the eternal state. 9.38.
As long as it rains even out of season and the earth remains soaked, one should extend the village boundary no further than one *krośa*, even if the area is vast. (9.39)

Medhātithi says: On the twelfth day, one should take auspicious, dry clay from a commendable place during the bright fortnight while remaining pure; having taken the clay, one should use a small amount without causing any injury to the earth. (9.40)
As long as it rains even out of season, and as long as the earth remains soaked,
a monk who observes his own duty should not wander;
he should reside for four months beginning with Āṣāḍha until the rising of Kārttika.
Atri said:
I shall declare the rule for the four-monthly rites (cāturmāsya) for ascetics of restrained self; by resorting to which one will always be liberated, without a doubt. 9.42.
The time beginning from the bright fortnight until the full moon of Āṣāḍha;
on some auspicious day therein, or even on a day chosen by resolve. (9.43)
Having gone to a pure, ordinary ground that is dry and free from gravel, stones, creepers, vines, clods of earth, and the like, the ascetic [should prepare his seat] upon sandy soil. (9.44)
Remembering Hari in the form of the Boar, who supported the earth,
and Vāsudeva, the sanctifier who dwells within all beings.
O Goddess, you have been consecrated by the Self-Existent One himself with the syllable *praṇava*,
since you were created by the God of gods for the sake of purity.
Likewise, O Goddess Earth, you have been consecrated by means of the syllable *praṇava*;
having thus consecrated the earth with these mantras accompanied by the *praṇava*, [one should proceed].

Beginning with "Trampled by horses," at every step: "Thou art lifted up"; "The earth is a cow"; "O clay, destroy [evil]"; "By thee destroyed"; "O clay, grant [blessings]"; "Her whose door is fragrance"; "The Sovereign. (9.48)
O Goddess, may that Keśava, the upholder of the earth, who rescued you with his fanged form of wrath, protect me along with you.
O Goddess Vasudhā, you are remembered as the support of all beings;
you are the protector, the purifier, the sustainer, and the granter of fearlessness to all creatures.
"O Goddess, you are Viṣṇukrāntā; you are the earth that has stepped across the universe.
O Mādhavī, together with Viṣṇu, protect me from all beings!"—having thus addressed Mādhavī, the sustainer of the world, he remained composed in spirit. (9.51)
O earth, you were given by Brahmā and consecrated by Kāśyapa;
O earth, destroy all that evil deed which has been committed by me.
With the two verses beginning "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," he should take auspicious clay. Then, with darbha grass in hand, the ascetic, seated upon them facing the east,
should undertake this vow for the rainy season, which lasts for four months.
For four months, Mādhava, the Lord of the World, will indeed go to sleep upon the body of Śeṣa together with Lakṣmī for the welfare of all beings.
And until that eternal one has risen from his sleep,
I shall indeed remain here for the welfare of all beings.
Having recited the verse "The sky is firm," he should then touch the earth;
by this very procedure, the mendicant [should do so] in the month of Āṣāḍha.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, or even on the full moon day,
if that full moon is conjoined with the Uttarāṣāḍhā constellation.
Having taken earth with the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," he should bring that earth;
then, with this very mantra, he should worship the sacred bathing places (tīrthas). || 9.58 ||
Having paid homage according to the prescribed rite to the ascetics in order of seniority,
the junior ascetic should offer earth to the elder ascetic.
Then one should worship one or two morsels of food with this mantra:
"Accept this auspicious clay, O mendicant, which removes all sins. (9.60)
"May this goddess, together with Viṣṇu, protect you and us.
Having thus taken the clay, one should perform the bath and other rites with it. (9.61)
Having thus brought clay, he should perform the cleansing rites with that clay gathered at that very time for as long as four months.
Starting from the first day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, which occurs on the following day, the ascetic should not travel for the four months, nor should he have his head shaved. (9.63)
One may have hair shaved on the day of the undertaking or the day of the rising;
however, even during shaving, one should never shave the hair below the throat, nor the crest-lock, the eyes, or the eyebrows.
If the commencement on the twelfth or the full moon day is obstructed by impediments due to lack of space, one should proceed until the fifth day of the dark fortnight.
If a mendicant travels beyond that point, he becomes liable for penance; if he goes there under a pretext, the monk should perform one *kṛcchra* penance. (9.66)
If one should travel more than a *krośa* beyond the boundary of a village that is situated in a wide area,
one should perform thirty *prāṇāyāmas* and recite [the mantra] three hundred times three.
This expiation applies to one who returns on that very same day. However, regarding one who has stayed there for the night, Vṛddhajābāli states the following expiation:
"In a village, one should not go beyond the boundary; in a large area, one should not go more than a *krośa*.
If someone, through negligence, should travel more than a *krośa*," [he must perform penance].
He shall be purified by a Prājāpatya penance, as well as by sixteen suppressions of the breath (prāṇāyāmas).
Vāyu said:
But that Brāhmaṇa initiated into yoga who should cause a division among the rainy-season [ascetics], becomes pure-souled through the Taptakṛcchra penance and is born again free from passion. 9.69.
Wherever physical danger is perceived in some calamity—whether in a famine, the collapse of a kingdom, or even during the rains—one should abandon that place. (9.70)
One should quickly abandon a country that is harassed by thieves, afflicted by famine and disease, or overrun by another [hostile] army, even during the rainy season. (9.71)
Atri says:
But if one should abandon shelter during the rainy season without any obstacle,
one should indeed recite three thousand [times] and likewise perform a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma).
If one should move to another place during the rainy season without obstacle,
one should indeed recite three thousand [mantras] and perform three hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma).
If one should pass through many villages suitable for habitation during the rainy season, one must perform a *kṛcchra* penance for each; thereby, one is liberated from that sin.
With the four mantras beginning with "samudrajyeṣṭhā," he sprinkles water upon his head;
with the mantra "saṃ naḥ śiśīhi," he scatters water in the four directions.
One should perform the consecration of the razor for the sick and the afflicted;
for an ascetic, acts such as shaving are recommended up until the fifth stage.
On the twelfth day of the month of Kārttika, or likewise on the full moon day,
having performed the ritual shaving, he should cast the remaining earth into the water while reciting the mantra "urv antarikṣa."

Then, when the next day has dawned on the thirteenth, or perhaps on the first day of the lunar fortnight, he should rise and set out for his desired region while reciting the verse beginning with "Three steps. (9.78)
Having recited these verses— "The earth for the three," "The three ṛcs," and "Those paths which are yours"— he should depart either toward the east or toward the north.
Gautama says: One should not stay in a village for a second night except during the rainy season. (GDh 3.21)

When the season has passed, he should not stay in a village for a second night; the meaning is that he should not stay in a single village for two days. Maskarī maintains that because of the mention of "village," there is no fault in staying in the forest. Although the phrase "not a second night outside the season" does not specify which season is meant, nevertheless, the rainy season (*vārṣika*) should be understood [as the one intended]. Śaṅkha states: "Beyond the two months of the rainy season, staying in one place is not prescribed. Furthermore, those two months of Śrāvaṇa and Bhādrapada are for one who is incapable [of wandering]; Devala says they constitute four months.
One should not dwell in one place for long, except during the rainy season. The four months beginning with Śrāvaṇa constitute the rainy season;
thus says Viśvarūpa. (9.82)
Satyakāma and Jābāla:

When the rainy season has arrived, whether in a village, a town, or a city, the mendicant should remain in that very place; he should not stay in that spot for even a moment beyond that time. If he stays out of ignorance, he should perform the Prājāpatya penance.
Furthermore, Atri says:
Having recited these verses, one may depart, either toward the east or toward the north;
one should dwell for a single night in a village, or remain seated in one place for a long time.
Like one who is blind, like one who is dull-witted, and like one who is deaf, insane, or mute. || 9.84 ||

One who proclaims one's name, lineage, conduct, country, clan, learning, family, age, behavior, vows, and character does not achieve success at all. By such proclamation, there is a loss of merit for the ascetic; of this there is no doubt. (9.85)

The wise man, relying on the hidden Dharma and remaining in a life of unrecognized conduct, should practice the Dharma without corrupting it, appearing as one who is deluded though he is actually undeluded. 9.86
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Goal and the State," in the Yatidharmasamuccaya. 9.87.
The tenth book: The Procedure for Expiation.
Now, the expiations are being stated. Regarding this, Vāyu says:
Expiatory rites are to be performed for those acts committed unintentionally;
others, however, maintain that they are also to be performed for those committed intentionally. 10.1.
But evil should be known to be threefold, arising from speech, mind, and body;
it persists day and night, by which this person is consumed. (10.2)
"Neither karmas nor even life-force remain," so says the supreme revelation;
therefore, once the life-force has been stabilized, one should immediately apply the rite of atonement.
