Through habituation, one delights in evil and increases it day by day; when this occurs through habituation or intentional thought, one should purify oneself with penance. One should purify oneself as long as the mind remains unsettled. (10.4)
If a yogi should commit some transgression through negligence, he should practice yoga alone; he should not perform any other expiation. (10.5)
When combined with breath control, withdrawal of the senses, meditation, and yoga, the defect born of negligence is destroyed—not by other vows that have been performed. (10.6)

It has been stated that when performed intentionally through repeated practice, it is the observance of a vow (*vrata*); when done through negligence, it is called *yoga*. Regarding this, Hārīta says:
"For one who delights in the practice of *yoga* in this world, even great sins are destroyed. (10.7) [cf.
8.56]. Atri says:
If an ascetic is unable to perform the Cāndrāyaṇa, the Parāka, the Kṛcchra, or the Sāntapana and other such penances, he should practice breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Whatever sin of men is destroyed by fasting for a single day, that same sin is certainly destroyed by the recitation of the *trikasahasra* three thousand times. (10.9)
Whatever sin a twice-born man may destroy by reciting [the mantra] three thousand times,
that entire sin is destroyed by a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) alone.
Whatever sin is destroyed by twice-born men through a thousand breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), that is completely destroyed in a mere moment by meditating on Hara. 10.11.
There is no means of purification for a mendicant other than breath control, recitation, and meditation;
therefore, an ascetic should practice those very things for the sake of his own purity. 10.12
A monk who performs a hundred breath-restraints day after day is liberated from these three—even if he has killed his father, mother, or teacher. (10.13)
Jamadagni said:
By means of constant practice of breath-control, meditations, and recitations, all sins are consumed just as fuel is by fire. (10.14)
Vyāsa says: In all minor offenses and even in the great sins,
one is purified by meditating on Brahman for a single quarter of the night.
Gālava said: "Beholding the Lord is the expiation for all [sins]. 10.16.
There may be yoga for one who is vigilant, for yoga is indeed considered supreme. For there exists nothing more beneficial for men than yoga. (10.17)
It is the most sacred of the sacred and the purifier of all purifiers;
therefore, the wise praise yoga as that which is appropriate for the patient one. 10.18
Jamadagni said:
"Alternatively, whatever the guru may say should be carried out without hesitation;
whether in punishment or in favor, the guru is the authority in all matters. (10.19)

Vāyu said: "But whoever should transgress [the rules] through actions of speech, mind, or body, all the members of the assembly, having reached a decision, should carry out whatever they declare. (10.20)
Atri says:
For a mendicant who has committed a minor offense (upapātaka), light food, the recitation of mantras (japa), silence, and bathing at the three times of day are specifically prescribed. 10.21.
Having performed a thousand suppressions of the breath (prāṇāyāma), one should recite the Praṇava ten thousand times;
thereafter, according to the rule, twenty-five sets of three thousand [recitations].
Having performed this vow in the forest, the mendicant (bhikṣu) becomes purified.
Now, the expiation for the omission of the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) is stated. Regarding this, Devala says:

"If the omission of the twilight devotions occurs through negligence on the part of one who is not ill, he is purified by the recitation of three thousand [Gāyatrī mantras]; there is no doubt in this matter. (10.23)
Garga says:
A mendicant who lets the twilight devotions pass is liable to perform penance;
he should recite the [sacred syllables] three thousand times and likewise perform one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma). 10.24.
Gālava said:
One should perform the ritual attendance while the sun is half-risen; however, having allowed the time to pass, one should indeed maintain twelve breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).
Now follows the expiation for wandering for alms. On this point, Devala says:

Having performed the *upasthāna* (worship), one should not remain for a long time. Having remained for a long time, one should perform sixteen *prāṇāyāmas*. Having performed the *upasthāna*, one should not fail to offer salutations to the deities, elders, and others; if one fails to do so out of ignorance, one should maintain sixteen *prāṇāyāmas*. Having performed the *upasthāna*, one should not neglect the collection of alms (*bhikṣā*); if one neglects it, one should perform thirty *prāṇāyāmas*. Having performed the *upasthāna*, one should not practice eating only a single meal (*ekabhikṣā*); if one should so practice, one must perform a *prājāpatya* penance. (10.26)
Bharadvāja:

He should avoid conversation and the like. If he does so out of ignorance, he should perform three *prāṇāyāmas*. Holding the bowl with the left hand, he should never move the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*) to the right. If he moves it out of ignorance, he should perform three *prāṇāyāmas*. Holding the bowl with the left hand, he should not let it touch the triple staff when it is on the right. Whenever he makes contact, he should perform six *prāṇāyāmas*. Having approached for the sake of alms, he should enter but not sit down. If he sits down anywhere, he should maintain twelve *prāṇāyāmas*. If a mendicant, through negligence, accepts alms offered by a *śūdra* or an *udakyā*, he should maintain sixteen *prāṇāyāmas*. Having placed the triple staff outside, he should neither beg nor accept alms. If he should accept them, he should maintain sixteen *prāṇāyāmas*. Having released the triple staff from his hand, he should neither beg nor accept alms. If he does so out of ignorance, he should perform one hundred *prāṇāyāmas*. (10.27)
Devala and Kāśyapa [declare that one should avoid] dogs, donkeys, camels, rats, cats, hyenas, monkeys, and pigs; as well as indigo, wood from a funeral pyre, human bone, and village cocks.
A jackal, an ungrateful person, a Śūdra who drinks liquor, one who has discarded his sacred thread, a naked man, and a twice-born who follows heretical paths—[these should not be looked upon]. 10.29.
One who betrays trust, one who reviles the gods and Brahmins, one who sets fire to houses, and likewise one who sells the Dharma; || 10.30 ||
Having touched a heap of impurities, a eunuch, or a *devalaka*,
an ascetic should place his bowl in a clean spot and go to a pure body of water.
Having performed purification according to the rule, the ascetic should wash with earth and water that part of the body which has been defiled, using twelve applications of earth.
Having purified all that with water, one should likewise perform the ritual bath;
having sipped water and become pure after eating, one should perform six breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).
Having purified himself repeatedly with the three verses beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā," and having performed the Aghamarṣaṇa rite in the water, he should perform the bath once again.
One should take up the alms-bowl after sprinkling it with water using the three [fingers], and likewise immerse it in water along with the hand for the sake of purification. (10.35)
Thus, when these [impurities] have come into contact with them, the alms of a monk become pure; if there is contact with something else in the bowl, then it becomes pure, and not otherwise. (10.36)
If there is contact with others— such as dogs, crows, or members of the lowest castes— in the vessel while one is eating,
then one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
Jamadagni says:

Upon touching a dog, a crow, a boar, a prostitute, a lecher, a donkey, or a camel, an ascetic who has been submerged in water while begging for alms may become pure by reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn. (10.38)
Vṛddha-Jābāli says:
A renunciant who, while wandering for alms, should touch a dog or an impurity, must, after taking his alms and bathing, perform six breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). 10.39.
One should make the alms pure with the Gāyatrī and the Praṇava;
then, having been sprinkled with the Vāruṇa mantra, it becomes ritually clean.
Garga says: If the bowl has fallen, one should take the alms and perform thirty breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). 10.41.
Gālava said: One should avoid that house where fish-meat is cooked; having entered there, one should perform twelve breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). || 10.42 ||
Devala says:
Whether one should collect alms outside the village or within the village,
if one accepts them in both places, one must perform the Sāntapana vow.
Jamadagni:
If alms are not obtained when one has entered a village for the purpose of begging, one should beg in a second village and then perform the Taptakṛcchra penance. (10.44)
If alms fall into the bowl, one should consume only a single portion;
for the sake of his own purification, the ascetic should perform one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma). 10.45.
While eating alms-food collected from many houses (mādhūkarī), one should avoid even consecrated food offerings (naivedya);
one is purified by the Prājāpatya penance—of this there is no doubt. (10.46)
If one eats honey-gathered alms-food after the offering has been dismissed, yet does not eat any other food thereafter, he becomes pure in just three nights. (10.47)
Gālava said: Having eaten another's food and alms-food on the same day, one should mutter the Gāyatrī ten thousand times. 10.48.
Devala said: If one has placed the offering in a vessel but does not apply the mantra, the ascetic becomes free from passion (viraja) by reciting [the mantra] three thousand times. || 10.49 ||
Having touched a woman in her courses, a corpse, a Caṇḍāla, a thief, one who is naked, a skull-bearer, an outcast, or a slanderer, a mendicant should discard the alms-food.
Having eaten the food of an outcast even once, an ascetic should perform an expiation;
by performing three Vajra-kṛcchra penances, he is purified—of this there is no doubt.
One should cook a handful of barley with cow urine;
on the new moon day, one should eat this. This is the great Vajra-kṛcchra penance.
One who has eaten the food of an outcaste should perform the Prājāpatya penance;
having eaten it once unintentionally, one is purified by the Prājāpatya. 10.53.
One should perform a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), or practice the quarter-penance (pādakṛcchra);
or else, having boiled śaṅkhapuṣpa for three nights, one should drink it with plenty of milk.
Hārīta says: When a cause for suspicion has arisen regarding the mixing of edible foods and drinks, I shall declare the purification of food; listen to me as I speak it. 10.55.
Having prepared it without alkaline salt, one should drink *brahmasuvarcalā*;
or for three nights, one should cause [the patient] to drink *śaṅkhapuṣpī* with milk.
Having boiled the leaves of the *pālāśa* and *bilva*, as well as *kuśa* grass, lotuses, and *udumbara* fruits, one should drink the water; thus one becomes purified in three nights.
Or again, by drinking the five products of a tawny cow according to the prescribed rite, one attains purification from the consumption of forbidden food. 10.58
Atri says:
Food from a single person, honey, meat, food defiled by excrement and the like, food not offered as *hantakāra*, and foods containing visible salt—[these should be avoided]. (10.59)
Having eaten any one of these, an ascetic should perform the Prājāpatya penance;
having eaten food with honey or meat, he should perform the Parāka penance. Furthermore, he should recite the *trikam* a hundred thousand times, provided that the recitation is performed for a year.
He who consumes water, the limbs of living beings, honey, or meat when in distress,
shall indeed recite the Trika-sahasra three thousand times and likewise perform one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).
Vṛddha-Jābāli says:
Having given what was not given out of compassion, or having accepted such a gift, one should perform the great Saumya-kṛcchra or even the Prājāpatya penance. (10.62)
A monk who eats the food of a single person out of courtesy or even out of greed shall be purified by the Prājāpatya penance, the Kṛcchra penance, and one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma). 10.63
Devala says: If one eats honey or meat that has been produced from a wound by worms,
one should observe three days of fasting and perform one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma).

Gālava says: Having eaten meat or honey, one should perform a *parāka* penance; having consumed betel-leaf, one should fast for a day and night; if done intentionally, one should perform a *prājāpatya* penance. (10.65)
Jamadagni says: Food from a single house, honey, meat, a *śrāddha* meal on the ninth day, food from a woman in childbirth,
and likewise salt that is not processed (natural salt)— these are not to be eaten by ascetics (*yatis*).
For the transgression of each one of these, purification is achieved through the Prājāpatya penance. || 10.66 ||
Austerity: Having eaten food defiled by the hair, insects, bones, or clothing of a rat, a cat, or a crow, an ascetic is purified by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). (10.67)
Bharadvāja says: "Whatever [is found] in the midst of food, such as fine hair, insects, or what has been struck by flies, and so forth. (10.68)
Devala says:
If one somehow happens to eat while there is a gathering of those who eat raw flesh (kravyāda),
one should first abandon the meal and afterwards perform a ritual bath.
One should recite [the mantra] three thousand times and perform one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma).
Jamadagni said:
"If the anus of a Brahmin while eating should ever discharge [feces], how can there be purification for him, given his state of being rendered impure by the remains of food? (10.70)
Having first performed purification, one should afterwards touch water;
having fasted for a day and night and bathed, one becomes pure by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If a monk should discard whatever remains of his alms-food, he must perform three breath-restraints for every morsel he eats. (10.72)
But having entered a village crowded with people during the rainy season when it is muddy,
one should apply three applications of clay to the shanks and seven to the feet.
Devala says:
If water from the hair or the beard falls into the alms-bowl, the ascetic should discard that alms-food; having discarded the bowl as well, he should fast.

After purging, vomiting, voiding feces or urine, or after the emission of semen, and after eating food given by a single person, one should bathe; then, having returned from begging alms, one should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) for each of those acts.
Having smelled the odor of liquor, as well as that of urine or feces, or the stench of a carnivorous creature, one must perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) for each. (10.76)
Upon suddenly seeing vomit, urine, or feces,
an ascetic shall become pure by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma) and should perform twice that amount of penance.
Gālava says: Having smelled the stench of putrid feces, urine, raw meat, or liquor, one should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) for each. 10.78.
One should always practice the observances (niyamas), but one should guard the restraints (yamas) even more than them;
except in times of distress, when one is incapable, or during the consumption of water, medicine, or food. (10.79)

In the case of sacrificial offerings, when following the wishes of a Brahmin, when eating flowers, roots, and fruits, with curds, milk, at the command of a guru, or when using cinnamon leaves for cleaning the teeth,
there is no transgression of the rules for Brahmins, provided they have received permission.
By the sound of their proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), the removal of sin is accomplished;
by performing that for those who have committed sins unintentionally, one is liberated from them. (10.81)
Baudhāyana says:

Now, regarding that which the teachers declare to be the Upaniṣad, they cite this: standing, silence, the postures, the ritual rinsing after the *savana* sacrifices, being engaged in the vows at the fourth, sixth, and eighth periods of the day, and the practice of subsisting on grains, oil-cakes, barley-gruel, curds, and milk. In this regard, one who observes silence should converse with the elders learned in the three Vedas, with teachers, with sages, or with others belonging to the various stages of life (*āśrama*) who are well-versed in scripture, joining tooth to tooth while facing inwardly, speaking only as much as is necessary; thus it is understood that there is no transgression. One should employ either standing, silence, or the *vīrāsana* posture, but one should not combine all three together. Wherever [the teacher] goes, one should follow him for however long is required; it is understood that in times of distress, there is no transgression. [This applies to one] who is engaged in standing, silence, the *vīrāsana*, the ritual rinsing, and the vows at the fourth, sixth, and eighth periods of the day. (10.82)
These eight do not destroy a vow: water, roots, ghee, milk, sacrificial oblation, the word of a Brahmin who desires one's welfare, the command of a guru, and medicine. (BDh 2.18.15–19) — Devala.
If someone, through negligence, should forget the conduct regarding sleep, he should recite it three thousand times; he is purified, of this there is no doubt. (10.84)
Now, the expiation for offenses committed at night is stated. Regarding this, Vṛddha-Jābāli says:
"If an ascetic eats at night when the time of twilight has arrived, [he must perform] the worship, the recitation, breath-control, and likewise the offering. (10.85)
All those [acts] of his become fruitless; an expiation is prescribed:
a fast for one night and sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma). 10.86.
Jamadagni said:
Ten breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) are prescribed for taking food at night;
likewise, one should perform them when taking water or earth during the night. (10.87)
If what has been taken is lost, one is not tainted by the law [of theft] when taking once from flowing rivers, from streams, and from temples of the gods. 10.88.
But having bathed at the time of twilight during the night, one should perform twelve breath-restraints;
with his self purified by these prāṇāyāmas, the ascetic becomes free from passion.

Śaunaka says: One should not remember previous sexual enjoyments. If one remembers them through negligence, one should sip water (ācamana), perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma), and sip water again. Upon seeing a woman through negligence, one should perform breath-restraints. Having engaged in sexual intercourse during sleep, one should mutter [the mantra] three thousand times and hold twelve breath-restraints. In the case of emission during sleep following intercourse, one should hold twelve [breath-restraints]. Having urinated twice, one should sip water again. || 10.90 ||
Kapila says: Having bathed after sexual intercourse in a dream, one should recite the mantra three thousand times; in the case of scratching or the flow of blood, there shall be a fast. 10.91.

Gālava says: One who intentionally emits semen should perform three *parāka* penances. If it occurs unintentionally during sleep while engaging with a woman, one should perform twelve *prāṇāyāmas*. If there is emission due to negligence while sleeping, one should perform twelve *prāṇāyāmas*. Upon seeing the secret organ exposed through negligence, one should perform three *prāṇāyāmas* for each instance. If this is seen in a dream, one should recite the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn. Having emitted semen while in a state of impurity, one should always perform sixteen *prāṇāyāmas*. Having intentionally caused the emission of semen, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance. (10.92)
Jābāli says: When one should perform the release of a white bull, whether out of desire or even through habit,
one should perform a hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) accompanied by three *parāka* penances.
If one should emit semen during the day through negligence, he must perform an expiation;
by fasting for three nights, he should practice one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).
If, due to weakness of the senses, one's seed is emitted upon seeing a woman through negligence,
sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) must be performed by him.
If a monk should intentionally discharge semen anywhere, he must perform three *prājāpatya* penances and one hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*). (10.96)
Vṛddhaparāśara said:
"O Vāsudeva, as long as the sun has not yet risen while you sleep,
I shall dwell here for the sake of the welfare of all beings."
The seven seers are stationed within the body;
they guard it constantly with vigilance. Seven waters go to the world of the sleeper there.
"The two gods who are wakeful, sleepless, and providers of the sacrificial feast" (VS 34.55).

One should lie down with these two mantras. If one does not do so, having performed six breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), one should lie down again with the two mantras. At the time of rising, one should rise with the mantra "Arise" (VS 34.56). If one does not do so, having performed three breath-restraints, one should rise again. || 10.99 ||
Now, regarding penances for the transgression of observances (*niyama*): concerning this, Vāyu says:
"Whatever vows belong to the mendicants (*bhikṣu*), as well as their secondary vows (*upavrata*), a penance is prescribed for the transgression of each one of them. (10.100)
But having approached a woman out of lust, an ascetic must perform penance;
he should carry out a Kṛcchra penance for one year, combined with breath-control exercises (prāṇāyāma).
Then, having experienced world-weariness and being concentrated in difficult meditation,
he should again attain detachment and wander for alms without sloth.

Kapila says: In the case of a single instance of sexual intercourse, there shall be fasting for twelve nights and the recitation (*japa*) of the *trikalakṣa* mantra. In the case of repetition, one shall fast for three nights and perform the recitation for a year. Having once approached a woman of the lowest caste (*antyajā*), one shall subsist on *bilva* and other fruits that have fallen of their own accord in the forest, having washed them; while meditating upon Brahman, he becomes pure at the time of death. 10.103.
Jābāli says:
Having approached a woman out of lust, an ascetic must perform penance;
he should practice the Sāntapana rite for one year, conjoined with breath-control (prāṇāyāma).
Gālava said: "Having once gone to Sādhāraṇī, one should perform the penance for the murder of a Brahmin. (10.105)
Atri:
For the sake of purification from the fault arising from a mortal sin (mahāpātaka), an ascetic (yati) should practice;
the yogi should likewise recite [the mantra] three hundred thousand times and perform ten thousand breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma).
Then the ascetic should recite the Praṇavas one hundred thousand times.
One is purified from a single instance of sexual intercourse with a woman through delusion by this prescribed rite;
likewise, in the case of repeated practice out of desire, one is purified by penance.
It is the wind. For that which is called "wealth" consists of these vital breaths (*prāṇa*) moving outside [the body].
He who takes away another's wealth takes away his very life-breaths. (10.108)

Having acted thus, that evil-minded ascetic, who has violated the conduct and stage of life, shall then fall into despondency and perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow for one year according to the procedure seen in the scriptures; so says the Śruti.
Then, at the end of a year, having once again diminished his defilements and having attained further world-weariness, the mendicant should once more practice begging for alms.
Gālava says: Having intentionally accepted wealth, cattle, land, sesamum, and so forth, one should perform penance as if one had fallen [from caste]. 10.111.
Jamadagni said:
Having abandoned wealth that has been obtained, one should observe three fasts;
by reciting the Gāyatrī ten thousand times, one is liberated from all sins. 10.112.
He himself said:
"If a wandering ascetic possesses land, cattle, or gold, seeing such a defilement, he should enter the water with his clothes on. (10.113)
Vāyu says:
One who speaks falsely while observing a fast should perform one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas).
A seeker of dharma, a renunciant, must not engage in untruthful speech. 10.114.

Gālava says: Having spoken a falsehood, one should fast for three nights. Having uttered a falsehood connected with dharma, one should fast for a day and a night and perform one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). || 10.115 ||
Jamadagni:
In the case of injury to speech, mind, or body toward mobile or immobile beings, one should purify oneself by means of whatever [act] caused the obstruction. 10.116.
When there is an application of speech, there is the punishment of speech; but the punishment of life pertains to the mind.
The punishment of action belongs to the body; through wisdom, one should prescribe detachment.
The rod of speech indeed destroys knowledge; the rod of the mind destroys the supreme goal;
but the rod of action, if unguarded, destroys the three worlds. (10.118)
The staff of speech consists in observing silence; the staff of action is fasting;
but the staff of the mind is the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma). 10.119.
When faults have arisen, there shall be expiation by this means;
however, if a very long time has passed, one should perform double the vow.
Gālava says: Having killed four-footed wild animals, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow;
for killing crabs, spotted deer, and the like, one should fast for ten nights.
But if a monk should intentionally kill domestic animals or wild beasts, he should perform the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra penance or the Cāndrāyaṇa. || 10.122 ||
Jamadagni says:
In the case of a chameleon, a lizard, a frog, a house-lizard,
or creatures such as ospreys, there shall be a ten-day period of eating only half a meal.

One should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow for killing a cat, a mouse, a snake, large fish, birds, or creatures such as mongooses; for a tiny ant, one should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) each time.
For a monk who kills a creature possessing subtle bones, an expiation is prescribed:
having performed thirty breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), he shall eat only half his usual portion for one day. (10.125)
Gālava said: Having performed the cutting of leaves, roots, sprouts, and flowers, one should maintain thirty breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). || 10.126 ||
Dattātreya says:
Having seen a Brahmin by mistake either naked or uninitiated,
one becomes pure by bathing with twelve applications of clay and changing one's clothes.
Hārīta says:
"He who feeds at a Śrāddha a twice-born man who is either naked or uninitiated offers semen, urine, and excrement to the ancestors. (10.128)
If one who has adopted the single-staff (ekadaṇḍa) order out of impulse or greed later falls into despondency, the wise man should take up the triple-staff (tridaṇḍa). 10.129.
Restrained in conduct, he shall perform the Prājāpatya penance for a period measured by months, bathing at the three sessions of the day and constantly reciting the Gāyatrī. || 10.130 ||
If, however, the one who subsists on air wishes to perform it quickly, he should remain in the water during the night; having emerged at dawn, he shall obtain the fruit of the Prājāpatya penance.
Having performed the recitation of the Gāyatrī eight thousand times when the sun has risen,
one is liberated from all sins, provided one is not a killer of an embryo.
When a confluence of all manner of sins has occurred,
the recitation of the Gāyatrī ten thousand times is the supreme purification.
One should recite the Gāyatrī together with the Vyahṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras three times while restraining the breath; that is called Prāṇāyāma.
One who is composed should perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) according to the rule;
the sin committed during a day and night perishes at that very moment. 10.135.
Whatever a twice-born man has done during the day by deed, thought, or word,
he becomes pure by sitting for the evening twilight prayer and performing breath control (prāṇāyāma).
He who constantly recites the Gāyatrī, which has a maximum of one thousand syllables, a middle of a hundred, and a minimum of ten, is not defiled by sin.
Sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas), accompanied by the vyāhṛtis and the syllable Om, performed day after day, purify even the slayer of an embryo within a month. (10.138)
For misfortunes, difficulties, and likewise for great sins,
the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances are the destroyers of all evil.
Saṃvarta said:
"You ought to hear the expiation for those who have fallen away from renunciation;
for if some evil-minded person, having renounced, should resort to a return to worldly life... (10.140)
He should perform the *kṛcchra* penance without weariness for six months continuously; this is the observed sequence of rules for expiation in the event of the death of an ascetic. 10.141.

He himself says: "For one who has committed the murder of a Brahmin or the killing of a guru, even if he is endowed with the four Vedas, one should prescribe the penance prescribed for the path of the Setubandha. (10.142)
On the path to Setubandha, he should beg alms from members of all four castes,
proclaiming his own deeds, while remaining without an umbrella or sandals.
"I am indeed a man of evil deeds, a perpetrator of great sins;
as a slayer of a Brahmin seeking alms, I stand at the doors of houses. (10.144)
Wandering through cow-pens, cattle-sheds, villages, and cities,
and visiting sacred fords (tīrthas), he went to the holy ocean.
Then one should behold the Setubandha, the bridge to Laṅkā across the great ocean,
ten yojanas wide and a hundred yojanas long.
Then, having seen the construction of the bridge built by Nala’s accumulation of effort at the command of Rāghava, and having seen the king, the lord of the earth,
performing the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha), one becomes instantly pure. (10.147)
Devala says: Having touched a woman in her courses, a prostitute, a woman who drinks liquor,
or the wood used for a corpse or its implements, one should bathe and recite the two [mantras] twice.
He himself says: "If the birth of a louse occurs on the body, an expiation is prescribed:
having performed one fast, one should practice six breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). (10.149)
Garga says:

Monks should not accept [alms] from one another. If, through negligence, they do accept them, they should mutter the verse "mitrasya carṣaṇīdhṛtaḥ" and perform three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma). 10.150.
Gālava says:
In the case of scratching [an animal] and the consequent flow of blood, there shall be a fast for one day and night. (10.151)
Jamadagni said: One should not think even in one's mind of mother, father, or son;
if there should be affection for them, however, one must perform sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). 10.152.
Satyakāma and Jābāla:

If one performs or causes to be performed a single *vaṣaṭkāra*, *svāhā*, *svadhā*, or *vaṣaṭkāra* [inappropriately], all of that becomes fruitless. An expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for that is prescribed: one who has employed [the rite] himself, having performed three *prājāpatya* penances, should hold twelve breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*). 10.153.
Satyakāma has declared the expiation for all those [transgressions] not specifically mentioned:
having committed a violation of what is prescribed, one should perform twelve breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). (10.154)

For one who is incapable, heavy or light penances should be prescribed in consideration of place, time, and other such factors. Some maintain that there is an option (vikalpa) due to the difference in the opinions of the sages. Likewise, others say that other duties as well as the penance for them should be applied from among the very duties of a householder.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "The Rules for Expiation," in the *Yatidharmasamuccaya*. 10.157.
The eleventh section:
the procedure for the final rites of ascetics (*yatīnāṃ saṃskāravidhiḥ*).
Now, the procedure for the final rites of ascetics is stated. Regarding this, Bodhāyana says:
I shall describe in its entirety the ritual for the funeral rites of ascetics (yatins).
Having bathed and purified his soul, a householder should perform the consecration of the ascetic. 11.1
Having placed the body upon a litter, adorned with perfumes and garlands,
and accompanied by the proclamation of cries of victory and the sound of kettledrums,
one should go toward the east or the north and take refuge in a pure place. (11.2)

On the bank of a river, at an *aśvattha* tree, in a temple, in a cow-pen, or beneath a sacred fig tree (*brahmavṛkṣa*), one should dig a sacrificial altar (*devayajana*) the size of a staff using the *vyāhṛtis*. Having sprinkled it with the seven *vyāhṛtis*, bathed [the image] with the *Puruṣasūkta*, and adorned it with perfumes and other offerings, one places it down with the mantra "O Viṣṇu, protect! One places the staff in the right hand with the mantra "Viṣṇu strode across this. With the verse "The swan dwelling in purity," one should mutter over the region of the heart. One should mutter the *Puruṣasūkta* between the eyebrows. With "Brahman was born," one should mutter over the region of the head. With "Earth has entered earth," one should pierce the crown of the head. There is a touching with the *Gāyatrī*. One should fill the sacrificial altar with the *praṇava*. The purification of the site is performed repeatedly with the *Gāyatrī*. If the harassment of jackals, crows, and the like should cause a defect, there will be drought in that region for the performer; therefore, one should fill it again and again. One should cover it with that. There is no impurity, nor water-libations. For an ascetic (*yati*), from carrying, digging, or touching, there is immediately the ritual bath of the conclusion (*avabhṛthasnāna*). At every step, a person obtains the fruit of a horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).
Thus said the Blessed One Bodhāyana. 11.3.
When one devoted to Brahman has died, his son, a disciple, or a householder should dig [the grave];
likewise, he must perform for him the Nārāyaṇabali with that very same [rite]. || 11.4 ||
There is no fire-rite, no water-offering, no Śrāddha, nor even the satiation of Brāhmaṇas;
everything dedicated to Nārāyaṇa should be performed according to the ritual for a single ancestor (Ekoddiṣṭa).
Sages know that this same procedure applies even when a person dies while traveling;
however, when the eleventh day has arrived, the pārvaṇa rite is prescribed.
One should never perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite for them;
by the mere taking up of the triple staff (*tridaṇḍa*), they do not enter the state of a *preta* at all. (11.7)
For this alone is sufficient for a monk who is devoted to solitude:
nothing is done by him, and he does nothing for anyone. (11.8)
Now another method is seen: as before, with the *vyāhṛti* mantras, having placed him [the fire] with those very same mantras, and having likewise prepared the pit with those same mantras. (11.9)
And having sprinkled that pit again with the seven *vyāhṛtis*,
[he should do so] with the mantra beginning with "The god Savitṛ for you" (*devo vaḥ savitā*) and "The flour has fallen" (*piṣṭapraskanda*).
Having given [the water] and set aside the carrying-net, he should set down the staff at his side;
with the words "Be my friend," and so forth, he should place the carrying-net upon his heart.
Having placed the water-purifier in his mouth with the mantra "yena devāḥ pavitreṇa," and having placed the *kuṇḍikā* in his right hand with the mantra "tvaṃ no agne," [he should proceed].
Having recited the mantra, "The earth has entered the earth," he likewise placed the vessel in his belly;
then, having been attended by the Hotṛ priests, he sprinkled it with the seven Vyāhṛtis.
One should fill the pit with the mantra; thus fire is kindled by fire, so that neither jackals nor dogs may lift it up again. (11.14)
A Brahmin should place the bodies of those monks who maintained the sacred fires either in a pit or in the earth;
for those who were without fires but had attained perfection, he should cremate their corpses.
The *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, water offerings, the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*), the period of impurity, and the funeral rites for the deceased—
these should be performed according to the prescribed rules during the year [of mourning] until the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is completed.
One should not perform any rite other than the *pārvaṇa* for a mendicant who has become one with Brahman.
Atri says:
A pure-souled householder who has a son should perform the funeral rites for an ascetic;
having placed the body, adorned with perfumes and garlands, upon a carrying-pole (śikya). || 11.17 ||
Having kindled a fire of chaff here for the sake of the funeral rites of the ascetic, one should carry him out amidst shouts of "Victory! and the sounding of kettledrums;
then, having gone toward the east or the north, one should perform the ceremony in a pure location.
Having dug the ground to the length of a staff using the *vyāhṛtis*,
and having sprinkled it with the seven *vyāhṛtis*, there a layer of wood should be prepared.
Then, having washed his body with sacrificial wood or other blameless materials according to his ability, he, pure in mind, [should recite] the Sāvitrī.

Having placed that [oblation] upon the wooden altar with the words "O Viṣṇu, protect the offering," he should place the purifier (pavitra) at the mouth [of the fire] with this very mantra: "The Purifier. (11.21)
With the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ," he should place the triple staff in his right hand;
with the mantra "yad asya" ending in "svāhā," he should place the sling in his left hand.
One skilled in the ritual procedure should place the vessel in Sāvitrī’s belly and the water-pot in her secret place, reciting: "The earth has entered the earth. (11.23)
Then, having been cast into a pit or upon wood, the body—equipped with all the ritual implements—is consecrated by the officiating priests, and the performer stands by it;
he should burn the body with chaff-fire until it has been reduced to ashes. (11.24)
Moreover, the wise who are skilled in the meaning of the Vedas cite this:

"The rites beginning with the impregnation ceremony and ending with those at the cremation ground are prescribed for the Brāhmaṇa; therefore, the householder performs the purificatory rite for the ascetic as well, accompanied by mantras. (11.25)
When an ascetic has deposited the sacred fires within himself and has uttered the final injunction,
his son, according to the prescribed rule, shall deposit the fires [within him] and cremate him with fire.

Even by means of the Hotṛ-ritual, or with the Gāyatrī, or with the Praṇava; when the father, established in action and having renounced the world, has passed away, his cremation must be performed by his sons, as well as the Śrāddha, the offering of rice-balls, and the water-libations.
From the very beginning, through his resolve, he should become a celibate ascetic;
for him, everything that must be done by a householder should be performed in the presence of Hari.
By merely carrying, burning, touching, or bathing with ascetics, a person becomes pure;
at every step, he obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice.
Śaunaka said:
For one who has desisted from all attachments and is devoted to the yoga of meditation,
neither cremation nor the offering of funeral cakes and water should be performed.
One should place the body of the meditating mendicant with the *praṇava* alone;
one should perform the sprinkling and the digging, indeed everything, with that very same [syllable].
"By merely bathing after carrying or even touching ascetics, one becomes pure;
all [those involved] shall individually obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice. || 11.32 ||
The Blessed Vṛddhayājñavalkya has said this very same thing. 11.33.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Consecration of Ascetics," in the *Yatidharmasamuccaya* composed by Yādavaprakāśa. 11.34.
